articles.title: Why Afghanistan’s Neighbors Have Not Backed Pakistan’s Strikes on the Taliban
articles.full_text:
China, Uzbekistan, and Tajikistan are less exposed to the impact of cross-border terrorism – and less willing to risk smooth relations with Kabul over the issue.
The eighth meeting of the Moscow Format consultations on Afghanistan in Moscow, Russia, Oct. 5, 2026.
On October 5, Moscow hosted the eighth meeting of the special representatives and senior officials from regional countries for the Moscow Format to discuss political and economic relations with Afghanistan and counterterrorism and counter-narcotics cooperation. The Moscow Format includes Afghanistan, China, India, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Russia, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan.
But the meeting failed to adopt a joint statement because the Pakistani and Afghan delegates disagreed over the language on terrorism. The Taliban objected to the frequent mention of terrorism in reference to Afghanistan. 
Russia’s special envoy for Afghanistan, Zamir Kabulov, said the Afghan delegates accepted similar language last year. He believed that the changed relations between Pakistan and Afghanistan might have caused Kabul’s objection this time.
The meeting was held only a week after the most recent confrontation between Islamabad and Kabul. On September 18 and 26, Pakistan suffered deadly terrorist attacks in its northwestern province, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, that together killed about 44 people and injured about 138. Pakistan responded with airstrikes on different targets in Afghanistan that it believes were the training camps and hideouts of the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and its associated factions responsible for the cross-border attacks.
At the Moscow summit, Pakistan’s delegation said the Taliban were complicit in those attacks in Pakistan because the terrorist groups were operating on Afghan soil with impunity. The Taliban said Pakistan was using military aggression in violation of international law for an issue that could be resolved through political negotiations.
The Moscow Format meeting failed to bridge these differences enough to allow for a joint communique. What’s noteworthy is that other countries that share borders with Afghanistan – such as China, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan – did not use their diplomatic capital to reach an understanding on language that included everyone’s concerns.
Afghanistan’s neighbors have different levels of concern about militancy there. Their strategies, especially on counterterrorism, are a function of the nature of their border with Afghanistan, the extent of the threat from militant groups on Afghan soil, and the Taliban’s scale of cooperation regarding those groups. From their perspective, military force is not the most effective solution to address the issue.
China shares a border of only about 92 kilometers with Afghanistan, high in the Wakhan Corridor, marked by rough terrain and the nearly 5,000-meter high Wakhjir Pass. In terms of a terrorist presence in Afghanistan, Beijing considers the East Turkestan Islamic Movement (ETIM) its main concern and has pressed the Taliban to act against the group. The Taliban have reportedly relocated ETIM fighters away from the border, and they now have a dispersed presence. Therefore, the immediate cross-border threat to China is smaller, and any movement across the pass is easy to detect. 
Uzbekistan similarly shares a short border of 144 kilometers with Afghanistan, almost entirely along the Amu Darya. Regular cross-border movement is concentrated at the closely guarded Termez-Hairatan road and rail crossing. But the militant groups in Afghanistan that concern Tashkent have shown only a limited capacity for cross-border attacks. There was one incident in 2022 of rockets being fired toward Termez, which didn’t cause any casualties. Therefore, the immediate cross-border threat is relatively small and easier to contain.
Tajikistan’s case is closer to Pakistan’s in terms of the long border and threat. Dushanbe shares about 1,374 kilometers of border with Afghanistan, much of which runs along the Panj River and passes through remote and mountainous territory and is difficult to monitor consistently. The cross-border threat therefore needs more immediate attention. In November 2025, two cross-border attacks from Afghanistan’s Badakhshan province killed five Chinese workers in Tajikistan. 
As for Taliban cooperation, Kabul has offered these countries help in investigations and has arrested suspects after cross-border attacks. 
Pakistan’s case is of a different magnitude on all these counts. 
Pakistan shares 2,640 kilometers of border with Afghanistan, where Pashtun and Baloch communities live on both sides. Afghanistan has never recognized the border since Pakistan’s founding. Islamabad has been fencing it since 2017, but militants continue to cross it. A disputed frontier with kinship networks on both sides gives militants far more routes and tricks to enter Pakistan than Afghanistan’s northern borders offer. 
Pakistan also faces a much larger threat. Its key concerns are the TTP, the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA), and the Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISKP). Islamabad charges that all three groups have a presence in Afghanistan, especially the TTP. U.N. monitors estimate the TTP, which has carried out the most frequent and lethal attacks in Pakistan, has about 6,000 fighters in Afghanistan. 
By September 2026, Pakistan’s terrorism situation had worsened sharply, with 1,232 militant attacks in nine months, already 169 attacks above those recorded in all of 2025. Consistent attacks on this scale raise domestic pressure to take firm action.
Moreover, the Taliban have shown limited willingness to cooperate with Pakistan on the issue of militant groups. The Taliban leadership describes TTP members as Pakistani refugees and refuses to classify them as militants. U.N. monitors report that the group enjoys greater liberty and support from Taliban authorities. Kabul has offered to relocate the TTP fighters away from the Pakistani border, but that step cannot stop the militant movement through the long and porous border with Pakistan. 
Pakistan has, therefore, asked for written guarantees that the militants would not use Afghan soil as a base for attacks in Pakistan. The Taliban have rejected this demand, which was why the Istanbul talks failed in November 2025.
Pakistan has said its operations will continue until the Taliban take verifiable action against militant groups on Afghan soil. Yet none of Afghanistan’s neighbors has publicly supported Pakistan’s airstrikes. China, Russia, and Iran have called for restraint and offered to mediate, and Uzbekistan urged a diplomatic resolution. China hosted informal talks in Urumqi in April but those ended without agreement. 
Whether in Urumqi or more recently in Moscow, repeated efforts at finding common ground have fallen flat. While none of Afghanistan’s neighbors is comfortable with the idea of cross-border terrorism, none of them has sanctioned Pakistan’s military retaliation, either.

articles.title: The US and China Cannot Slow the AI Race, But They Can Make It Safer
articles.full_text:
The United States does not need to trust China, share frontier models with China, or slow its own AI development to have a national security interest in AI safety cooperation.
The most important shift in artificial intelligence (AI) is not that models are becoming more intelligent, but that they are becoming more capable of acting.
Much of the first wave of AI safety governance focused on misinformation, bias, deepfakes, privacy violations and harmful content. Those risks remain. But increasingly capable AI agents can plan, write and execute code, use tools, obtain credentials, and interact with external systems. Recent incidents in which OpenAI’s autonomous systems slipped past their constraints show that as agents gain tools and autonomy, the boundary between a model and the outside world becomes harder to enforce.
That makes AI safety a collective-action problem. The AI superpowers face a prisoner’s dilemma. If one laboratory slows while competitors continue, it may lose its edge. Disclosure creates a similar tension: reporting failures can make the wider ecosystem safer, but the discloser bears the costs and may expose vulnerabilities to attackers. Governments face the same strategic impasse as the firms. Washington fears that slowing its AI development will allow China to catch up; Beijing fears that doing so will leave it further behind. 
Yet cooperation can be narrow on AI safety. The United States does not need to trust China, share frontier models with China, or slow its own AI development to have a national security interest in such cooperation. It has an interest in ensuring that AI-enabled cyber incidents are contained before they cascade through third countries, shared software infrastructure and global supply chains. China has the same systemic interest.
This collective action has significant implications for middle-power countries. Helping others repair a vulnerability can be a form of systemic containment and a public good.
U.S. President Donald Trump has rejected calls to slow U.S. AI development, framing continued technological leadership as essential to winning the AI race. On September 29, he convened major technology companies at the White House, where six firms – OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, xAI and Nvidia – signed a voluntary accord built around four layers of oversight: internal capability assessments, internal audit teams, independent external auditors, and board-level review. His administration ordered federal agencies to replace the term “artificial intelligence” with “super intelligence,” presenting the technology as a source of economic and strategic leadership. 
Taken together, these moves point to a U.S. approach combining continued AI power with developer responsibility, voluntary industry controls, external scrutiny, and ex-post legal accountability.
China approaches the problem through a more centrally coordinated system. In May 2026, guidelines on AI agents, issued jointly by the Cyberspace Administration of China, the National Development and Reform Commission, and the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, made “safety and controllability” a baseline requirement for agent development and deployment. Governance is tiered, with tighter filing, testing and recall requirements for agents used in sensitive sectors. 
On September 14, China’s AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0 reiterated “safety and controllability” while updating its classification of AI risks and associated technical and governance measures.
Despite their institutional differences, the two approaches converge on one point: neither country wants safety policy to halt AI development, and both increasingly recognize that greater autonomy creates new problems of control.
AI systems rest on overlapping technological foundations. Chinese AI development has relied heavily on U.S. chips and, in some cases, U.S. cloud infrastructure. Export controls may weaken those hardware links, but the stronger case for joint risk management lies in the software and services AI systems share.
Standards, certificates, identity infrastructure, model repositories, and open-source libraries support trust across networks. A compromised root certificate or a maintainer’s credentials can put the entire dependency tree at risk.
AI risks vary along two dimensions: severity of harm and whether responsible actors can recognize it in time. The biggest danger is severe and invisible harm, where nothing visibly breaks for days or weeks, yet time compounds the severity of the incident. An AI agent could quietly corrupt records, act on instructions planted in its memory or in documents it consults, or appear cooperative while accumulating access beyond operator intent. Infrastructure may operate normally while the means to disrupt it are already in place. 
The dependencies and shared risks determine which code a system runs, which credentials it accepts, and which updates it trusts. Harm can cross borders quietly even when models and their owners remain separate.
That makes the speed of response critical. Delays in detecting a breach, assigning responsibility or authorizing a shutdown can allow damage to spread. Both China and the United States therefore need warnings to reach personnel with the authority and technical means to respond.
There is no obvious diplomatic agreement that can resolve the paradox built into the AI race: it rewards speed and secrecy, while safety depends on collective restraint and disclosure.
China-U.S. cooperation should instead focus on measures that improve safety without requiring either side to slow unilaterally, transfer its most advanced models, or expose commercially and strategically sensitive capabilities. Four areas stand out:
Before the Trump-Xi summit, American and Chinese security experts in a long-running bilateral dialogue proposed red lines around nuclear systems, human control over consequential cyber operations, and a dedicated mechanism for AI incidents. 
When an AI agent can search, authenticate, write code, call external tools, and act within minutes or seconds, where should human intervention occur? Requiring approval for every step would undermine the autonomous value of AI agents; waiting until something goes wrong may make intervention too late.
The harder questions concern permissions, escalation thresholds, shutdown mechanisms and which actions should always require explicit human authorization. Researchers could cooperate on these engineering challenges without sharing model weights, training data, or proprietary frontier capabilities.
Sandboxing, monitoring, permission controls, and model-level refusals are often treated as established safeguards. 
The underlying technical risk is broad: with appropriate tools and access, advanced models could identify previously unknown vulnerabilities and develop exploits across well-protected systems without step-by-step human direction. The key question is not whether a developer has guardrails, but whether they still work as agents become capable enough to search for ways around them.
While frontier AI labs in the U.S. have voluntarily disclosed instances of their models escaping from sandboxed environments, public reporting from China on comparable containment failures remains limited. This lack of transparency shouldn’t stop the two sides from working together. Washington and Beijing could develop compatible methods for testing sandbox escape, scope violations, unauthorized tool use, shutdown resistance, and failures of human intervention. Independent auditors, potentially from trusted third countries, could help verify the results.
Cyber attribution has always been challenging. AI makes it harder.
A defender discovering unauthorized access may be looking at a state-directed operation, a criminal actor using AI, a human-directed autonomous agent, or an agent that has exceeded its instructions while pursuing a legitimate task.
Between strategic rivals, that ambiguity is especially dangerous when the trust deficit widens. An autonomous system interacting with critical infrastructure could be mistaken for reconnaissance or preparation for attack before either government understands what happened. 
American and Chinese experts have already identified this risk: autonomous cyber exchanges could move faster than governments can determine whether an operation was deliberate, accidental, or unauthorized.
Washington and Beijing are unlikely to agree routinely on the attribution of contentious cyber incidents. They could instead develop common technical expectations about the evidence that should be examined before an AI-enabled incident is escalated politically, including agent logs, credential use, tool-invocation records, model provenance, human authorization, and network telemetry. In the first hours of a major cross-border incident, governments and trusted responders should be able to exchange technical indicators, containment measures, and patch information without first deciding who is responsible. Exchanging such information need not imply an admission of responsibility.
Cybersecurity has struggled with remediation for decades. Critical infrastructure is fragmented across hospitals, utilities, telecommunications networks, ports, government agencies, and private vendors. A vulnerability may be understood and a patch may exist, yet deployment can still take days or weeks.
articles.summary: The United States does not need to trust China, share frontier models with China, or slow its own AI development to have a national security interest in AI safety cooperation.

articles.title: Myanmar’s Leaders Tried to Erase My Rohingya Identity 11 Years Ago
articles.full_text:
The repression of Rohingya identity is connected to Myanmar’s broader failure to establish an inclusive political order. It’s time for ASEAN to realize that.
In July 2015, I was invited to the residence of U Aung Thaung, a senior and influential leader of Myanmar’s Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP), in Naypyidaw. We discussed the approaching general elections and parliamentary nominations for the constituencies in northern Rakhine state.
What happened during that meeting has remained outside the public record for more than 11 years. I want to disclose it now because the political question at its center – the recognition of Rohingya identity and rights – remains unresolved. It is also relevant to how ASEAN engages with Myanmar’s military leadership today.
I was elected to Myanmar’s house of parliament, the Pyithu Hluttaw, from Buthitaung township of Rakhine state in November 2010 as a USDP candidate. In the summer of 2015 I was preparing to secure my office for another term. But, during our private conversation, U Aung Thaung proposed a condition that went far beyond ordinary electoral politics.
As I recall it, he told me that he, the USDP leadership, President U Thein Sein, and then Commander-in-Chief Min Aung Hlaing did not accept “Rohingya” as an ethnic identity. He urged me to stop advocating for that identity and to persuade my constituents to identify themselves as “Bengali” instead. He presented this change as a pathway toward obtaining citizenship documentation and restoring political participation. He also advised me to give a media interview stating that “there is no Rohingya but Bengali,” without mentioning our private meeting and his name.
My parliamentary nomination, he indicated, depended on my willingness to support that position.
I could not ask my constituents to surrender their identity in exchange for the possibility of receiving documents, voting rights, or another parliamentary term. Political representation should protect the rights of a community, not become an instrument for bargaining those rights away.
U Aung Thaung encouraged me to consult my constituents and reconsider. I subsequently informed community leaders and constituents about the conversation. They supported my position and we were all on the same page. I did not disclose the meeting to the media at that time because of the political consequences of making such an account public while living in Myanmar.
During my visit, I saw large portraits of President Thein Sein, Min Aung Hlaing, and nationalist Buddhist monk U Wirathu in an office at the residence. An assistant told me that the office also served U Wirathu whenever he comes to Naypyidaw. These are my recollections of what I saw and I was told 11 years ago.
The statements about Thein Sein and Min Aung Hlaing were made to me by U Aung Thaung. I cannot claim that I heard either man personally authorize the proposal. But U Aung Thaung confirmed the proposal with Union Immigration Minister U Khin Yi, today’s USDP chairman and speaker of Pyithu Hluttaw, over the phone in front of me.
The central proposition was unmistakable: I was being asked to abandon public advocacy for the identity of the people I represented as a condition of continuing my political career.
On August 4, 2015, I resigned from the USDP. Two days later, I applied to contest the upcoming Pyithu Hluttaw election as an independent candidate for Buthitaung.
On August 22, the Maungdaw District Election Subcommission rejected my candidacy. Its decision concluded that my parents had not been Myanmar citizens at the time of my birth in 1965. I appealed, together with concrete documents, to the Rakhine State Election Subcommission, which upheld the rejection on September 1, 2015. The Union Election Commission subsequently affirmed the decision, communicating its ruling in a letter dated September 6, 2015.
This outcome presented a profound contradiction in my political life.
The same Union Election Commission had formally recognized me as an elected member of parliament following the November 7, 2010 election. Its recognition certificate, dated January 10, 2011, identified me as the elected representative of Buthitaung and recorded my citizenship card.
Five years later, election authorities found me ineligible to stand for the same parliamentary seat because they now considered the evidence of my parents’ citizenship insufficient.
The State Election Subcommission acknowledged that my father possessed a national registration card, which serves as a primary document for full citizenship, and that my maternal grandparents also held national registration cards. Nevertheless, it concluded that those records did not adequately establish the citizenship qualifications required under the election laws.
I maintained that I had submitted the same family citizenship documentation in both electoral processes. The surviving recognition certificate and 2105 rulings represent contrasting official outcomes, although a complete comparison of the underlying applications would require examination of the original 2010 candidate file.
I believe the circumstances of my exclusion cannot be separated from the political pressure I experienced over my Rohingya identity. But the official election decisions do not themselves establish that my refusal of U Aung Thaung Thaung’s proposal caused my disqualification.
In November 2015, I publicly described the disenfranchisement of Rohingya voters and candidates in an opinion article for the New York Times. What I did not reveal then was the private conversation that had proceeded my departure from the USDP. I am revealing it now not simply to revisit my personal experience, but because it illuminates a continuing political problem.
For decades, Rohingya identity has been contested by successive Myanmar authorities, often through the characterization of the community as “Bengali” migrants. Questions of citizenship, documentation, and political participation have been intertwined with that dispute. The consequences extended beyond elections.
The mass atrocities committed against Rohingya in 2017 drove hundreds of thousands of Rohingya people into Bangladesh and intensified international demands for accountability. The Myanmar military coup in February 2021 subsequently plunged the country into wider political and humanitarian crisis.
Today, the Rohingya question cannot be treated as an isolated refugee-management problem. It is connected to Myanmar’s broader failure to establish an inclusive political order in which citizenship and fundamental rights are protected without discrimination.
This why ASEAN’s diplomatic engagement with Min Aung Hlaing deserves close scrutiny.
Regional governments have legitimate reasons to maintain channels of communication concerning humanitarian access, armed conflicts, migration, and regional security. Diplomatic contact is not necessarily equivalent to recognition or endorsement. But engagement must be judged by what it achieves for people affected by Myanmar’s crisis.
For Rohingya, discussions of repatriation are incomplete unless they address the conditions that forced people to flee and the rights they must be able to exercise upon return. A refugee cannot be expected to regard return as durable when questions of identity, citizenship, personal security, and political belonging remain unresolved.
ASEAN should therefore make these issues substantive elements of its discussions with Myanmar’s authorities. They include equal citizenship rights, recognition of the right to self-identification, meaningful political participation, protection against further atrocities, accountability for grave violations, and conditions for voluntary, safe, dignified, and sustainable return. The wider realities of Myanmar’s conflict must be taken into account. The aspirations of people resisting military rule, the safety of civilians across the country, and political future of ethnic communities cannot be separated from efforts to resolve the Rohingya crisis.
My experience in 2015 taught me how readily the question of identity could become a condition imposed upon political participation. The documents from my parliamentary career show that official recognition in one election offered no assurance of eligibility in the next.
Eleven years later, I remain convinced that Rohingya rights cannot depend on whether individuals agree to relinquish the name by which they identify themselves.
ASEAN cannot settle Myanmar’s political future on its own. But it can insist that engagement address the rights and security of the people whose lives are at stake.
articles.summary: The repression of Rohingya identity is connected to Myanmar’s broader failure to establish an inclusive political order. It's time for ASEAN to realize that.

articles.title: Why Kim Jong Un Should Want a 4th Summit With Donald Trump
articles.full_text:
Here’s what Pyongyang’s Foreign Ministry might be telling Kim about a possible summit.
In this Feb. 27, 2019, file photo, U.S. President Donald Trump shakes hands with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un at the Sofitel Legend Metropole hotel in Hanoi, Vietnam, for their second summit meeting.
U.S. President Donald Trump’s push for a fourth summit with Kim Jong Un has so far been rejected by the North Korean leader, who may be playing hard to get. However, based on our decades analyzing North Korea, participation in countless face-to-face meetings with North Koreans – official and unofficial – and numerous visits to North Korea, we think that some in Pyongyang may believe their country could benefit greatly from a fourth summit, though not in terms of what Washington may think. 
In view of North Korea and Kim’s experience, especially his three summits during Trump’s first term in office, and Pyongyang’s analysis of the president’s current foreign policy, the North Korean Foreign Ministry would emphasize the following points that lay out a strong case with Kim Jong Un for a fourth summit.
First, it would point out that because of Kim’s policies in the military and economic fields, taking advantage of shifts in international geopolitics, especially Pyongyang’s close relationship with Russia and China, North Korea is in a position of strength for a summit, should the chairman choose to proceed. 
The United States and Trump, on the other hand, are in a much weaker position than before. The president’s overconfidence and erratic personality will almost certainly result in missteps that further weaken the U.S. position. And he doesn’t grasp that another summit will greatly benefit North Korea, which is now working in opposition to Washington. 
The ministry would add that, as Kim has said many times, the past – the previous summits in Singapore, Hanoi, and at the Demilitarized Zone – is gone. Back then, the chairman focused on improving relations with Washington in return for putting his nuclear program on the table and creating space for North Korea to modernize its economy. 
But today, another summit would improve North Korea’s global position by supporting its friends – China and especially Russia – undermining Washington’s influence abroad, and, hopefully, nudging Trump to accept Pyongyang’s growing nuclear arsenal. The ministry would also observe that, more than ever, Trump’s missteps have made the situation ripe for creating tensions in the already fraying South Korea-U.S. alliance.
Just as in the past, should Kim decide to proceed, the timing and venue of a new summit will be the subject of considerable back and forth with the Americans. In this instance, the North Koreans may believe the result of a summit could be more consequential because of Trump’s personality and his growing domestic political weakness.
The ministry would applaud Kim Jong Un’s policy of delaying a summit decision to take advantage of Trump’s eagerness to meet and extract unilateral concessions has already resulted in victories. The president has shortened one South Korea-U.S. exercise and left a cloud hanging over the rest. 
Trump has also inched away from Washington’s long-standing pursuit of denuclearization and toward accepting North Korea as a nuclear power. That appears to have had the added benefit of setting off an internal debate. The State Department continues to back denuclearization, contradicting Trump’s position and sending confusing signals to U.S. allies.
Looking ahead, the North Korean Foreign Ministry would predict that if the Republicans lose the upcoming November congressional elections, as expected, nothing will save Trump from a greatly weakened situation. As a result, he may be anxious to make even more concessions to paint any outcome – even simply holding a meeting with Kim – as a personal victory. 
North Korea’s Real Assessment of President Trump
While North Korea’s media have avoided direct criticism of Trump and continued to note Kim’s personal relationship with him, in private, foreign ministry analysts probably believe that his worst personality traits, evident in 2018 and 2019, have only become worse. These, in turn, will provide openings to reach agreements that further support Pyongyang’s strategy.
They would emphasize seven traits that will affect Trump’s performance at a North Korea-U.S. summit. First, at 80, he is seven years older than when the last summit was held and has declined physically and mentally. As the aged typically do, he has good days and bad days. Second, he reacts well to flattery, more so than ever. Third, Trump has a higher opinion of himself and his negotiating ability than in the past, even in the face of repeated failures. Fourth since he is more likely to rely on his gut feelings rather than expert advice, Trump will act impulsively. Fifth, he is losing his grip on reality. American media often laugh at many of his claims. Sixth, Trump has rolled out the red carpet at summits with presidents Vladimir Putin of Russia and Xi Jinping of China, despite their opposition to Washington’s global interests. He mistakenly believes that flattery can overcome policy differences. 
Perhaps even more important, Kim’s advisors will point out that Trump does not understand strategic thinking. Past summits with North Korea have demonstrated that he has no grasp of the wider picture; the U.S. war with Iran again underlined his short sightedness. It is doubtful he will understand that the North’s new objectives are different from the past and inimical to U.S. interests.
Given this analysis of Trump, North Korea’s Foreign Ministry would conclude that he will either repeat standard U.S. positions or come up with his own on the spur of the moment without expert advice from his staff. 
Trump knows denuclearization is not in the cards. Instead, he may float the idea of a nuclear freeze. If he does bring it up, the chairman could simply repeat his insistence that Pyongyang needs a strong deterrent. From his perspective, that deterrent is not just to maintain North Korea’s security but an absolute requirement for regional balance, especially given the growing danger of Japanese militarism. 
The president may also repeat his proposal made at the 2019 Hanoi summit for a moratorium on further testing of intercontinental-range ballistic missiles (ICBMs) that can reach the United States. South Korean President Lee Jae-myung advanced the same idea at the recent United Nations General Assembly session. The proposal wouldn’t include the shorter-range missiles that target Seoul and Tokyo. As a result, it will prove controversial in South Korea and could create new tensions in U.S. relations with Japan.
The ministry would suggest that Kim could easily parry such a proposal by insisting that any moratorium on ICBM launches must include other countries with those missiles. That would be consistent his position that North Korea is now a global power and cannot be expected to make concessions other nuclear powers will not. And, of course, neither the United States nor the others will be open to that idea,
Trump is likely to dangle sanctions relief for North Korea – a centerpiece of past summits – in return for concessions. The ministry would note, however, Pyongyang’s success in avoiding those restrictions with assistance from Moscow and Beijing, as well as the billions of dollars North Korea earns from illicit cyber activities. As a result, Kim should not see sanctions as the card that Washington once imagined them to be. Still, lifting them could have some secondary political value for North Korea, enhancing its international standing and further normalizing its status. 
Moreover, a proposal to lift sanctions could backfire and cause problems for the United States. It could stir up trouble in the Western bloc in the United Nations Security Council since lifting restrictions would face stiff resistance from Britain and France. On the domestic front, fiddling with sanctions would spark criticism from both Trump’s own party and political opponents. While he will not care, such policy turmoil further weakens the United States.
Just as in the past, the president will probably showcase grandiose, even far-fetched, and unachievable schemes to modernize North Korea’s economy. He has done that more recently with a proposal to turn Gaza into a modern coastal metropolis. Pyongyang’s position is quite clear – foreign aid is poisoned candy and should be rejected out of hand unless the chairman decides otherwise.
Finally, Trump can be expected to try to interfere with North Korea’s strong support for Russia in its war with Ukraine. However, the ministry’s America watchers would note that Washington has consistently underestimated the chairman’s commitment to the new relationship with Moscow. Presumably, few if any in the White House read Kim’s last letter to Putin expressing continued full support for Russian operations in Ukraine. Just how hard Trump will push is an open question given his zigzagging approach to the war and his hopes for a better relationship with Putin.
The Foreign Ministry will argue that a Trump-Kim meeting represents a golden opportunity to secure important objectives while only taking tactical steps that appear to be concessions. It will also open doors to significant strategic gains. It would recommend the following steps.
Kim’s overall summit approach should showcase his statements over the past year that North Korea is seeking “peaceful coexistence.” That theme has mesmerized the Americans. However, meaningless formulations used before by nuclear weapons states, such as “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought,” would cloak the North’s real objectives. So would any pledge to “work for peaceful resolution of outstanding differences.”
All of this will appeal to Trump who is determined to declare peace in his time and secure the Nobel Prize. In reality, highlighting “peaceful coexistence” would put North Korea in a position to protest virtually any steps the United States takes in the region as contradicting Washington’s assertions of a desire for peace.
While Trump’s aides are sure to warn him ahead of time, the ministry would recommend that Kim press the president to go beyond his random public statements on the North’s nuclear capabilities to put it in writing, perhaps in a summit declaration. Any acknowledgment of North Korea’s nuclear arsenal coming out of the meeting, even only verbal, will create turmoil in Seoul and Tokyo.
The chairman should certainly encourage Trump to reduce the U.S. military commitment to South Korea. He will be pushing on an open door. Trump has made it clear in the past that he is willing to further limit U.S. military activity in and around the Korean Peninsula. One possibility is ending joint South Korea-U.S. military exercises. The ministry would caution that it is unclear how far the president will go. But its experts would point out that he has also been consistently looking to draw down U.S. forces in the South for years.
Finally, North Korea’s diplomats would recommend that Kim seriously consider accepting any offer Trump makes to recognize the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea as a sovereign state. Embassies in each capital could serve as a formal line of communication after decades of hostility. In theory, they can be framed as a step to reduce tensions and avoid accidental war. In practice, they will do neither.
articles.summary: Here’s what Pyongyang’s Foreign Ministry might be telling Kim about a possible summit.

articles.title: New Governor, Old Problem: Koja Confronts US Base-Related Crimes in Okinawa
articles.full_text:
Whoever is governor, waves of Okinawan anti-base sentiment and protest will continue in the wake of every violent crime.
Okinawa Governor Koja Genta (left) lodges a written protest over the murder of a woman, allegedly by a U.S. Marine, with Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae (center) and Chief Cabinet Secretary Kihara Minou, Oct. 7, 2026.
Okinawa’s September 2026 election made headlines as incumbent Denny Tamaki was ousted by the Liberal Democratic Party’s (LDP) preferred candidate, Koja Genta. Koja became the first LDP-backed candidate to win the position since Hirokazu Nakaima in 2006. 
Tamaki and his predecessor, the late Onaga Takeshi, vocally opposed the expansion of the U.S. Marine Corps’ Camp Schwab in Henoko and were generally critical of Okinawa’s excessive base burden, relative to other Japanese prefectures. Newly-elected Governor Koja was perceived by the LDP-led Japanese government to be more favorable to the U.S. bases in Okinawa, specifically the completion of the relocation of Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Ginowan City to Camp Schwab. 
Perhaps most emblematic of the shift in the Okinawan Prefectural Office was Koja’s abolition of the Henoko New Base Construction Issue Countermeasures Division, the office that had handled legal, environmental, and political issues surrounding the construction. Instead, Koja’s administration created the Early Return Countermeasures Office, which is less overtly critical of the Henoko project. 
Only days after his inauguration, however, Koja has had to confront the same perennial problem that his predecessors faced: crimes (allegedly) committed by U.S. military personnel in Okinawa and their impacts on the Japan-U.S. alliance. 
On October 3, Okinawan police arrested a U.S. Marine on suspicion of murdering Anna Yagi, an Okinawan woman. While it remains to be seen if the U.S. soldier is convicted of the crime, this incident represents an unfortunate continuity of crimes committed by U.S. soldiers in Okinawa, particularly against women. In recent years, for instance, a U.S. Marine was convicted of attempted rape, and a U.S. Air Force member was found guilty of the kidnapping and rape of a minor; in both cases the victims were female. 
As the U.S. and Japanese governments increasingly worry about conflict with China in the Taiwan Strait, which borders Okinawa, they must work to prevent these crimes to ensure the stable operation of their alliance. 
Crimes Committed by U.S. Servicemembers Contribute to Okinawa’s “Base Burden”
Several factors impact Okinawans’ perception of the prefecture’s “excessive base burden.” One is the fact that Okinawa hosts 70 percent of the U.S. soldiers stationed in Japan, but Okinawa’s landmass is just 1 percent of Japan’s total area. Okinawa also has a contentious and traumatic history with Tokyo, which increases suspicions that the central government doesn’t have the prefecture’s best interests in mind.  
A major factor that contributes to the perception of the U.S. bases as burdens is the negative externalities that periodically come from U.S. bases and troops. That includes various forms of chemical pollution, such as Agent Orange (historically) and per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) (in recent years), and other environmental issues.  
Crimes attributed to U.S. military personnel are another type of negative externality. Violent crimes such as sexual assault and murder may be especially likely to mobilize protests against the U.S. military presence, in part because of the strong emotions that they can invoke. These events serve as opportunities for anti-base activists to remind Okinawans and mainland Japanese citizens alike of the island prefecture’s traumatic history involving both mainland Japan and the U.S., such as the Battle of Okinawa during World War II. Through this lens, crimes committed by U.S. military personnel in Okinawa are interpreted as further examples of the ways that the U.S. and Japanese governments have and continue to marginalize Okinawa in the name of national and regional security.
Unsurprisingly, anti-base protests in Okinawa often occur after a crime such as the murder of Anna Yagi. For example, the 1995 kidnapping and rape of a 12-year-old girl by U.S. servicemen kicked off a massive wave of protests against the U.S. bases, and more recently, the 2016 murder of Rina Shimabukuro by a U.S. contractor was followed by protests with tens of thousands of participants. 
Despite the election of Koja to the governorship, which some observers may interpret as a sign that Okinawans are deprioritizing base politics, protests are likely to follow Yagi’s murder. They have already started in Tokyo, as well as Naha, the capital of Okinawa Prefecture. 
The Threat Perception of China Can’t Overshadow Crimes
For some observers, Koja’s election win signaled that Okinawans’ concerns about potential Chinese hostility in the nearby Taiwan Strait may trump their concerns about the “burdens” from the U.S. bases. Koja himself stated that “the fact that the security environment around Okinawa has become more severe is something we can’t help but acknowledge.” He said that “we have to have the ability to defend ourselves and deter aggression,” presumably referring to the U.S. and Japanese Self-Defense Force (SDF) bases in the prefecture. 
However, it would be a mistake to assume that the perception of China as a threat to Japanese and Okinawan security will automatically counteract the negative impacts that crimes committed by U.S. soldiers have on public opinion toward the U.S. military, at least in the short term. Recent research has suggested that threat perception does not always increase support for a U.S. military presence. 
Some of my own research found that crimes committed by U.S. personnel have a negative impact on public opinion toward the U.S. military. Furthermore, it is unclear if the presence of U.S. bases makes locals feel more or less secure, particularly in the event of a military conflict, especially given Iran’s recent attacks on U.S. military installations in the Middle East. In Okinawa, surveys suggest that a majority of residents worry that military bases (which could include SDF bases as well) in the prefecture could serve as military targets. 
Therefore, although recent surveys suggest that Okinawans, like mainland Japanese citizens, are wary of Chinese military aggression, U.S. and Japanese officials should not assume that threat perceptions will automatically result in Okinawan public support for U.S. bases, particularly when a crime linked to U.S. personnel is in the headlines. 
An Ounce of Prevention Is Worth a Pound of Cure
If the U.S. and Japanese governments believe, as they say, that the bases in Okinawa Prefecture are crucial to regional security, they need to take more proactive measures to prevent rather than react to crimes allegedly committed by U.S. military personnel. Even if Anna Yagi’s accused murderer is ultimately found innocent, the damage to civilian-military relations between U.S. soldiers and Okinawans is already done. 
For his part, Koja has issued a formal protest with the U.S. military and expressed his “outrage” at the crime. Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae has lodged a “strong protest” with the U.S.; meanwhile, U.S. officials have temporarily prohibited U.S. soldiers from going off base in Okinawa. However, reactive actions by officials are not new, and Okinawans are wary of the crime, protest, and apology routine. As one Okinawan resident put it, “I am deeply disappointed by the same kinds of government comments we have been hearing for decades – that they will protest or that they take the matter seriously.” 
One of the biggest elements in preventing such crimes against civilians is the training that U.S. soldiers receive when they deploy to a specific location. Such training may impact soldiers’ perceptions of the host communities in which they live and with which they interact, as well as how they interact with host community civilians. In the case of Okinawa, a recent study suggested that the orientation materials that U.S. Marines are exposed to depict Okinawans as obstacles to be overcome and the media as agitators of anti-base sentiment. In doing so, these materials delegitimize opposition to U.S. bases, instead of asking how U.S. troops can avoid stoking anti-base sentiment. This study drew on training materials from the 2010s. Since then, the materials have hopefully been updated in a way that seeks to better understand where Okinawan anti-base sentiment comes from and the role of individual U.S. soldiers in facilitating (or inhibiting) the Japan-U.S. relationship. 
The U.S. military and its municipal and gubernatorial partners also have a role to play in shaping the narratives around the U.S. military presence in Okinawa, which may help ameliorate the negative impacts of crimes on civilians’ relationships with U.S. soldiers. Recent studies suggested that contact between U.S. soldiers and civilians in base-hosting countries can facilitate positive public opinions of the U.S. military. The same research found that contact combined with exposure to base-related crime – being the victim or having a friend or family member who is a victim of such crime – does not consistently lead to negative attitudes toward the U.S. military. Thus, creating and strengthening the relationships between U.S. troops and the community members that host them is essential to maintaining a positive Japan-U.S. alliance. This can include activities such as base festivals, English or Japanese language courses, or other exchanges. 
Anna Yagi’s murder comes at a time of other high-profile cases of violence against women, and joins a history of crimes committed by U.S. military personnel against women in Okinawa. For the stability of the Japan-U.S. security alliance, it is imperative to facilitate more positive relationships between U.S. soldiers and Okinawan citizens; crimes attributed to U.S. soldiers have the opposite effect. While the United States has tried to address this issue in the past, it is clearly not enough, as Koja has said. 
Until the U.S. military and its Japanese partners can solve this puzzle, waves of Okinawan anti-base sentiment and protest, which threaten the Japan-U.S. relationship, will continue in the wake of every violent crime.

Perhaps most emblematic of the shift in the Okinawan Prefectural Office was Koja’s abolition of the Henoko New Base Construction Issue Countermeasures Division, the office that had handled legal, environmental, and political issues surrounding the construction. Instead, Koja’s administration created the Early Return Countermeasures Office, which is less overtly critical of the Henoko project. 
Only days after his inauguration, however, Koja has had to confront the same perennial problem that his predecessors faced: crimes (allegedly) committed by U.S. military personnel in Okinawa and their impacts on the Japan-U.S. alliance.

articles.title: Debunking Alarmist Narratives on the ‘China Air Base’ in Laos
articles.full_text:
The most widespread narratives regarding the Laos-China Support and Training Center lack evidence and demonstrate a limited understanding of air power.
A satellite image shows the construction of the China-backed air strip in Ban Keun, Vientiane province, Laos, Jan. 3, 2026.
The opening of the Laos-China Joint Support and Training Center and the Friendship Aviation Academy in Ban Keun, Laos on September 29 has sparked an intense media storm. China hawks claim that the innocuous airfield represents Beijing’s third overseas military base, following the Djibouti facility in East Africa and the Ream Naval Support facility in Cambodia, and the first Chinese air base in Southeast Asia. 
International media has framed the Ban Keun facility as a “base” or an “air base,” and the training aircraft spotted on satellite imagery as “attack aircraft” or “light attack aircraft.” Further, alarmists warn that China could extend the airfield’s runway and expand its infrastructure to enable power projection across mainland Southeast Asia and beyond, or to use the facility for intelligence collection. Still others have proposed that an enlarged base could facilitate bomber operations or to out-flank or surround Vietnam. 
Critically, however, whether due to intentional framing or simple ignorance, many of the above claims lack evidence and realism. This article attempts to debunk some of the more persistent and glaring narratives repeated in the media and expert commentary regarding the new airfield and its purpose.
First, images of Ban Keun airfield taken by a commercial satellite provider Vantor and shared first by Reuters show eight Chinese-made JL-8/K-8 basic jet trainer aircraft on the facility’s apron. The aircraft are termed as “light attack aircraft” or “attack aircraft” by media. That is an inaccurate framing, making the aircraft appear more threatening by nature than they actually are. 
The K-8 is a joint China-Pakistan training aircraft project, operated by many countries, including in the region by China, Laos, Myanmar, and Pakistan, among others. The K-8 is primarily a basic or intermediate training aircraft. The type typically feeds into phases two and three of a flight training syllabus, like introduction to jet flight and advanced jet training, and an introduction to tactical flight, before moving on to more advanced and higher performance trainers.
In the Lao People’s Liberation Army Air Force (LPLAAF), the phase one elementary training is carried out on Chinese-build SAIC LE-500, the K-8 is used in the phase two and three basic jet training, and the Russian YAK-130 is used for phase four tactical training. 
Unlike Myanmar’s air force, which has reportedly employed the K-8 in a light attack role, there is no evidence of LPLAAF use of the type in that role. Tellingly, no visual evidence of the type participating in exercises or carrying air-to-ground munitions has surfaced in the aircraft’s almost a decade of service in Laos. Thus, framing the Laotian K-8 as a “light attack aircraft” is simply an inaccurate description, which causes confusion and alarm.
In contrast, the Russian advanced jet trainer is a substantially more capable platform than the K-8 and can be armed with various air-to-air and air-to-ground munitions for ground support.
Another persistent claim suggests that Ban Keun airfield is a Chinese “air base” with a long runway and a “large” apron for aircraft parking, supposedly capable of supporting Chinese military power projection across mainland Southeast Asia.
However, the airfield’s single runway is approximately 2,000 meters in length, which, in fact, is not very long for a military airfield. Other major LPLAAF operating locations like the Wattay International Airport in Vientiane and Xieng Khouang (Phonsavan) air base have runways extending to approximately 3,000 m and 2,500 m, respectively, measured in Google Earth. 
By way of comparison, neighboring Thailand’s military airfields are generally built to 3,000 m length. Similarly, the People’s Liberation Army Air Force (PLAAF) fighter bases in the Southern Theater Command area have 2,500 m runways, while bomber bases at Shaodong and Leiyang have longer, 3,000 m runways. 
The 2,000 m runway at Ban Keun was not built to support power projection but, instead, to handle training aircraft.
In addition, claims that the facility has a large apron for aircraft parking and potential for significant expansion to support power projection are also incorrect. Judged from the available satellite imagery, the airfield’s apron is in fact relatively small and can only support a dozen trainers with associated sun shelters, hangars, and maintenance infrastructure. 
To support sustained power projection operations, the airfield should have truly vast aprons, numerous aircraft shelters, and large fuel and munitions “farms,” which can be seen in similar imagery from Chinese air bases across the border. 
None of this is visible at Ban Keun. What can be parsed out is an airfield with modest infrastructure suitable for the stated intended training role.
Some experts have proposed that together with the Cambodia-China Support Center in Ream (often framed as a Chinese naval base), the Ban Keun “air base” will help China “encircle” Vietnam. Writing for the Interpreter, Hunter Marston suggested that “Beijing has effectively pulled off an end run around Hanoi’s air and maritime flanks.” 
Such statements demonstrate limited understanding of air power’s key attributes and China’s existing military posture and options to project power in the South China Sea or mainland Southeast Asia. Air power allows maneuver in the third dimension (altitude). Its key attributes – speed, reach, and ability to overfly any terrain – provide military aircraft significant operational flexibility.  
The PLAAF does not have to base its combat aircraft physically in Laos to attempt to “surround” or “encircle” Vietnam. It can do so from its current bases within the Southern Theater Command and the South China Sea.
Under the Southern Theater Command, the PLAAF has an extensive network of well-equipped air bases that stretch from Hunan and Guangdong provinces in China’s southeast to Guangxi and Yunnan provinces in the south, directly bordering Vietnam, Laos, and Myanmar. In addition, Hainan Island, Woody Island in the Paracels, and Fiery Cross Reef, Subi Reef, and Mischief Reef in the Spratlys provide the PLAAF with a chain of well-equipped operating locations for any regional contingency. 
Importantly, from its current bases, such as Mengzi in Yunnan Province or Bose/Tianyang in Guangxi Province, PLAAF combat aircraft can comfortably reach anywhere in mainland Southeast Asia. Moreover, operating from China’s Spratly outposts, the PLAAF can reach nearly all corners of the subregion. The reach of China’s air power can be further expanded by the growing fleet of indigenous aerial refueling aircraft. 
The PLAAF’s primary combat aircraft in the Southern Theater Command area of operations – such as the JH-7A, Su-30MKK, J-16, and J-20 – are designed for long combat radius, extending from 600 nautical miles to up to 1,000 nm. The smaller J-10C can also reach more than 600 nm with drop tanks. With such operational flexibility, PLAAF strike aircraft can execute multipronged attacks against targets up to central Vietnam from their existing bases. Dispatched from Woody Island or Fiery Cross Reef in the South China Sea, Chinese fighters can easily cover the entirety of Vietnam and more, offering options for multiple approaches.
As a result, there is no reason for Beijing to position its bombers forward to the Ban Keun airfield to project power across mainland Southeast Asia and the Gulf of Thailand and Gulf of Bengal in conflict. With an estimated combat radius of 1,350 nm combined with the use of long-range precision-guided weapons, China’s H-6K bombers can cover all the above areas while operating from their home bases at Shaodong and Leiyang in Hunan Province. Any forward deployment of Chinese bombers would occur within the Southern Theater Command area, Hainan Island, or the Spratlys, offering the PLAAF multiple options and operational flexibility. 
Experts have suggested also that China could deploy spy aircraft, surveillance radars, and signals intelligence gathering systems to Ban Keun. Commenting on the matter for the South China Morning Post, Abdul Rahman Yaacob proposed that China could use the facility for “keeping an eye on Vietnam” and to “monitor air activities deep into Myanmar, Thailand, and Vietnam.” Others have noted that the facility offers improved reach for Chinese spy planes to monitor U.S. military activity up to the Singapore Strait.
However, it is unclear from such commentary what the purpose of increased monitoring of mainland Southeast Asia is. 
Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, and Cambodia all hold very close relations with Beijing. When it comes to Vietnam, which has maritime disputes with China in the South China Sea, Hanoi’s military bases can be easily monitored from Southern Theater Command area of operations, with little additional benefit from dispatching such capabilities to Laos.
These assertions are among the most frequently disseminated narratives regarding the Laos-China Support and Training Center. Many are pure speculation that fuels unnecessary alarmism – particularly those that lack evidence and demonstrate a limited understanding of air power, its key attributes, and China’s regional air projection capabilities.
What the official statements and available evidence suggest is that the Ban Keun facility is a joint training facility to help the LPLAAF develop its capacity for the future and meet its own modernization goals. 
China has assisted the Lao air force (and the broader civil aviation sector) not just through hardware sales (i.e., the LE-500 and JL-8 for the LPLAAF and the C-909 for the Lao Airlines) but also by developing the entire aviation ecosystem, including infrastructure, management, maintenance, and training. This is the context in which the Laos-China Joint Support and Training Center and the Friendship Aviation Academy should be viewed.
articles.summary: The most widespread narratives regarding the Laos-China Support and Training Center lack evidence and demonstrate a limited understanding of air power.

articles.title: Central Asia’s Leaders Gather in Turkmenistan for 8th Consultative Meeting
articles.full_text:
Grand outcomes aren’t necessary at every meeting to prove the value of a format. But at a certain point, the lowest hanging fruit has been picked.
On October 8, Turkmenistan hosted a flurry of region meetings in Avaza, including the 8th Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan, and the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) Council of Heads of State, as well as related foreign minister-level meetings. 
According to Turkmen state media, Turkmen President Serdar Berdimuhamedov laid out “five key objectives,” which included “building the potential of the six-party format,” ensuring lasting peace and stability in the region, joint efforts “to transform Central Asia and Azerbaijan into key transport, logistics, energy, and industrial hubs on the continent in the East-West and North-South directions,” creating the conditions for “accelerated technological growth and the active implementation of artificial intelligence,” and finally, expanding “cultural, humanitarian, educational, and civilizational ties.”
These were all vaguely, and inoffensively, stated, as per Turkmen diplomatic style.
Remarks from Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev were more ambitious and concrete – or at least more readily accessible. Mirziyoyev remarked on the atmospheric change in Central Asian regional diplomacy. He pointed to the completion of the Treaty on Friendship, Good-Neighborliness and Cooperation for the Development of Central Asia in the 21st Century. The treaty was signed during the fourth Consultative Meeting of Central Asian Leaders in 2022 by the presidents of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan. It took until 2025 for Tajikistan to sign on, and Turkmenistan only did so earlier this year, in July during a visit by Kazakh Foreign Minister Yermek Kosherbayev to Ashgabat.
Mirziyoyev did not remark on the gap between 2022 and 2026 for all five countries to sign onto the treaty; he also didn’t address the fact that while Azerbaijan has joined the grouping – and is taking over as chair – it isn’t a party to the treaty. 
This is, perhaps, by design. Mirziyoyev did remark that “we do not seek to create cumbersome structures.”
The friendship treaty codifies this position, baking in possibilities while committing to little beyond words and consultation. The treaty lays out commitments to cooperate across a wide range of areas and build relations “on the basis of mutual respect, equality, understanding and comprehensive consideration of each other’s interests.” 
But it contains hints of possible future pathways. For example, its Article 5 states that the parties “shall provide each other with comprehensive support and mutual assistance in matters of preventing threats to their independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity.” It goes on to stipulate that should a situation arise that “poses a threat to the security, sovereignty and territorial integrity” of one of the parties, “appropriate consultations” may be held bilaterally or within the consultative format “in order to determine measures that will contribute to the effective prevention of the threat that has arisen.” That’s a long-winded diplomatic way of saying that should a crisis develop, the Central Asian states may act together to confront it. 
Of course, history – and the track records of other regional groupings such as the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) or the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) – suggest that defaulting to inaction is the most likely outcome, even amid a crisis. 
It’s hard to divorce the friendship treaty, which was signed by Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan in July 2022, from the Russian invasion of Ukraine earlier that year. Similarly, Tajikistan only joined after its long-standing border disputes with Kyrgyzstan were settled. Turkmenistan, which maintains a foreign policy of “positive neutrality,” is the most surprising signatory by far – but that it did sign on may reflect less a change of heart in Ashgabat than the low commitments demanded by the treaty.
Grand outcomes aren’t necessary at every meeting to prove the value of a format. But at a certain point, the lowest hanging fruit – the ability to sit around a table together and discuss priorities amicably – has been picked. Mirziyoyev – and Kazakh president Kassym-Jomart Tokayev – have made clear that they have grander ambitions for what Central Asia can accomplish collectively. The economic sphere – particularly trade, transit, and investment – got special attention from both presidents and represents the next lowest hanging fruit. Who can argue with expanding trade?
In his remarks, Tokayev noted that intraregional trade amounted to approximately $13 billion, representing 8 percent of total trade turnover between the countries. He set the aim of reaching $20 billion. Tokayev suggested deepening regional trade cooperation, linking across borders the logistics centers most of the countries in the region are building. “In the near future,” he said, “we can link them together to build regional value chains. We have all the conditions for expanding cooperation in investment, energy, industry, and other strategic areas.” Tokayev referenced the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, or the Middle Corridor, while also noting that “North-South route, in cooperation with Russia, remains particularly important for Kazakhstan.”
Mirziyoyev argued that “economic cooperation must be elevated to a new level.” He noted the importance of continuing to address trade barriers, but looked to the future: “We have already reached a point where standard mutual trade is no longer sufficient; we need to create finished products together.”
Mirziyoyev closed with a focus on the youth and cooperation, saying that “it is important that students, young professionals, scientists, researchers and representatives of creative professions have more opportunities to communicate, learn from one another and work together.”
That’s a great sentiment, but delivered in light of virtual silence on the matter of Dr. Ikboljon Qoraboyev it rings hollow. Qoraboyev was a well-known Uzbek international relations professor at a top Kazakh university. He was was detained this summer in Kazakhstan, apparently on espionage charges, and there has been very little said officially about the case – either by Astana or Tashkent – since. It serves to highlight the distance between remarks delivered at a round table and the reality of what it takes to inspire and support cooperation and collaboration. 
There is much hard work ahead for Central Asia.

articles.title: Why Is China Proposing Reciprocal Nuclear Laboratory Visits?
articles.full_text:
While China and the U.S. still disagree on the size of nuclear forces and the path of arms control, can they exchange meaningful information on certain technical issues?
Crews at Los Alamos National Laboratory in New Mexico, the U.S., repackage waste to be shipped to the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant, Dec. 20, 2011.
On October 6, CNN reported that the United States and China are engaged in informal, preliminary discussion on reciprocal visits to nuclear facilities. According to the report, the idea was first raised by the Chinese side in meetings with U.S. officials this year, during which the two sides discussed U.S. Department of Energy national laboratories and their Chinese counterparts. The same source also indicated that the U.S. side is willing to discuss visits to nuclear test sites. 
At the China-U.S. leaders’ summit held in September, the two sides agreed to build “a constructive relationship of strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness, and reciprocity.” According to CNN, however, they didn’t discuss reciprocal nuclear facility visits at the summit.
Reciprocal laboratory visits could serve to test the feasibility of limited nuclear transparency and give the broad political goal of “strategical stability” something concrete to work on. The question is whether the two sides can learn about each other’s nuclear institutions, their roles, and some of their activities, without harming their own national security. 
In the mid-1990s, the United States and China set up the “U.S.-China Lab-to-Lab Technical Exchange Program” (CLL). Nuclear weapons laboratories under the U.S. Department of Energy and Chinese institutions including the China Academy of Engineering Physics participated in the project. The exchanges were conducted by scientists from both countries responsible for the technical management of nuclear forces, under the supervision of both governments, and were initially limited to nuclear arms control and nonproliferation. The program listed a shared goal: the exchange of information about the operation and management of nuclear facilities, while safeguarding the national security interests of both countries. 
China hosted American scientists at its nuclear weapon laboratory and the Lop Nur test site, and showed them a variety of facilities. According to a U.S. participant, the United States authorized only small scale, restricted exchange on nuclear material protection and nuclear arms control verification technologies. Although the U.S. side had initially expressed a willingness to host Chinese scientists at the Nevada Test Site on a reciprocal basis, it withdrew that commitment later. 
The two sides also ran into other obstacles. In 1996, for example, regarding a joint analysis plan for seismic data from mining activities on both sides, the China Academy of Engineering Physics declined to participate because the work was outside its scope. The Northwest Institute of Nuclear Technology also declined, out of concern that the data might be used to estimate the yields of China’s past nuclear tests. 
In the late 1990s, the program was halted as China-U.S. relations worsened. In particular, a 1999 U.S. Congressional report accused China of stealing nuclear technology, which Beijing allegedly used “to fabricate and successfully test its next generation of nuclear weapons designs.” Scientists from both sides tried to revive the program during the administrations of Presidents George W. Bush and Barack Obama, without success.
This history shows that laboratory exchanges were a form of contact China and the United States have tried before, where information sharing and confidentiality requirements coexisted. While the experience of the 1990s cannot directly explain China’s current motivation for reviving the idea of reciprocal visits to nuclear facilities, it left a precedent. Whether the concept of reciprocal visits described in the CNN report aligns with the experience of such limited exchanges needs to be considered together with China’s current position on nuclear transparency.
China’s official position stresses transparency of intentions, but it also insists on protecting national security. The 2025 White Paper on Arms Control stated: “Given the current international security situation, transparency in intentions and policies is the most practical significance.” The 2026 NPT Compliance Report noted, however, that “inappropriate transparency may also undermine strategic stability” and advocated that nuclear weapon states should raise transparency step by step, in accordance with their own security environments and actual circumstances. 
The report also noted that in March 2026, China organized a visit by permanent representatives to the United Nations, disarmament ambassadors, and high-level representatives from nearly 20 countries to the decommissioned 816 nuclear facility in Chongqing. Beijing included this in the section on “transparency and confidence-building measures.” A visit to a decommissioned facility does not prove that China would open an active nuclear weapon laboratory in the same way. But it shows that China already uses facility visits as a way to explain its nuclear policy to other countries.
Visits to active laboratories, however, may sit in a middle ground between policy transparency and transparency about nuclear forces. Nuclear weapons research institutions also undertake specialized work in areas such as arms control and nonproliferation. The earlier CLL program set out to explore ways of sharing selected information about nuclear materials and facilities while protecting sensitive national security information. The exchanges at that time covered how a nuclear weapons research institution can organize its arms control work, staff its operations, and carry out management. These issues go beyond a nuclear policy statement, but there is no need to discuss the number of warheads, deployment locations, or readiness status. 
In addition, professional exchanges among nuclear agencies can foster a better understanding of each other’s working methods. Following the 1997 CLL program export control workshop, a Chinese representative stated that the workshop had given him a clearer understanding of the functional relationships among the U.S. government, laboratories, and technical experts. If the new reciprocal visits include such substantive dialogue, the laboratories could serve as a starting point for limited transparency: providing access to institutions and personnel in the nuclear field without immediately delving into discussions regarding the numbers, deployment and use of nuclear forces.
Such professional engagement could also become part of China-U.S. strategic nuclear dialogue. Chinese expert Li Bin has suggested that strategic nuclear dialogue could take place at various levels and involve different partners, and that Track 1.5 dialogue could include diplomatic departments, the military, and nuclear weapons laboratories. He also stressed that transparency should be a tool for achieving strategic stability.
Finding a form of openness that both sides can accept is only the first step. Laboratory visits could also allow each side to ask direct questions about specific work and hear the other side explain the purposes of its activities and technical judgments. If these discussions can correct misunderstandings and are carried forward by participants into their respective policy debates, they may reduce overreactions stemming from misreading. This is also where limited transparency can contribute to strategic stability.
Laboratory visits will not automatically resolve the conflict between nuclear strategy and the security interests of China and the United States. But they could serve as a limited test for the China-U.S. nuclear relationship in a new period. While the two sides still disagree on the size of nuclear forces, deployment, and the path of arms control, can they first exchange meaningful information on certain technical issues and keep talking afterward? If so, this limited transparency could provide a concrete example of the “strategic stability” called for by the leaders of both countries.

articles.title: India’s Energy Transition Is Complicated, But Progressing
articles.full_text:
While coal continues to dominate India’s power supply, the country is also building clean energy at one of the fastest rates in the world.
Across Western climate commentary, India is frequently portrayed as a coal-dependent laggard whose rising emissions threaten to offset progress elsewhere. This framing obscures a more complex reality: While coal continues to dominate India’s power supply, the country is also building clean energy at one of the fastest rates in the world. Understanding this contradiction requires reassessing how climate progress is conventionally measured.
The concerns behind India’s continued use of coal are real. India recorded the world’s largest absolute rise in emissions in 2024, and thermal power still generates around 70 percent of its electricity. Yet these figures describe where India stands today, not where it is heading.
At the 2015 Paris climate conference, India pledged that 40 percent of its installed power capacity would come from non-fossil fuel sources by 2030. It reached that goal in November 2021, almost a decade early. After raising its target to 50 percent, India crossed that threshold in June 2025, this time five years ahead of schedule.
As those figures suggest, India’s renewables expansion is significant. India’s non-fossil fuel energy capacity passed 300 gigawatts in July 2026, more than half of its total installed capacity. The country added a record 55 gigawatts of clean capacity in the 2025–26 financial year and now ranks third in the world for installed renewable energy. On July 29, 2025, renewables met more than half of India’s electricity demand, a record share and, in the Indian government’s words, “a remarkable sign of change.”
Many of today’s high-income economies industrialized on coal for over a century before shifting to cleaner energy. India is attempting to do both simultaneously, expanding electricity access and industrial growth for 1.4 billion people while building one of the largest clean-energy systems in the world. 
Yet significant challenges remain. The largest is the gap between capacity and generation. Although more than half of India’s installed capacity is now non-fossil, these sources produce under a third of the electricity the country consumes. Solar output peaks in the afternoon while demand often peaks in the evening, and the storage and transmission networks needed to bridge this gap are still under construction. Until they are complete, coal will remain the backbone of reliable energy supply.
Rising demand compounds the difficulty. Rapid economic growth, urbanization and more frequent heatwaves are driving up electricity consumption, which is why India’s total emissions continue to climb even as its power mix becomes cleaner. Clean capacity is being added quickly, but demand is rising almost as fast.
Heavy industry presents a further hurdle. Steel and aluminum are among the hardest sectors to decarbonize. Indian exporters now face carbon border rules in key markets; the Global Trade Research Initiative estimated that Indian steel and aluminum exporters may need to cut prices by 15 to 22 percent to remain competitive in Europe. Smaller firms struggle the most with the cost of measuring and reporting emissions.
Finance is the final, perhaps most binding, constraint. A transition of this scale requires enormous investment, much of it in grids and storage with long payback periods. At COP29, India objected to the new climate finance goal of  $300 billion a year, which was less than one-fourth of the $1.3 trillion that developing countries had demanded.
Still, India continues to push forward. Its national carbon market became operational in January 2025, providing industry with a price signal to reduce emissions. The growth of India’s fossil fuel emissions is projected to have slowed sharply in 2025. 
Energy transitions are rarely linear, as recent Western experience shows. During the 2022 energy crisis, several European countries temporarily returned to coal to maintain supply before renewable growth resumed. This was a reasonable response to an emergency, and it illustrates that every country balances climate goals against energy security and affordability. India faces the same trade-offs at a lower income level and with more people still gaining reliable power.
International partners can also play a constructive role. Expanded financing for grid infrastructure and battery storage would directly address India’s generation gap. Mechanisms that recognize domestic carbon pricing, such as India’s carbon market, could ease the burden of border carbon rules on smaller exporters. The International Solar Alliance, which India co-founded, already offers a strong base for wider cooperation on clean technology and supply chains 
Coal will remain part of India’s energy mix for some time, and the obstacles ahead are real. But measuring climate commitment through coal dependence alone risks misreading one of the world’s largest clean-energy transitions. 
Assessments of India’s climate performance should therefore shift their focus. Rather than asking whether India still uses coal, the question should be whether it is moving decisively away from it. A fairer yardstick would weigh a country’s direction of travel, per capita emissions, and historical responsibility alongside its current energy mix. After all, the average Indian emits about 2.2 tonnes of carbon dioxide a year, less than half the global average, and India has contributed under 4 percent of cumulative carbon dioxide emissions since the industrial revolution.
Future analysis of India’s climate role should account for both its achievements and the constraints shaping its choices.
