The young women protesting against patriarchy are not intimidated by authority. They are demanding accountability from Home Minister Amit Shah while also lampooning him. Student wings of the opposition Congress and leftist parties organized protests against the failure of the Delhi Police to enforce the law. These protests were held amid ongoing protests in Delhi calling for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over election process irregularities.
Youth anger about women’s safety forced the Supreme Court to address the issue. Describing the recent spate of rapes as a clear “systematic failure” on the part of law enforcement authorities, a two-judge bench said that “accountability needs to be fixed.”
The judges stressed the need for a focused approach to prevent rapes and not on penalty. Merely installing CCTV was not enough, it pointed out, calling for the Delhi Police to monitor it around the clock. Better policing and patrolling would “instill fear in criminals,” it said, adding that public spaces, including parks and buses, should not ​become “high-risk” zones because of poor lighting and poor surveillance. Having strict laws was not enough, the court said, calling for effective implementation of laws to discourage serious offences like rape. The court will be taking stock of the progress made on its directives again next month.

articles.title: Anwar is Bargaining Myanmar Lives For Political Gain – And He Will Lose
articles.full_text:
Min Aung Hlaing should not be trusted to resolve a refugee crisis that is a direct result of his own past policies.
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim (right) and Myanmar’s President Min Aung Hlaing at the Perdana Putra Complex in Putrajaya, Malaysia, Oct. 8, 2026.
This week, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim received Min Aung Hlaing, Myanmar’s junta chief, who led the 2017 genocide against the Rohingya, to arrange the transfer of 200,000 refugees, including Rohingya, back to Myanmar. The first deportations have already begun.
The plan is not just morally bankrupt. It makes no practical sense. It appears driven by months of coordinated online hate speech against Rohingya refugees in Malaysia and the targeting of community leaders by authorities, including the recent arrest of Zafar Ahmad Abdul Ghani.
In case anyone needs reminding, Min Aung Hlaing is the subject of an arrest warrant from the Argentine Federal Court for commissioning the atrocities against Rohingya as commander-in-chief. Prosecutors at the International Criminal Court have also requested an arrest warrant for him on similar grounds. He is yet to face justice, and the military remains as brutal as ever. He led the coup in 2021 and has razed half the country in the years since in his desperate bid for power. He still represents the Myanmar military, an institution whose sole purpose is to exploit the population through force, as it has for more than 50 years, and is the root cause of all Myanmar’s suffering.
Deporting refugees to Myanmar under an agreement with Min Aung Hlaing is a violation of international law and the fundamental principle of non-refoulement. And it will not ease the burden of the Myanmar crisis on Malaysia or the wider region; indeed, it will worsen it.
Time and time again, Min Aung Hlaing has proven that he can’t be trusted, not only by the people of Myanmar, but also by our neighbors. He has treated ASEAN with contempt since the coup, ignoring the basic requirements of the Five-Point Consensus, which called for an immediate cessation of violence, inclusive dialogue, and humanitarian access to the country. This is the precise reason why the refugee numbers continue to grow.
Min Aung Hlaing is also not the sole arbiter of power in Myanmar. He controls less than half of the country. He does not even control northern Rakhine State, the Rohingya homeland. That region, and most of Rakhine, is now largely held by the Arakan Army, which is committing its own grave abuses against Rohingya.
Just last week, the military bombed a market in Kyauktaw township in Rakhine State, killing nearly 50 civilians, including Rohingya. Where then will these refugees be returned to? To the killing field? Or will they be housed in internment camps outside Sittwe alongside 120,000 other Rohingya who have been confined there for 14 years? Or will they be left to face the exploitation of trafficking networks and armed groups, including the military, that will forcibly recruit them and send them to die on the front lines?
The plan will fail, while emboldening Min Aung Hlaing and fueling instability, making a lasting solution harder to reach.
Malaysia has offered safety to Myanmar refugees, and those refugees have in turn contributed to Malaysia’s economy. But this is not a permanent solution. Of course, Anwar has an obligation to address the issue, and he is right to pursue diplomatic efforts in that regard.
But if he genuinely wanted to improve the situation and resolve the crisis, rather than reacting to populist pressure, these are a number of diplomatic steps he would take. The first is to work through ASEAN and the U.N. to secure a nationwide ceasefire in Myanmar and uninhibited humanitarian access to all parts of the country, including by defining concrete benchmarks to measure Min Aung Hlaing’s implementation of the Five-Point Consensus.
Second, he should support efforts to hold Min Aung Hlaing and leaders of the military and other armed actors to account for the genocide and decades of grave violations against Rohingya and other civilians across Myanmar. The same principles that Anwar applies to Palestine apply in Myanmar: without an end to impunity, the devastating cycles of violence will not end.
Third, Anwar should develop a diplomatic strategy that responds to the reality of Myanmar’s multiple centers of authority, engages Myanmar’s legitimate authorities and stakeholders, and works toward inclusive dialogue for a genuine political solution.
Fourth, he should lead a coordinated international effort to dismantle the regional human trafficking networks that are flourishing in the conflict, exploiting the most vulnerable and fueling the refugee crisis.
Finally, he needs to consider how a mission of independent international monitors could be stationed in Rakhine State, with a mandate to monitor and report on the protection of civilians, as a means of building confidence towards the eventual sustainable, voluntary, and dignified return of Rohingya and other refugees from Myanmar.
Rohingya and other Myanmar refugees want nothing more than to return safely to our homes. We are not objecting to Anwar’s plans because we want to live the rest of our lives in insecurity and exile; we are objecting because we know it will only make things worse.
And deep down, I believe Anwar knows this too. These are not the actions of the wise and principled leader whose release many human rights activists and I supported. These actions are a dangerous betrayal that bargains away our lives, in the vain hope of short-term political gain.

articles.title: In a Diplomatic Shift, Malaysian PM Hosts Myanmar’s Min Aung Hlaing
articles.full_text:
While the talks focused on the repatriation of refugees, Anwar also appeared to endorse Myanmar’s reintegration into ASEAN.
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim (left) and Myanmar’s President Min Aung Hlaing attend a welcome ceremony at the Perdana Putra Complex in Putrajaya, Malaysia, Oct. 8, 2026.
Malaysia’s Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim met today with Myanmar’s military-appointed leader Min Aung Hlaing, pledging to work for Myanmar’s reintegration with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
Min Aung Hlaing arrived in Myanmar yesterday evening for a two-day visit, part of a campaign of diplomatic outreach aimed at shoring up key diplomatic partnerships normalizing his country’s relationship with the Southeast Asian bloc.
After being granted an official welcome at the Perdana Putra Complex in Putrajaya this morning, Min Aung Hlaing held a one-on-one meeting with Anwar, the Malaysian state news agency Bernama reported. This was followed by a meeting involving senior ministers and officials from both countries. Min Aung Hlaing also spoke to Malaysian business leaders late yesterday, urging them to invest in his country.
In a post on X after the meeting, Anwar said that his half-hour discussion with Min Aung Hlaing “focused on the plight of Myanmar refugees in Malaysia and the prospects for their voluntary, safe and dignified return, regardless of ethnicity.” He added, “I believe direct dialogue and negotiations with President Aung Hlaing and Myanmar’s leadership are essential to securing a lasting resolution.”
Both Anwar and the Malaysian Ministry of Foreign Affairs had previously indicated that this would be a primary point of discussion. The two nations recently agreed to the repatriation of around 5,000 Myanmar nationals currently being held in Malaysian immigration detention centers. The first batch of 1,476 people departed Malaysia via ship on September 29.
Speaking to the press after the meeting, however, Anwar suggested that his engagement with Myanmar extended beyond the refugee issue. Indeed, according to Reuters, he said his government had ongoing concerns about the situation in Myanmar but was willing to respect outstanding differences. He also appeared to endorse the normalization of Myanmar’s relations with ASEAN, , which has excluded Myanmar from its summits since late 2021, for its lack of effort to implement its Five-Point Consensus conflict resolution plan.
“I would say that we and our part in Malaysia, will do whatever is possible to make sure that we enhance this collaboration and ultimately, take ​Myanmar as part of ​our community of ⁠nations, without prejudice, and particularly in the context of ASEAN,” Anwar said. According to Bernama, Anwar also “welcomed Myanmar’s efforts to pursue reforms and policy adjustments aimed at addressing the country’s complex challenges.”
Malaysia is the fifth member state of ASEAN to host Min Aung Hlaing since he took office as president in April, after trips to Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, and Vietnam. It is also the first nation from maritime Southeast Asia to take such a step.
The visit marks a significant diplomatic shift for Malaysia, which had previously been among the ASEAN member states most critical of the military coup of 2021. Speaking last month, Anwar justified the invitation to Min Aung Hlaing on the basis that Malaysia needed an authority to negotiate with on returning Myanmar nationals who he claimed were in Malaysia illegally.
This has become a pressing domestic political issue for Anwar this year, due to the growing public hostility toward Myanmar asylum seekers, particularly Rohingya Muslims. Large numbers of Rohingya have come to the country since 2017, when the Myanmar military launched an ethnic cleansing campaign that pushed more than 740,000 from their homes in Rakhine State into Bangladesh. Around 126,000 Rohingya asylum seekers are currently registered with the U.N. refugee agency in Kuala Lumpur, around half of the agency’s total. Both Anwar and his government have claimed that the refugees have become a financial burden, a security risk, and a source of social discord.
Needless to say, Anwar has drawn heavy criticism both for acquiescing to the repatriation of refugees to a country still wracked by civil war, and for hosting Min Aung Hlaing, whose policies prompted many refugees to flee the country in the first place.
In a statement, the Burmese Rohingya Organization U.K. noted that Min Aung Hlaing is the subject of an international arrest warrant by the Argentine Federal Court for genocide and crimes against humanity allegedly committed against the Rohingya between 2012 and 2017. It urged Anwar to order Myanmar’s arrest on the Argentine warrant, stating that “he belongs on trial, not on a red carpet.”
The Malaysian Foreign Ministry said in a statement yesterday that Anwar’s engagement with Min Aung Hlaing was consistent with the principles of the Five-Point Consensus, and that it followed a decision made by ASEAN at its last summit “to continue constructive and principled engagement with Myanmar.” During bilateral meetings between the Malaysian and Myanmar delegations today, Anwar also said that he emphasized “the importance of inclusive dialogue to realize peace and reconciliation efforts in Myanmar” and expressed Malaysia’s “readiness to facilitate this process towards sustainable peace.”
Interestingly, when Min Aung Hlaing spoke at the joint press conference in Putrajaya, he said that his administration would only take back refugees who were confirmed to have Myanmar citizenship. As Jonathan Head of the BBC noted on X, this effectively rules out most Rohingya, who have been denied citizenship by successive Myanmar governments.
While this is in some ways good news – civil society groups have expressed concern that any Rohingya returned to the country could be confined to ghettos in Rakhine State or conscripted into the military – it does raise the question of whether Anwar’s outreach to Min Aung Hlaing, and the reorientation of Malaysia’s policy toward Myanmar, will address its stated domestic political purpose.
In any event, the fact that Malaysia, previously the ASEAN state that was most outspoken about Myanmar, has accorded de facto recognition to Min Aung Hlaing’s quasi-civilian government suggests that full normalization with the bloc is likely just a matter of time.

articles.title: How Indonesians Are Being Recruited Into the Russian Army
articles.full_text:
So far, Jakarta is yet to come to grips with problem that has arisen alongside President Prabowo Subianto’s efforts to build a closer relationship with Russia.
A building in Borodyanka in Ukraine, destroyed during the Russian occupation of the region around Kyiv, Apr. 8, 2022.
On September 18, Indonesia’s ambassador to Russia, Jose Tavares, told the state news agency Antara that his embassy had taken dozens of calls from families who believed their relatives had been recruited into Russia’s army by agents on social media promising large salaries. Jakarta has so far dealt with these cases one by one, in line with standard consular procedures. On September 19, the Indonesian embassy sent a note verbale, a formal diplomatic letter, asking the Russian Foreign Ministry to verify the names, and bring home those who failed Russia’s medical examination. Arrmanatha Nasir, the career diplomat who was sworn in as foreign minister on October 1, has inherited that approach.
However, the current approach is ill-equipped to handle a problem that has arisen alongside President Prabowo Subianto’s efforts to build a close relationship with Vladimir Putin’s Russia. Indonesian institutions have been promoting Russia as a labor destination, including in a special economic zone that assembles attack drones, even as they warn their citizens against the job offers that might lead to the frontlines in Ukraine. Meanwhile, Jakarta counts the personal closeness between Prabowo and Putin as an asset, yet it has made no public use of that closeness to aid the citizens caught in this recruitment trap.
Most of the public record on these cases comes either from one of the warring parties or from the recruits and their families. Ukraine’s foreign intelligence service said on August 27 that it had documents on at least eight Indonesians who were recruited into Russia’s army. However, Kompas noted that the documents are Russian e-visa notices, while Russia’s embassy in Jakarta called the release a disinformation campaign. Meanwhile, a man who told Republika that he was among those named said that an agent had promised him a security job and then pushed him into a military contract, although he had failed his medical examination in Moscow. He was in hospital when he spoke to the newspaper, after a Ukrainian drone had taken one of his fingers. In Natuna, the parents of a 30-year-old man said that a comrade had reported him killed by a Ukrainian drone on September 20, which the regent of Natuna still called uncertain and unclear 10 days later.
The cases point to three problems, the first of which is that recruitment follows the logic of labor migration long before it turns into military service. Hartyo Harkomoyo, Indonesia’s deputy ambassador in Moscow, told RRI that most recruits are promised civilian jobs, some of them as drivers, builders, cooks, or nurses under Russia’s Defense Ministry. Some are recruited from Indonesia through social media, and others from among Indonesians already in Russia, especially students. A content creator from Central Java told Republika that a Russian contact on social media had offered him a post in a government ministry or a large company and paid for his flight and his e-visa. The contract he was handed in Moscow was a military one, written in Russian, which he could not read. An Indonesian man filmed by Ukrainian soldiers after his capture in early September said he had been working as a cleaner when he was put into uniform and sent to the front.
The case of the man from Natuna shows the same path from a civilian job to the frontline. According to his family, the young man had worked as an electrician in the Philippines before going to Russia with seven other Indonesians. He believed he had been hired to deliver food to the troops. The head of his neighborhood said that he refused a transfer to a combat unit because it was not in his contract. He could not leave because his passport was being held. And yet, the migrant-worker protection office in his province found no record of him as a registered worker.
The second problem concerns the fact that Indonesian institutions themselves opened a formal labor channel to Russia this year. In January, the Ministry for the Protection of Migrant Workers (KP2MI) welcomed a plan by the aluminum producer RUSAL to take 50 vocational-school graduates, with departures scheduled for September. They presented it as part of Prabowo’s “SMK Go Global” program. A month later, KP2MI named Russia a new placement destination in manufacturing and shipbuilding. It also said it had received a draft Memorandum of Understanding from Russia’s Federal Service for Labor and Employment. In the same meeting, the deputy minister received a warning from the defense attaché in Moscow that Indonesians should beware of well-paid job advertisements for private military companies, suggesting that the Ministry knew of the risk from the start.
The West Java provincial labor office went further in June, when its one-stop service for migrant workers advertised jobs for women aged 18 to 24 in Russia’s Alabuga Special Economic Zone, with salary in dollars and a flight paid by the employer. The United States Treasury sanctioned the company that runs the zone in February 2024 for producing Iranian-designed Geran-2 attack drones under a contract with Russia’s military. An Associated Press investigation found that young African women recruited there, with offers of work in hospitality and catering, ended up assembling drones. The West Java advertisement, now marked closed, names no employer and gives no number of applicants or departures. No documented recruit is known to have left through these channels. Their effect is to present Russia, including the defense industry, as an ordinary destination for Indonesian workers.
In July, Indonesia’s embassy in Moscow warned Indonesians against taking job offers on tourist visas and signing contracts in a language they could not read. The warning did not mention military service, and a month later the embassy’s own job fair for Indonesians in Russia, held on August 17, listed Alabuga SEZ among the employers, beside RUSAL, En+ Group, and Rusagro. The ambassador presented the fair as a way to widen Indonesians’ chances to work and build careers in Russia. Indonesia’s national placement system still listed 76 places in Russia on October 1. Among them, 60 places are for fishery workers whose placement permits were issued on September 1.
The third problem is that Jakarta’s response to these recruitment traps has treated the issue as a series of separate cases. The Foreign Ministry’s spokesperson said on September 18 that the government would look into claims of fraud and exploitation, protect any Indonesians found to be victims, and prosecute recruiters. She added that any verified service in a foreign army would be seen as an individual act that does not represent the policy of the Indonesian government. Tavares described the embassy’s note verbale to the Russian Foreign Ministry as a request for verification and clarification. Meanwhile, KP2MI’s deputy minister, Christina Aryani, said the recruits had been lured by advertisements and declined to treat the cases as trafficking without proof of exploitation, thereby leaving any kind of repatriation for the Foreign Ministry to negotiate. Moreover, as of press time, the ministry’s online travel advisory for Russia still said nothing about recruitment.
I would suggest that the reason for this restraint lies in the relationship itself. Prabowo has met Putin five times since taking office, and in Vladivostok last month, he offered Indonesia to Russian businesses as a natural entry point to ASEAN. A government that has invested this much in the relationship at the presidential level is unlikely to seek a public quarrel with Moscow over a few dozen citizens. Therefore, it treats each case as a matter of individual choice and consular care. Friction between KP2MI and the Foreign Ministry, visible in Aryani’s remarks, explains why the cases pass between agencies, but not why no one has raised them with Moscow at the political level. The cost of that restraint falls on the men themselves, because Moscow has little reason to act on the cases of a partner that has not raised them at the political level publicly.

Jakarta should also bring its own labor channels into line with its warnings. Until Russian employers can be checked, KP2MI and the provincial labor offices should stop placing Indonesians with firms tied to Russia’s defense industry, beginning with the Alabuga SEZ. The cost would be small, since the national placement system lists more than 2,200 places in Slovakia and more than 1,400 in Poland, against 76 in Russia.
Indonesia’s warnings also need to reach the people whom the recruiters already reach on social media. The Foreign Ministry and KP2MI could run Indonesian-language warnings on the same platforms where the advertisements appear. The Communications Ministry could also ask Meta to enforce its own ban. Colombia offers a working model, since its Foreign Ministry has added an awareness campaign to a screening protocol in its passport offices for applicants who say they intend to fight abroad.
Lastly, Indonesia need not act alone, since other states in the region face similar recruitment challenges. Indonesia, the Philippines, and Cambodia could take the matter up together in ASEAN, which would raise the political cost to Moscow of recruiting in Southeast Asia.

Treating them as a series of individual cases narrows it in the same way, because it leaves the routes that brought them to Russia intact. articles.title: From Military Base to Pax Silica: Clark and Capas in Philippine History
articles.full_text:
The history of U.S. involvement in the region demonstrates how domestic political dynamics can get entangled with regional and global geopolitics.
New Clark City in the Philippines is in the news for being the site of the planned industrial hub of the Luzon Economic Corridor under the United States-led Pax Silica coalition. It is part of the Clark special economic zone and also covers the municipalities of Capas and Bamban in the province of Tarlac. The history of this place can help us better understand the political narratives in favor of and opposed to Pax Silica.
As the colonial ruler of the Philippines in the first half of the 20th century, the U.S. established an air base in Angeles in the province of Pampanga in the central part of Luzon, the country’s biggest island. After the end of World War II, the Philippines became an independent republic but the U.S. maintained the Clark base in Pampanga. It soon became the largest overseas U.S. military camp and a crucial hub during the Cold War era. In 1991, Clark was turned over to the Philippine government after the Senate rejection of the U.S. bases treaty. It was converted into a commercial area and designated a special economic zone to attract investments.
Today, Clark is a strategic business center since it is only less than a two-hour drive from the capital region of Metro Manila. Its international airport is already one of the country’s busiest aviation terminals.
Meanwhile, Capas is outside of Clark but it used to host Camp O’Donnell, an American military reservation. Thousands of prisoners during World War II died in a “death march” from Mariveles in Bataan to Capas. The communist-led New People’s Army was also established in this rural municipality in 1969.
Parts of Capas were incorporated into the New Clark City, which was originally envisioned as a government center and alternative capital to decongest Metro Manila. Sports facilities were built here when the country hosted the Southeast Asian Games in 2019. The stadium cauldron was reported to be overpriced, which implicated key allies of former President Rodrigo Duterte.
The pandemic affected the development of New Clark City and there has been no substantial discussion about the earlier plan to build a new capital in the area.
It generated attention again when it was named as a possible location of the Luzon Economic Corridor, a trilateral initiative unveiled in 2024 between the Philippines, the U.S., and Japan. This was confirmed last April after the Philippines officially joined the Pax Silica coalition.
In several social media posts, U.S. Undersecretary of State Jacob Helberg stated that the hub will be a “forward deployed industrial base” aimed at securing vital supply-chain inputs for American companies and its allies.
“Four thousand acres. Roughly one-third the size of Manhattan – the equivalent of everything from Times Square south to the very tip of the island,” Helberg added, referring to the land “gifted” by the Philippine government for the Pax Silica project.
After this, concerns were raised about the project’s potential grave impact on energy and water resources in the provinces of Pampanga and Tarlac. Farmers and indigenous peoples said their communities have been threatened with eviction to give way for the rise of the industrial hub.
In response, authorities said data centers will not be a component of the Pax Silica site, although these facilities will still rise in other parts of Luzon. They also assured local communities that consultations will be conducted, even if they initially denied that there were residents in the project site.
The Philippine government also assured the public that the country’s laws will prevail and no immunity will be granted to foreign investors in the hub. Nevertheless, concerns persist about the role of Pax Silica in supporting the military operations of the U.S. in the country and in the Asia-Pacific. What is clear is that it is seen as a counterpart to the China-led World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization.
Negotiations are ongoing and expected to continue for the next two years. A framework deal could be signed next month during the summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, and it could be the highlight of U.S. President Donald Trump’s visit to Manila.
Pax Silica is more than just a real estate transaction since it is touted as the next big opportunity for the Philippines to promote industrial development through mineral processing and technology transfer. The history of Clark and Capas is a reminder that local political dynamics can get entangled with regional and global geopolitical issues. The Pax Silica hub will rise on a land that hosted foreign bases, military operations that led to war atrocities, and protests that represented the Filipino people’s assertion of sovereignty.
As the Philippines under the government of Ferdinand Marcos Jr rushes forward with this bold initiative, the challenge is to address the criticism that this is another unfair deal that favors the country’s former colonizers rather than a development blueprint that prioritizes the national interest.

articles.title: Trade Agreement With US Close to Completion, Thai Prime Minister Says
articles.full_text:
Anutin Charnvirakul said that he expected to sign the Agreement on ⁠Reciprocal Trade during President Donald Trump’s next visit to Asia.
Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul addresses a meeting on the economic impacts of the Iran war in Bangkok, Thailand, Mar. 2, 2026.
Trade negotiations between Thailand and the United States are in the final stages and an agreement is expected to be signed as soon as next month, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said yesterday.
Speaking at a forum ​in Singapore, Anutin said negotiations on the Agreement on ⁠Reciprocal Trade (ART) are now on “the last ​paragraph” and that he ​expected to sign the final agreement during U.S. President Donald Trump’s next visit to Asia, Reuters reported. This could take place during the ASEAN Summit in the Philippines on November 16–18, which Trump has confirmed he is attending, or the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meetings in Shenzhen on November 18–19. Trump’s attendance at the latter summit has not yet been confirmed.
Anutin said that he received a ​letter from the U.S. president last week ​confirming the deal is at its final stage. “He ‌told ⁠me that I was to make sure that my people and the United States Trade Representative would write ​up the ​final clause,” the Thai leader said.
The U.S. is Thailand’s largest export market, and the country’s imports of Thai goods totaled $91.3 billion in 2025, according to U.S. government figures.
Bangkok and Washington have been negotiating a “reciprocal” trade deal with the U.S. since Trump’s initial “liberation day” tariff day announcement in April 2025, which hit Thailand with a 36 percent tariff.
In October 2025, the U.S. and Thailand announced a “framework” for an agreement on reciprocal trade, which reduced the tariff to 19 percent in exchange for a Thai pledge to “eliminate tariff barriers on approximately 99 percent of goods, covering a full range of U.S. industrial and food and agricultural products.” Under the framework, Thailand also promised to purchase more American energy, agricultural products and aircraft in order to close its $71.7 billion goods trade surplus with the U.S.
However, the negotiation of a final agreement has been complicated and delayed by recent shifts in U.S. tariff policy. In February, the U.S. Supreme Court struck down the “liberation day” tariff regime.
As a workaround, Trump imposed a temporary 10 percent global tariff under Section 122 of the Trade Act, which expired in July. The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) also used Section 301 of the U.S. Trade Act of 1974, which allows Washington to investigate and impose tariffs on foreign countries for unfair trade practices. In March, it initiated two separate investigations, one examining 60 nations’ alleged failures to take action on forced labor, and another examining excess industrial capacity on the part of 16 major trading ​partners.
Thailand was a target of both investigations, and in June, it was hit with a 12.5 percent tariff in the forced labor probe. The USTR has also accused Thailand of maintaining a “structural overcapacity” in three sectors – automotive and parts, machinery, and rubber products – although this investigation has not yet been concluded.
The Commerce Ministry says Thailand and the U.S. have already agreed on the main substance and principles of the ART, leaving technical teams to settle remaining details and legal wording. Thailand’s aim, according to The Nation, “is to keep the eventual overall tariff burden around the previous 19 percent benchmark, or at least no higher than that faced by regional competitors.”
The finalization of the ART would undoubtedly be a positive development for the U.S.-Thailand relationship, which has not been helped by the drawn-out negotiations. In August, Bloomberg reported that Thailand was going so far as to consider using military cooperation as leverage in the trade talks. According to its report, which quoted an unnamed Thai official, Bangkok was preparing to warn the Trump administration that steep U.S. tariffs might force it to scale back military cooperation, including the Cobra Gold exercises that have been a cornerstone of the U.S.-Thailand alliance since the 1980s.
Thailand’s government denied the reports.

However, the negotiation of a final agreement has been complicated and delayed by recent shifts in U.S. tariff policy. In February, the U.S. Supreme Court struck down the “liberation day” tariff regime.
As a workaround, Trump imposed a temporary 10 percent global tariff under Section 122 of the Trade Act, which expired in July. The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) also used Section 301 of the U.S. Trade Act of 1974, which allows Washington to investigate and impose tariffs on foreign countries for unfair trade practices. In March, it initiated two separate investigations, one examining 60 nations’ alleged failures to take action on forced labor, and another examining excess industrial capacity on the part of 16 major trading ​partners.
Thailand was a target of both investigations, and in June, it was hit with a 12.5 percent tariff in the forced labor probe. The USTR has also accused Thailand of maintaining a “structural overcapacity” in three sectors – automotive and parts, machinery, and rubber products – although this investigation has not yet been concluded.
The Commerce Ministry says Thailand and the U.S. have already agreed on the main substance and principles of the ART, leaving technical teams to settle remaining details and legal wording. Thailand’s aim, according to The Nation, “is to keep the eventual overall tariff burden around the previous 19 percent benchmark, or at least no higher than that faced by regional competitors.”
The finalization of the ART would undoubtedly be a positive development for the U.S.-Thailand relationship, which has not been helped by the drawn-out negotiations. In August, Bloomberg reported that Thailand was going so far as to consider using military cooperation as leverage in the trade talks. According to its report, which quoted an unnamed Thai official, Bangkok was preparing to warn the Trump administration that steep U.S. tariffs might force it to scale back military cooperation, including the Cobra Gold exercises that have been a cornerstone of the U.S.-Thailand alliance since the 1980s.
Thailand’s government denied the reports.
Trade negotiations between Thailand and the United States are in the final stages and an agreement is expected to be signed as soon as next month, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said yesterday.
Speaking at a forum ​in Singapore, Anutin said negotiations on the Agreement on ⁠Reciprocal Trade (ART) are now on “the last ​paragraph” and that he ​expected to sign the final agreement during U.S. President Donald Trump’s next visit to Asia, Reuters reported. This could take place during the ASEAN Summit in the Philippines on November 16–18, which Trump has confirmed he is attending, or the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meetings in Shenzhen on November 18–19. Trump’s attendance at the latter summit has not yet been confirmed.
Sebastian Strangio is Southeast Asia editor at The Diplomat.
articles.summary: Anutin Charnvirakul said that he expected to sign the Agreement on ⁠Reciprocal Trade during President Donald Trump's next visit to Asia.

articles.title: The Lessons the Taliban Have Learned
articles.full_text:
Afghanistan’s leaders haven’t changed ideologically. But five years after returning to power, they have learnt from where the “first emirate” went wrong.
A Taliban checkpoint in Balkh province, Afghanistan.
In the female section of an upscale restaurant in Kabul’s Shar-e Naw, a waiter brings me a menu and a form. Only two lines are filled in: one bears an Italian name, the other a local one. The waiter explains that guests are required to fill it in at the request of the Ministry of Interior. It is for the guests’ own safety, he emphasizes, slightly uneasy. It is hard to tell if he believes it.
I look at the form. It asks for the guest’s name, date of birth, passport number, address in Kabul, as well as when they visited the restaurant. 
“It is for your security,” the waiter repeats. I give him the blank form back. “I feel secure without it,” I say. He doesn’t insist. He takes my order and disappears.
Five years after the withdrawal of NATO troops from Afghanistan, and into the rule of the Taliban, the group’s control over the country is stable. While the Taliban might not have access to the newest surveillance technologies, their infiltration of local communities is high. They had learned their lesson from their first period of rule, the emirate that ended in 2001 with the U.S. invasion, a United Nations official tells me.
“You can say that fundamentally, ideologically, they haven’t really changed. But in terms of control, consolidation, management, messaging, they are far more sophisticated now,” he says. “The first emirate was a brand new experiment. The second emirate is still an experiment, but they have learned a lot of lessons. They are smart.”
Kabul still reminds me of its former self, as if time had stopped. The streets are bustling with life; street vendors cover the pavements, selling products ranging from food and cigarettes to clothes and electronics. The new regime is seen in the details: fewer women walk the streets, less rubbish lies scattered across the city center – a lasting feature of the corrupt rule back in the Republic days – and the streets seem less chaotic. But at first glance, the changes are small, sometimes imperceptible.
Everyone I speak with says that the country has become safer. Twenty years of war and decades of fighting have taken their toll on people. The Taliban, while brutal and devoted to anti-modern ideas, has nevertheless brought peace. The paradox is that the Taliban were the main perpetrators of violence during the Republic days. It was due to their attacks on cars that traveling between provinces used to be dangerous and caution was advised. Since they took power, traveling between different regions of Afghanistan has suddenly become possible.
Now, Taliban checkpoints cover the whole country. Some of them are stricter, with soldiers standing under the white flag bearing the Shahada, the Islamic declaration of faith, and the Taliban symbol, checking travel permits meticulously. Other checkpoints are more relaxed, and it is enough to slow down and let the Taliban gaze into the car.
There are few roads that the group does not control. To leave their place of residence, drivers need special permits, and so do tourists. A letter from “Afghan Tour,” a unit responsible for travelers, is required to travel and stay in another province. It is unclear what its purpose is, other than surveillance.
In Kabul, the “Afghan Tour” official says that getting a travel letter requires paying for an expensive tour. But it is possible to get it in Bamyan, another province, for a small fee. Most other regions also issue such letters in exchange for booking an inexpensive “tour” with an official guide. It is unclear if its price is official or simply a bribe paid for obtaining the letter. It is also hard to call it a tour.
As part of the “tour” I book to stay in Mazar-i-Sharif, the local guide shows me into the Blue Mosque, the shrine of Imam Ali, first built in the 12th century before Genghis Khan leveled the original building to the ground. But the tour included little in terms of a history lesson. The guide complained about his low earnings, suggesting I pay extra for his time. Then he demanded that I share my local contacts with him. For my own safety, of course.
Today the new Taliban administration is stable. Ministries work, and courts solve disputes without the need to pay bribes, I am told. 96 percent of the poppy fields have been eradicated and hundreds of addicts who formerly squatted on Kabul’s streets and under bridges have been forced into rehabs. This is the kind of “stability” I know all too well from Central Asia’s autocracies, Afghanistan’s neighbors: they are brutal and relentless, but the pavements are clean.
According to a recent report from Human Rights Watch, censorship of local media outlets and restrictions on freedom of expression have intensified, while journalists, activists, academics and other regime critics have faced repression, torture, and arbitrary arrests. 
“The Taliban always accuse us of being spies, it’s hard to work these days,” one local photojournalist told me.
Women have been denied basic rights, such as the right to education beyond sixth grade. A woman visiting her parental home who does not return to her husband can be deemed a criminal. That includes survivors of domestic violence. A woman accused of touching, shaking hands with, or hugging a man who is not her mahram, a close male relative with whom marriage is prohibited, can spend a year in prison. Two months if a girl or a boy is seen dancing.
A new “Preachers’ law” defines Muslims as followers of the Hanafi school of Islam. Local Hazaras, or Ismaili minority groups, are now officially deemed heretics. 
“Many Ismailis now hide their faith,” one man from the community tells me. He lost his job in a school in Badakhshan due to his faith.
All that in the name of the “peaceful and clear sky above us,” as Uzbekistan’s late President Islam Karimov used to say in justifying his own repressive rule. 
Except that this is not the reality for most Afghans. 
While the war might be over – except for skirmishes in Badakhshan province and regular attacks from Pakistan – Afghanistan is hardly facing a post-war recovery. The withdrawal of U.S. and NATO troops and the coming to power of the Taliban, a government recognized only by Russia, meant that the United Nations mandate became much more restricted in scope. Cooperation with the de facto Taliban authorities has focused mostly on securing people’s very basic needs.
Most international non-governmental and governmental organizations, and media, have left, and with them hundreds of local jobs disappeared. The biggest difference is noticeable in large cities: Kabul, Herat, or Mazar-i-Sharif, where previously educated, English-speaking men and women could find employment and develop careers. As another local journalist told me, during the Republic days he could support his family working as a photographer and videographer. Now, work is scarce. He has not had any projects for several months.
“The situation seems to get worse every day and every year. Unemployment has reached a very high level, especially for people like me who work in the arts and creative fields,” he says. “People of Afghanistan are facing many other serious problems, including unemployment, untreated illnesses, hunger, poverty, and lack of adequate shelter. I do not see a clear government plan to address unemployment at its roots.”
According to the United Nations, more than 17 million people, or 40 percent of Afghanistan’s population, are projected to face acute food insecurity. And the situation is worsening. While following the U.S. withdrawal, thousands of Afghans left the country in search of a better life, this trend is now reversing – though not voluntarily.
Over the last few years, Iran and Pakistan have forced millions of Afghans to return home. Even the European Union, including Germany, a country with the largest Afghan population in the region, began to deport people back despite fears of torture and imprisonment upon arrival. This has put a massive strain on the already impoverished nation with very limited resources. As the U.N. official told me, at the time of 9/11, in 2001, Afghanistan’s population was around 20 million. By the time of the return of the Taliban, twenty years later, it had doubled. Over the last five years of the second emirate, the population has grown by 5 million, and currently totals around 45 million.
“There has been almost triple pressure on resources, on communities, on infrastructure and humanitarian needs. And development hasn’t kept up. People are coming back to a country and to communities that are not equipped to sustain them,” the U.N. contact told me. “Even though we see economic growth, it’s not keeping up with population growth. And then on top of that a lot of people are coming back to urban areas, which is putting even more pressure on urban systems.”
In other words, over the past five years the population grew by 12.6 percent, while at the same time, the amount of skilled work opportunities fell amid the withdrawal of the West. Women have been banned from a number of professions, which pushed many families into even deeper poverty. While traditionally conservative and impoverished rural areas have not seen much change, cities, where women were more emancipated under the Republic, have experienced the greater shifts.
In Kabul, I meet with several young women, the friends and family members of my girlfriends who have long left the country. They are a lost generation. Unable to study beyond sixth grade, unable to follow their passions and have careers, they often live online. Some learn English, others open small businesses selling handmade accessories on Instagram, one of the few avenues left for Afghan women to make a living. But pressure is high.
A friend hosted a get-together for women in a female section of a Kabul restaurant. She was summoned by the Taliban. The meeting was deemed suspicious. She still hasn’t told her parents and brothers about the interrogation. That would mean she would not be allowed to leave the house on her own. For her own safety. My friend is a brave, educated woman with good English. She wants to work and develop new skills, something that the local government sees as sinful. Her very existence is a threat to the system.

articles.title: China’s High-Tech Ambitions Have a Blue-Collar Status Problem
articles.full_text:
Most Chinese still view vocational schools and skilled labor as low status and undesirable.
As China celebrated its dominance at the Asian Games that concluded days ago in Nagoya, Japan, its achievement at another global sporting festival in Shanghai has been largely overlooked. In the 2026 edition of WorldSkills, what the organizers call an Olympics for vocational skills, the Chinese team topped the medal table with 41 gold, 11 silver, and 4 bronze medals. In fact, the Chinese team has topped the medal table five straight times in the biennial competition, a phenomenon that has been attributed to the country’s unparalleled investments in providing systematic coaching and training for athletes in the same way it does for the regular Olympics.
Beyond simply winning medals, the Chinese authorities felt the need to drum up public interest in the competition. Local and national media, and even governments, covered WorldSkills extensively while it largely went unnoticed in other countries. Given that whatever prestige that China earns from WorldSkills is largely geared toward a domestic audience rather than an international one, it begs the question of why China would even bother with prompting something that leads to little gain in global stature. 
The answer to the question may be found in a February 2026 announcement from the Chinese Ministry of Education (MoE) suggesting vocational school reforms. The document criticized the current system’s lack of connection between education and employers, producing few skilled industrial workers essential for driving China’s next generation of high-tech manufacturing. 
China’s 2026-2030 Five-Year Plan emphasized that manufacturing remains central in ensuring the technological self-sufficiency underlying long-term economic growth and safeguarding national security. The MoE implied that the country’s vocational schools, without reforms, would be incapable of producing the human resources needed to achieve that goal.
But for vocational schools to urgently produce talent for high-tech manufacturing, they need more than just an appropriate curriculum. They also need the best raw talent that China has to offer. Here is where vocational schools fall short. 
China’s university enrollment increased from 1 million in 1999 to 9.6 million in 2020. The country’s brightest increasingly aspire to join the ranks of what used to be a tiny segment of the intellectual elite signaled by a university diploma. The expanding path toward college education has cemented a social hierarchy in which a bachelor’s degree followed by white-collar work is seen as more desirable than a vocational one followed by a career in manual labor, no matter how technically sophisticated. 
That norm of high-education aspirations is most clearly seen in study abroad. My primary job as a college admissions consultant leads me to interact with hundreds of Chinese families who are first and foremost attracted to higher-ranked institutions with well-recognized names. In choosing between the likes of the American Ivy Leagues and the British Oxbridge, they care less about what practical skills they can acquire, but whether the degrees indicate a highly competitive environment, and by proxy, the intelligence of successful applicants. Despite much cheaper costs and clear paths for employment, very few indicate interest in English-language higher-education programs in Germany and other European countries anchored by technical apprenticeships.
It is this cultural norm that the MoE must fight against as it seeks to overhaul the vocational school system in China. The proposed collaboration with major manufacturers will help. In a slowing economy, many applicants may be interested in blue-collar work with the likes of Huawei and Xiaomi, rather than a bachelor’s degree that comes with unemployment afterwards. But without changing the cultural norms of seeing technical education as “lower” than the university one, vocational schools in China, no matter how reformed, can still only attract those who are not afraid to be seen as desperate and obtuse enough to work on the factory floor.
Hence the glowing coverage of WorldSkills. The prestige of China’s medalists is about bringing pride not just to the country, but to their professions. And to further bestow status, China is turning hundreds of vocational schools into diploma-granting colleges, slapping bachelor’s degrees on vocational training. If better prospects for jobs do not bring brighter talent into technical education, the hope is that erasing the difference in visual appearance between universities and vocational schools can break down the hierarchical thinking.
It remains to be seen whether China’s dwindling ranks of youngsters will be sufficiently lured by the more attractive job prospects offered by manufacturing. As Chinese firms wow domestic and foreign audiences with fully automated dark factories, the image of grittiness associated with manufacturing is being chipped away. But will that overcome an ingrained educational culture that sees the work of the brain as higher in social status as that of the hand, even if the hand is increasingly replaced by robotics? It will depend on whether the Chinese mentality will evolve as fast as the country’s approach to industrial policies and technologies.

articles.title: The Quiet, Careful Growth of Philippines-Taiwan Ties
articles.full_text:
Manila is exploiting the space between its One China policy and functional cooperation with Taipei.
On October 2, the Philippine Coast Guard commissioned BRP Sarangani, a retired Taiwanese Coast Guard cutter formerly known as the Kinmen. The transfer is unusual because Taiwan only transfers decommissioned vessels to states that officially recognize Taiwan’s statehood, which the Philippines does not. 
Furthermore, the vessel did not sail from Kaohsiung to Manila under the Taiwanese flag, government-to-government, the way Taipei’s other patrol-vessel donations have gone to Palau, the Marshall Islands and Tuvalu – states that recognize the Republic of China (Taiwan). Instead, the Philippine nongovernmental organization We Protect Our Seas (WPS) Foundation quietly acquired the Kinmen, renamed it, repainted it, and handed it to the Philippine Coast Guard in a ceremony that never mentioned where the ship had come from.
The reason for this indirect approach is obvious: the Philippines adheres to the One China policy and would not like to provoke China. Unofficial engagements with Taiwan, carried out by states like the United States, France, Singapore, the United Kingdom, and Germany that formally recognize China, are a global default. China explicitly tolerates their economic and cultural relations with Taiwan. 
So what makes the Philippines’ engagement with Taiwan different, and why is Manila engaging with Taiwan so extensively now when its relationship with China is tenser than in the past two decades? 
For most of the above-mentioned states, Taiwan policy is about standing up for democracy and alliance management, conducted at a safe distance – being geographically far away from the immediate threat of military conflict with China. However, the Philippines is in close proximity to Taiwan. The Philippine province of Batanes lies south of Taiwan, near the Bashi Channel, placing it closer to spillover from the Taiwan conflict. 
Adding to this are 200,000 Filipino workers currently in Taiwan, whose evacuation during a Taiwan crisis would pose an emergency for the Philippine government. Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has publicly stated that Taiwan’s security is inseparable from the Philippines’ own, making clear that Taiwan is a national security question rather than an elective foreign policy stance.
Yet Manila must tread carefully. Anything it does with Taiwan that upsets China is directly visible in Chinese assertiveness in the South China Sea, affecting Filipino sovereignty and fisheries. 
The Philippines’ increased engagement with Taiwan predates the Marcos administration. Taiwan is the Philippines’ ninth-largest trading partner, with established cooperation in education, agriculture, and healthcare and growing interest in semiconductors and start-ups. Under Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte (in office from 2016-2022), the Philippines and Taiwan signed a bilateral investment agreement in 2017 – the first major investment agreement in the last 25 years – under Taiwan’s New Southbound Policy, with cooperation extending across trade, investment, education, and labor mobility. But this engagement made sense given that the Philippines was in a state of rapprochement with China. 
What has changed now is the strategic significance of Philippines-Taiwan engagement. Economic and cultural ties are increasingly accompanied by institutional and maritime cooperation. In April 2025, the Philippines eased restrictions on official exchanges with Taiwan, facilitating travel for economic and trade-related purposes. This was highlighted by Taiwanese Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung’s visit to Manila, the second such foreign minister visit to the Philippines since 1975. Taiwan’s subsequent proposal to open a second representative office in Cebu to deepen the “Taiwan-Philippine Corridor” further signaled an effort to deepen institutional engagement. 
Maritime cooperation has become increasingly apparent. What began as crisis management following the 2013 killing of a Taiwanese fisherman by Philippine personnel has created a basis for maritime cooperation, despite the absence of diplomatic recognition. 
The WPS Foundation confirmed that the recently transferred vessel, BRP Sarangani, will support maritime patrols, search and rescue, humanitarian assistance, disaster response, and training. The transfer of vessels between two coast guards without requiring an overt government-to-government transaction demonstrates how institutional informality can create political space for cooperation that formal diplomatic relations might otherwise constrain.  
Last year, the Philippine and Taiwanese Coast Guard conducted patrols in the Bashi Channel. Taiwan’s Coast Guard is also planning to send vessels to visit the Philippines in 2027, the first visit since the Philippines switched its recognition from the ROC to the People’s Republic of China in 1975.
But why is the Philippines doing this now, when China has become more assertive? One plausible explanation is that the Philippines sees little benefit in restraining its engagement with Taiwan. Chinese pressure in the South China Sea continued despite Manila’s previously cautious approach to Taiwan, giving Philippine policymakers fewer reasons to believe that restraint will win China’s goodwill. 
At the same time, the Philippines cannot match China militarily or economically. Deepening ties with Taiwan offer the Philippines a way to widen its strategic and economic options at a relatively low cost. Manila can strengthen cooperation with a partner that provides investment, technology, and security benefits, while also engaging with an issue that China considers highly sensitive. Whether this amounts to deliberate tit-for-tat is difficult to establish, but the effect is clear: the Philippines has less incentive than before to keep its Taiwan relationship within narrow limits simply to avoid displeasing China. 
While the Philippines has steadily expanded its engagement with Taiwan, it has stopped short of turning that engagement into overt alignment, as seen in the vessel transfer through a non-governmental organization and the Philippine government’s refusal to publicly recognize it as a formerly Taiwanese vessel. Manila has repeatedly affirmed that its One China policy remains “consistent, clear and unchanged” and that “economic, cultural, and functional cooperation with Taiwan” does not violate it. This caution reflects Manila’s awareness that spillover from a Taiwan crisis would be unavoidable. articles.summary: Manila is exploiting the space between its One China policy and functional cooperation with Taipei.

articles.title: The Strategic Implications of China’s Military Facility in Laos
articles.full_text:
Ban Keun poses only a limited direct threat to the South China Sea or Taiwan, but it will enhance China’s ability to place pressure on U.S. naval forces.
A PLA Air Force J-10 fighter takes part in the 2021 International Army Games.
China inaugurated an air force support and training center in Laos on September 29, marking China’s third overseas military facility. Analysts have noted that the arrangement could expand the People’s Liberation Army’s military presence in Southeast Asia and strengthen China’s regional interests, although there is currently no evidence that Beijing has deployed large-scale forces at the site.
According to China’s Ministry of National Defense, the China-Laos Joint Support and Training Center and the China-Laos Friendship Aviation Academy have formally begun operations at Ban Keun Airport. The two facilities are mainly intended to assist in the training of Lao Air Force pilots and will be jointly maintained and operated by China and Laos. Beijing has not disclosed details regarding the number of Chinese personnel or the equipment stationed there.
China has emphasized that the facilities comply with the laws of both countries and with international law, and that they are “not directed against any third party.”
Ban Keun Airport is significant because it is China’s first publicly acknowledged overseas military facility centered on airpower. This differs from China’s overseas facilities in Djibouti and Cambodia, which have largely been associated with naval operations.
China’s continued use of the “joint training center” model – also used in Cambodia – suggests that the PLA may be pursuing a gradual approach to expanding its overseas military presence. Ban Keun Airport may initially operate as a jointly used China-Laos facility, while allowing the Chinese presence to increase over time.
Geographically, Ban Keun Airport is located in Vientiane Province in northwestern Laos, around 45 kilometers from the capital, Vientiane. During the Vietnam War and the Laotian Civil War in the 1970s, the area had been part of the local airfield network used for tactical support operations, but it later ceased operations.
Satellite imagery suggests that construction work began around October last year, and by September this year the facility had already reached a considerable scale. Its longest runway is approximately 2,000 meters. From a geographic perspective, Ban Keun occupies an important location near the center of mainland Southeast Asia. It is also close to the China-Laos Railway, just north of Vientiane, giving the site convenient transportation access. This means that personnel and equipment sent from China would not necessarily have to rely solely on air transport. The China-Laos Railway could also be used to move personnel and certain equipment into Laos. For an overseas joint support base, this logistical advantage is highly significant.
A similar consideration may also apply to China’s other joint support facility in mainland Southeast Asia, at Ream in Cambodia. To a considerable extent, the future possibility of railway links extending directly into southern Cambodia may also enhance the logistical value of such a facility.
From the perspective of operational radius, however, Ban Keun Airport is unlikely to be primarily intended for operations in the South China Sea. China already has military facilities on Woody Island that can serve as forward bases for power projection in the area.
The greater significance of Ban Keun lies in its potential role as a transit base for the PLA Air Force. From this location, Chinese forces would have a certain level of operational reach toward Myanmar and farther south toward Singapore. For this reason, outside observers may view the airport’s most important function as providing the PLA Air Force with an additional staging and transit airfield for operations in Southeast Asia.
For the same reason, although Ban Keun currently poses only a limited direct threat to Taiwan Strait security, it still has significance for China’s broader ability to project military power abroad and to place pressure on U.S. naval forces operating around Singapore. For the United States, Singapore and Thailand are both important logistical and replenishment locations, particularly during periods when U.S. aircraft carriers are rotating or undergoing maintenance. These locations would potentially fall within the operational range of aircraft operating from Ban Keun. 
From a broader strategic perspective, China’s decision to establish a military airfield near the center of mainland Southeast Asia is therefore noteworthy. In the future, the facility could also be used to complicate U.S. military operations in the Gulf of Thailand, the Andaman Sea, and even the Strait of Malacca. This is the broader geostrategic significance of Ban Keun Airport.

articles.title: AI and the Risk to Democracy
articles.full_text:
The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Dr. Matthew Botvinick  – author of “AI and Political Reform: The Risk to Democracy and How to Respond” (Princeton University Press 2026), world-renowned AI researcher and neuroscientist, senior fellow at Yale Law School and member of the technical staff at Anthropic, leading research on AI and the rule of law – is the 529th in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.” 
Explain how AI will pose fundamental challenges to constitutional democracy.
We are in a remarkable political moment right now, where two trends are converging. First, AI is generating feelings of insecurity and vulnerability across society. Second, in many democracies, trust in government institutions is low – in the U.S., trust is at historic lows. This is a combustible combination, because it provides ideal conditions for what has been called “the demagogue’s playbook,” where populist sentiment is exploited by political leaders to undermine democracy. 
Democracy has always been vulnerable to this risk. The problem now, though, is that AI dramatically raises the stakes. As others have noted, if an authoritarian government can get a foothold, AI makes it much easier for such a government to entrench itself, through surveillance and control of the information citizens can access or share. So the problem is two-fold: AI is creating conditions that can be exploited by aspiring authoritarian leaders, and it is also making available tools that such leaders might use to achieve their goals.  
It is important to add that all of this is about risks, not certainties. In fact, if democracies rise to meet the moment, AI might prove to be a benefit to democracy, rather than a detriment. The first order of business is to get our institutional houses in order, instituting government reforms – in emergency law, surveillance law, separation of powers, and free speech doctrines – that increase democratic resilience. If we can do that and make it past the immediate challenge, then we can start thinking about how AI might be used to empower and inform citizens, support democratic deliberation, and enhance government transparency and accountability. If we are careful and strategic, AI may be a boon rather than a curse. 
Examine the dynamics between rising powerful AI systems and eroding democratic institutions and implications for political and economic freedom.
Democracy depends on a balance between the power of government and the power of society. What keeps that balance in place is a combination of two things. On the government side, to keep power in check, it must be subdivided. Things must be structured to prevent perfectly coordinated action, which would make abuse of power too easy. This is why we have separation of powers and traditional checks and balances. On the societal side, in contrast, adequate power depends on factors that support coordinated action – the news media, the activities of civil society, a free marketplace of ideas, free and fair elections, and so forth. 
All of this means that democracies face danger when (1) the checks and balances within government erode, and (2) when the ability of society to engage in collective action is diminished. 
If we are not careful, AI will threaten to do both of those things. My book unpacks this in a number of ways but let me give just two examples. On the government side, AI might over-empower the executive branch relative to legislative and judicial branches, if AI is used to automate perfect obedience to central executive authority. On the society side, the ability of citizens to act in concert could be undermined by AI-enhanced surveillance or propaganda. Society’s power decreases, government power increases, and the balance required for democracy is lost.
Again, these are risks, not inevitabilities. If we act wisely, AI could enhance society’s capacity for collective action, and keep government’s power in balance, through exactly the means I mentioned earlier. But that won’t happen without strategic and proactive interventions. 
Analyze how the propagation of AI fuels authoritarianism in China and the United States.
The situation in China stands as a warning of what is possible. China’s use of AI to monitor and control its people has been detailed in excellent books like Josh Chin’s and Liza Lin’s “Surveillance State.” The importance of AI is this: Cheap and ubiquitous sensors, cameras for example, and online activity like that on social networks generate huge amounts of data. Finding the most important bits within that flood of information, and making sense of larger patterns, is a difficult problem. AI solves that problem, matching analytic capacity to the scale of the data. The result is that there is no place to hide from an authoritarian government’s gaze – that, of course, is the situation in China. 
The current challenge in the U.S. and other democracies is to leverage AI for legitimate law enforcement and national security needs, without creating tools that are too easy to abuse. The U.S. has a long history of such abuse, running from FDR and J. Edgar Hoover to the activities revealed by Edward Snowden. This time, we must act to ensure civil liberties and the rule of law ahead of such problems, rather than only in reaction to them. 
Explain why there can be no genuine AI safety without democracy and the rule of law.
I’m really pleased to see that people across society, people who have no direct involvement in the AI industry, are now talking about AI safety. It’s the right moment for that conversation, as AI systems become more capable and also increasingly permeate our activities, from commerce to education to science and beyond. 
But there is one part of the AI safety conversation that is not getting enough public attention, and it’s the one you’ve brought up: the fact that constitutional democracy is absolutely mandatory for AI safety. To see this point clearly, imagine an AI system that is safe in every way: It cannot launch cyberattacks, cannot escape human control, cannot create bioweapons, and so forth. Now picture this AI system in two settings. The first is a democracy with free and fair elections, an open marketplace of ideas, protection of civil liberties, and robust rule of law. The second is an authoritarian state, with none of those features. 
In that latter setting, our hypothetical “safe” AI is anything but safe. It will, quite reliably, be used to oppress dissent and enforce political compliance. Again, we needn’t read science fiction to understand what that looks like; it is playing out in many countries today, not only China but also Venezuela, Russia, some Gulf states and elsewhere. The take-home message is very simple: As we pursue AI safety, through technical and regulatory means, we must also work to assure that our democracies are robust and resilient as well. Real AI safety absolutely requires that.  
Assess how U.S., Chinese, and other AI companies should be held accountable for the political and economic impact of their technologies on their societies and the global community.
Here I should start by stating clearly that I am speaking in a purely personal capacity, rather than on behalf of Anthropic. That said, I think the answer to the question follows directly from the points I just made about the connection between AI safety and democracy. Any company that purports to care about AI safety – and this includes all of the major AI labs – has a responsibility to use whatever power it has to protect and enhance the health of democracy, both where the company is based and worldwide. 
It is important to acknowledge that this responsibility faces the AI industry with an extremely tricky task. Our tendency is to worry about the economic and political power of AI companies, and of course corporate power has been a recurrent problem in the U.S. and other democracies. However, at the same time, people underestimate how vulnerable corporate power – including the power of the AI labs – is to government power, especially when authoritarian tendencies seep into a democracy’s leadership. 
Over recent decades, democratic backsliding around the globe has more often involved the subjugation of corporate power by government than the opposite. And when authoritarian-leaning governments bring companies to heel, they gain access to their assets, which here include AI. So we need to watch the relationship between government and industry power very carefully and support the labs when – as we hope – they stick their necks out to defend democratic institutions and the rule of law.

articles.title: Russia’s Wildberries Finding Fertile Ground in Central Asia
articles.full_text:
The Russian e-commerce retailer has announced yet another new logistics facility, this time in Uzbekistan.
A Wildberries pickup point in Bashkortostan, Russia.
During World War II, Soviet authorities moved industry and people – often forcibly – away from the frontier in Europe into the heartland of Eurasia. The strategic relocation of factories and critical production to the Urals, Siberia, and Central Asia fundamentally changed economies across the union. 
Now, amid a different war on the European front, Russian industry is looking again to Central Asia for relative safety to continue conducting business. 
Wildberries & Russ, the parent company of Russia’s largest e-commerce retailer, Wildberries, reportedly signed an investment agreement this week with the Uzbek Ministry of Investment, Industry, and Trade to expand its logistics capacity in Uzbekistan. The deal comes in the wake of an early August announcement from Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Trade and Integration that Wildberries would expand its warehouse capacity in that country.
Starting in July 2026, Ukraine began targeting major Wildberries warehousing facilities in Russia. Through mid-August, Ukrainian drones had struck at least 20 Wildberries hubs, many of them near Moscow. According to the Moscow-based e-commerce consultancy Data Insight, as reported by DW in mid-August, Wildberries had lost 480 billion rubles worth of goods ($5.7 billion) and a third of its warehouse space. 
As The Diplomat’s Albert Otkjær pointed out in August, WIldberries’ effort to build out its warehousing capacity in Kazakhstan predates the current crisis – though not the February 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine. Wildberries’ expansion into Kazakhstan began in 2023, when the company opened its first logistics center in Astana, followed by a warehouse complex in Almaty. In September 2023, Wildberries opened a sorting center in Uralsk, the company’s fifth logistics center in the country. 
Similarly, in May 2023 Wildberries opened its first logistics center in Uzbekistan, in the Tashkent region, followed by plans for a second in Fergana. In October 2023 Wildeberries announced that it would build another logistics center in the Tashkent region.
The recently announced deal pertains to a planned logistics hub in the Zangiata district of the Tashkent region, to be built on a a 67.3-hectare site. According to the company, the facility will generate at least 7,500 jobs. 
As such, the wave of attacks this summer targeting Wildberries is not the sole motivation for its efforts to expand capacity in Central Asia. Those efforts began earlier. The region is, even absent the ongoing conflict, a large market for Russian companies and a bridge deeper into Asia. Factoring in the war in Ukraine only deepens the commercial logic for expansion into Central Asia.
It also deepens the risks. Ukrainian authorities have justified the strikes on an ostensibly civilian enterprise by arguing that Wildberries warehouse are “involved in supplying the Russian military with drone components, navigation equipment, and other gear,” as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in late July. 
Similarly, Ukraine justified attacks on Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) infrastructure near Novorossiysk – in November 2025 and July 2026 – given the critical importance of oil revenues to the Russian war machine. But collateral damage to Kazakhstan’s export of oil through the CPC led to pushback from both Astana and Washington. In February 2026, Ukraine’s ambassador to the United States said that Kyiv had received a formal demarche from Washington. The complaint, Ambassador Olga Stefanishyna said, cited the risks posed to “American investments which are being performed through Kazakhstan.”
In early August, Bloomberg reported, citing a U.S. official, that Ukraine had agreed to not strike CPC infrastructure critical to Kazakhstan’s oil exports in the Black Sea, as well as avoid striking non-Russian vessels – provided they’re not separately sanctioned or carrying Russian cargo. 
Could Ukrainian drone strikes target Wildberries facilities in Kazakhstan or Uzbekistan? It’s highly unlikely, though not impossible as the war drags on. Such a strike would mark a significant expansion of the conflict and be ruinous to Kyiv’s relations with the Central Asian states, and likely the United States, too, given Washington’s intercession on Kazakhstan’s behalf in regard to the CPC.
