articles.title: Poland’s President in the Philippines: Black Hawks, ASEAN, and US Defense Interests
articles.full_text:
Could Nawrocki’s visit to Manila serve to promote further Black Hawk sales across ASEAN, potentially benefiting U.S. industrial interests?
Polish President Karol Nawrocki shakes hands with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos, Jr. during talks in Manila, the Philippines, Oct. 6, 2026.
President of Poland Karol Nawrocki arrived in Manila on October 5 for a three-day official visit to the Philippines. It is the first visit by a Polish president to the Philippines since diplomatic relations were established in 1973.
According to Marcin Przydacz, secretary of state and head of the International Policy Bureau of the Chancellery of the President of the Republic of Poland, the visit is part of a broader Polish strategy to strengthen the country’s position among the countries of the Global South. Nawrocki described the visit as an opportunity to seek backing for Poland’s continued presence in the G20 by gaining informal support from the Philippines, which is chairing ASEAN this year. Nawrocki also described the trip in the context of a broader strategy of engaging with the Global South – a direction that has recently been highlighted in Polish foreign-policy discussions. 
There is also a military cooperation angle, raising the question of possible broader American defense interests within the Polish administration and opposition. 
In August, PZL Mielec, an aerospace manufacturer based in Poland, completed the delivery of 32 S-70i Black Hawk helicopters to the Philippine Air Force. The Philippines had previously ordered 16 helicopters from Mielec in 2019.
PZL Mielec presents itself as a Polish company: the helicopters are manufactured in Poland and the workforce is Polish. But since 2015, PZL Mielec has been owned by Lockheed Martin, one of the world’s largest U.S. defense contractors.
This makes Nawrocki’s visit to the Philippines particularly interesting.
Former Polish Defense Minister Mariusz Błaszczak, now a leading opposition figure and a strongly pro-American and Eurosceptic politician, has argued that Europe is effectively helpless against Russia and that Poland should rely on the United States rather than Europe for its security. He was also highly critical of the EU’s SAFE program, an EU initiative providing up to 150 billion euro in loans for defense investment. Błaszczak has argued that the program could push the United States out of Europe and questioned its compatibility with Poland’s reliance on U.S. defense technology.
In July 2026, Błaszczak, together with a group of MPs with the conservative party Prawo i Sprawiedliwość (PiS), submitted a parliamentary interpellation concerning the lack of new orders for S-70i Black Hawk helicopters from PZL Mielec. The MPs warned that the end of the Philippine contract could put the future of S-70i production in Poland at risk.
Supporting PZL Mielec can be presented as supporting Polish jobs and industrial capacity, but it also directly supports the commercial interests of Lockheed Martin.
Ironically, it may be easier for the Polish president to persuade the ASEAN countries to place an order than Poland’s own Ministry of Defense.
Given the tense relationship between Nawrocki and the Polish government led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, as well as Nawrocki’s alleged close relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump, one possible aim of the Philippine visit could be to encourage the government in Manila to consider another contract, or to promote PZL Mielec and its capabilities through the Philippines at the ASEAN level.
Given the ownership structure of PZL Mielec,  Błaszczak and Nawrocki’s political alignment, and support for stronger U.S. defense ties, the timing raises questions. Within the span of a few months, a parliamentary interpellation called for new orders for PZL Mielec, the factory completed its Philippine contract, and Poland’s president made his first-ever visit to the Philippines.
Could Nawrocki’s visit also serve to promote further Black Hawk sales across ASEAN, potentially benefiting U.S. industrial interests?
President of Poland Karol Nawrocki arrived in Manila on October 5 for a three-day official visit to the Philippines. It is the first visit by a Polish president to the Philippines since diplomatic relations were established in 1973.
According to Marcin Przydacz, secretary of state and head of the International Policy Bureau of the Chancellery of the President of the Republic of Poland, the visit is part of a broader Polish strategy to strengthen the country’s position among the countries of the Global South. Nawrocki described the visit as an opportunity to seek backing for Poland’s continued presence in the G20 by gaining informal support from the Philippines, which is chairing ASEAN this year. Nawrocki also described the trip in the context of a broader strategy of engaging with the Global South – a direction that has recently been highlighted in Polish foreign-policy discussions. 
There is also a military cooperation angle, raising the question of possible broader American defense interests within the Polish administration and opposition. 
In August, PZL Mielec, an aerospace manufacturer based in Poland, completed the delivery of 32 S-70i Black Hawk helicopters to the Philippine Air Force. The Philippines had previously ordered 16 helicopters from Mielec in 2019.
PZL Mielec presents itself as a Polish company: the helicopters are manufactured in Poland and the workforce is Polish. But since 2015, PZL Mielec has been owned by Lockheed Martin, one of the world’s largest U.S. defense contractors.
This makes Nawrocki’s visit to the Philippines particularly interesting.
Former Polish Defense Minister Mariusz Błaszczak, now a leading opposition figure and a strongly pro-American and Eurosceptic politician, has argued that Europe is effectively helpless against Russia and that Poland should rely on the United States rather than Europe for its security. He was also highly critical of the EU’s SAFE program, an EU initiative providing up to 150 billion euro in loans for defense investment. Błaszczak has argued that the program could push the United States out of Europe and questioned its compatibility with Poland’s reliance on U.S. defense technology.
In July 2026, Błaszczak, together with a group of MPs with the conservative party Prawo i Sprawiedliwość (PiS), submitted a parliamentary interpellation concerning the lack of new orders for S-70i Black Hawk helicopters from PZL Mielec. The MPs warned that the end of the Philippine contract could put the future of S-70i production in Poland at risk.
Supporting PZL Mielec can be presented as supporting Polish jobs and industrial capacity, but it also directly supports the commercial interests of Lockheed Martin.
Ironically, it may be easier for the Polish president to persuade the ASEAN countries to place an order than Poland’s own Ministry of Defense.
Given the tense relationship between Nawrocki and the Polish government led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, as well as Nawrocki’s alleged close relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump, one possible aim of the Philippine visit could be to encourage the government in Manila to consider another contract, or to promote PZL Mielec and its capabilities through the Philippines at the ASEAN level.
Given the ownership structure of PZL Mielec,  Błaszczak and Nawrocki’s political alignment, and support for stronger U.S. defense ties, the timing raises questions. Within the span of a few months, a parliamentary interpellation called for new orders for PZL Mielec, the factory completed its Philippine contract, and Poland’s president made his first-ever visit to the Philippines.

articles.title: Pakistan’s Solar Revolution is Reshaping its Power Sector
articles.full_text:
Solar power generation has expanded rapidly in recent years and has overtaken nuclear power generation for the first time.
Pakistan’s solar power generation has surpassed 20 percent of the country’s total electricity production. While this transition toward clean energy is a positive development, it is the outcome of an unplanned shift in the country’s energy landscape.
According to the World Nuclear Industry Status Report (WNISR) 2026, solar generation in Pakistan reached an estimated 36.3 terawatt-hours (TWh) in 2025. This accounts for roughly 21.6 percent of Pakistan’s total electricity generation after growing about 85 percent in a single year.
The WNISR report offers important background on this transformation. In Pakistan, solar-led power generation has not only expanded rapidly in recent years but has also overtaken nuclear power generation for the first time. The report further notes that Pakistan installed roughly twice as much solar capacity in five years as France managed in a decade.
Moreover, Pakistan imported more than 58 gigawatts (GW) of solar panels from China between the beginning of 2017 and mid-2026. Of this, around 40 GW arrived in just two and a half years, from 2024 to mid-2026. These imports over such a short period illustrate how quickly Chinese solar manufacturing found a major market in Pakistan amid falling panel prices and surging domestic electricity costs.
The surge has made Pakistan the second-largest single-country import market for Chinese solar panels, just behind the Netherlands. This data underscores the scale and speed of the change underway in the country.
Besides, the solar generation figures coming out of Pakistan are likely underestimations for several reasons.
A substantial amount of privately installed solar capacity across the country remains unregistered and does not pass through the state-controlled grid. In many cases, much of this capacity is installed on rooftops and industrial sites, where households and businesses generate and store power for their own use without becoming part of the national grid. This trend has largely been driven by high electricity tariffs, frequent load-shedding and the falling cost of Chinese solar panels. All of this has created a strong incentive for consumers to bypass the national grid system altogether.
While this shift is likely reducing the demand for grid-supplied electricity, it is impacting Pakistan’s power sector challenges and the country’s mounting capacity-related debt significantly.
For instance, as high-usage households, businesses, and industrial consumers leave the national grid, power distribution companies and remaining customers are left to shoulder a heavier burden of fixed costs. This essentially means that capacity payments for underutilized power plants continue in Pakistan. At the same time, overall electricity consumption recorded by distribution companies has declined across the country.
This situation has put coal-based power agreements reached by Pakistan previously with local and international firms under intense scrutiny. While solar adoption is surging across the country, Pakistan remains committed to long-term contracts that require heavy fixed payments to coal plant operators even if their plants remain idle or operate well below capacity. As a result, long-standing power purchase commitments have become a major financial burden for Pakistanis, even as they grapple with pressures due to the current economic strains facing the country.
It is important to note that Pakistan’s 23 loss-making state-owned enterprises accumulated roughly $1.24 billion in losses in the first half of Financial Year 2026. This is roughly equivalent to around $10 million per working day. At the same time, total state-owned enterprises’ debt, excluding sovereign guarantees, rose 14 percent to approximately $36.5 billion.
In this context, the rapid growth of solar power generation is not only a story of clean energy access and cost savings for those who can afford panels, but it is also accelerating financial stress within the formal power sector and complicating efforts to manage circular debt and capacity obligations of the Pakistani state.
For example, for ordinary consumers who remain fully dependent on the national grid, costs will likely continue to rise as the customer base continues to shrink. Meanwhile, for the energy market as a whole, the transition raises fundamental questions about planning, tariff design and the future role of large-scale coal and nuclear power in a system increasingly shaped by solar power generation.
That said, Pakistan’s energy future will depend on better planning and reform by the state. Policymakers should reorganize and renegotiate power-sector contracts and grid management to fit the new reality shaped by widespread solar power generation.
Without proactive reforms, the gap between solar power consumers and the struggling national grid will only continue to widen and strain the economy.

articles.title: As Tide Turns Against Modi, More Parties Back INDIA Bloc Protests
articles.full_text:
Police detained scores of opposition lawmakers, who held a sit-in to press their demand for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
Congress leader Rahul Gandhi holds up the Indian national flag while standing on a metal barricade put up by Delhi police to prevent the INDIA bloc’s march to the headquarters of the Election Commission of India in New Delhi, India, Oct. 6, 2026.
Police detained scores of opposition lawmakers, including Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi, his sister and Congress parliamentarian Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, and Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav, on the evening of October 6, in a bid to clear the INDIA bloc of opposition parties’ sit-in protest at Akashvani Bhavan in New Delhi.
Delhi Police subsequently registered complaints against the detained opposition parliamentarians for entering a government building without permission.
The detention of the leaders came at the end of a day of protests called by the INDIA bloc, which is demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. They accuse Kumar of vote chori (stealing votes) by overseeing an electoral process that has benefited Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
The call for Kumar’s resignation gathered momentum after an investigative report in The Indian Express revealed that Kumar made unilateral decisions and issued orders despite two other election commissioners raising objections “at least 14 times over the last 10 months” to issues relating to the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the electoral rolls.
At a meeting on September 30, leaders of the INDIA bloc decided on a schedule of protests to press their demand for Kumar’s resignation. The October 6 march was the first of several planned demonstrations in the coming weeks.
The plan was to march from parliament to the Election Commission building. However, legislators were blocked by police and barricades from reaching the planned destination. It did seem initially that the Modi government had scored an early victory against the opposition.
However, the Gandhi siblings quickly changed the plan and headed to Akashvani Bhavan, located adjacent to the Election Commission building, and continued their sit-in protest there.
The march saw the participation of most of the INDIA bloc’s constituents. However, the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) and the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) stayed away. While the DMK is miffed with Gandhi for aligning with its rival, the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam, to form the government in Tamil Nadu, the AAP’s decision seems motivated by factors that are more complex and controversial.
The Congress party has long suspected the AAP of being the “BJP’s B-team” – that is, it believes the AAP’s electoral strategy of opposing the Congress strengthens the BJP.
Interestingly, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which led the Jantar Mantar protests in July, did not participate in the INDIA-led march on October 6, although it too has called for Kumar’s resignation. Indeed, its leaders were quiet on social media through much of the day’s dramatic events, posting mild support only later, as criticism of their silence mounted on social media.
The CJP is widely believed to be close to the AAP. Of the 12 members of its core team, six – including its leaders Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das, and Ashutosh Ranka – “were either directly associated with the AAP or supported it publicly,” The Print reported.
Indeed, apprehension over the CJP’s likely links with the AAP kept the Congress away from the July protests at Jantar Mantar. Although Gandhi did subsequently meet activists of the leftist organizations, he has maintained distance from the CJP.
The rift between the Congress and the AAP is over 15 years old. In 2011, India Against Corruption, a grouping of NGOs, civil society organizations, and right-wing activists, held massive protests against corruption in the then Congress-led coalition government. The IAC movement not only birthed the AAP but also severely weakened the Congress, paving the way for the BJP’s victory in the 2014 general elections.
For many Congress leaders and their supporters, the Jantar Mantar protests evoked memories of the 2011 IAC protests. They believe that the Jantar Mantar protests, although directed against the BJP government, would end up benefiting the AAP and the BJP rather than the opposition.
There are other important differences between the INDIA bloc and the CJP.
On October 5, Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge said the Congress and its INDIA bloc partners have three “non-negotiable demands” – the resignation of CEC Kumar, annulment of the ongoing Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls, and restoration of voting via ballot paper instead of electronic voting machines. It wants a level playing field in elections.
The CJP, meanwhile, is calling on opposition parties to boycott elections.
An opposition boycott of elections could deprive the election of legitimacy. However, a boycott could benefit the BJP. The BJP would get a few friendly parties to contest the election to lend the process legitimacy. At a time when mass support for the BJP is declining and support for the opposition parties is growing, staying away from elections would hurt the latter’s interests.
Such sharp differences among opposition forces can only weaken their efforts to defeat the BJP. The BJP can be expected to step up efforts to deepen these divisions in the coming months.
While last week, the INDIA bloc showed some signs of unity at its meeting, the October 6 demonstrations have upset some partners. What was supposed to be a joint INDIA event turned into a “Rahul Gandhi show” that showcased only the Gandhi siblings and the Congress party, they are complaining.
Meanwhile, the AAP, the DMK and the CJP appear to be rethinking their strategy of staying away from INDIA-led protests. In a sharp about-turn, the DMK today expressed solidarity with INDIA’s protests. “This government doesn’t want Rahul Gandhi to protest against Gyanesh Kumar,” it said today, after deriding him on October 6. And AAP participated in today’s protests.
The CJP and leftist organizations have called for protests in Delhi on October 10. Will the INDIA bloc back their effort? Importantly, can the Congress overcome its misgivings to extend them support? It seems unlikely at this point.
Building a mass movement is always challenging. Given its stellar role in leading India’s independence struggle, the Congress has immense experience in this regard and needs to draw on that experience. It will need to consult partners and pull together with them if it is serious about taking on the Modi government successfully.

articles.title: Why the Mecca Agreement Might Fail
articles.full_text:
If each member preserves its own partnerships while expecting the others to absorb its security risks, what does the promise that an attack against one is an attack against all mean when a crisis arrives?
On August 7, 2026, Turkiye’s Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Saudi Arabia’s Mohammed bin Salman, and Pakistan’s Shehbaz Sharif jointly signed the Mecca  Joint Defense Agreement, which commits their countries to collective defense and expands defense cooperation. It builds on the Saudi-Pakistani Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement of September 2025. On August 31, their foreign ministers, defense ministers, and military chiefs met in Istanbul, announcing a secretariat in Saudi Arabia, initially headed by a Pakistani secretary general, alongside cooperation in military technology and production.
The most important question about the Mecca agreement is whose war they are prepared to fight. Although the text of the agreement is not publicly available yet, according to a Pakistan Foreign Ministry statement, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye, and Pakistan have agreed that an armed attack against any one of the three states shall be regarded as an attack against them all. However, with a look at their conflicting interests, one can easily predict that they will struggle to agree on what should happen next.
What makes one doubt whether such an accord could realistically function is the agreement’s central weakness: its publicly announced terms do not specify which forces would fight, under whose command, or on what timetable. All parties to the accord want greater security while retaining the freedom to decide which regional conflicts concern them. But when countries commit to collective defense, they must also agree on when and how they will defend one another, what strategic purpose the accord serves, and which threats they consider common. They must also be clear about who decides when military action is necessary, how they will share the costs, and how far each country is prepared to go if the conflict escalates; what economic interests they are willing to sacrifice, whether greater financial contributions give one country greater authority, and how they will reconcile their competing ambitions.
The first problem is that all three countries aspire to lead the Muslim world, but each has a different idea of what that leadership means. For instance, Erdoğan’s Turkiye invokes its Ottoman heritage to project authority beyond its borders. Turkiye’s reconversion of the Hagia Sophia into a mosque in 2020 to restore symbols of its Ottoman past was part of that ambition. In a 2018 speech to provincial muftis in Ankara, Erdoğan presented Turkiye as a country entitled to shape the Muslim world’s future because of the authority its Ottoman predecessors once exercised. Since Erdoğan’s rise to power, nostalgia for an imperial and caliphal past has helped shape Turkiye’s claim to leadership in the Muslim world today. 
Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, bases its claim to leadership on its custodianship of Mecca and Medina and its established position in Islamic diplomacy. In the meantime, while Mohammed bin Salman wants to preserve that position and keep religion as a source of legitimacy, he is also making the kingdom a center for investment, technology, and regional diplomacy to serve the country’s economic and political ambitions. Saudi Arabia therefore wants a form of Islamic leadership that reinforces its own position, which raises the question of how far it would support an alliance that also strengthens Turkiye’s competing claim to that leadership. 
For its part, Pakistan has long sought to turn its military strength into a claim to leadership of the Muslim world. This ambition is visible in how its leaders have explained the purpose of its nuclear program. Prime Minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto famously said that other civilizations already possessed nuclear capability, writing: “Only the Islamic civilization was without it, but that position was about to change.” He was presenting Pakistan’s nuclear ambitions as an achievement that would alter the position of the entire Islamic civilization. Almost half a century later, addressing religious scholars in December 2025, Field Marshall Asim Munir, Pakistan’s first chief of defense forces and the country’s top military official,  declared: “Among all Muslim countries, Allah has given Pakistan the honor of helping safeguard the Haramain,” referring to Islam’s holy sites in Mecca and Medina. Munir was thereby presenting Pakistan’s military role as a religious responsibility extending beyond its borders, giving Islamabad another basis for claiming a special position in the Muslim world. 
Further, in 2020, Foreign Minister Shah Mahmood Qureshi threatened to organize Muslim countries outside the Saudi-led OIC over Kashmir. Pakistan has therefore shown a willingness to challenge the existing framework of Muslim diplomacy led by Saudi Arabia or Turkiye when it fails to serve Pakistani priorities, and this is where these ambitions could become difficult to reconcile with Saudi Arabia and Turkiye’s.
These three countries have also had differences in their foreign policies, and those differences have sometimes led them to work against one another’s regional objectives. For instance, during the 2017 blockade of Qatar by Saudi Arabia, it was Turkiye that sent troops and food supplies to Doha, helping Qatar to resist pressure from Saudi Arabia and its partners. Pakistan has also resisted Saudi expectations of military support. In 2015, after Riyadh requested Pakistani troops, aircraft, and warships for its intervention in Yemen, Pakistan’s parliament voted to remain neutral; this refusal showed that close relations did not mean Islamabad accepted Riyadh’s judgment about when military action was necessary. 
Pakistan has also not shown up to defend Saudi Arabia against the current attacks by Iran, despite the so-called “NATO-like” agreement that both countries signed last September. Most recently, on September 11, Saudi Arabia announced a precautionary shutdown of its East-West pipeline following drone attacks that Riyadh said originated in Iraq. The pipeline provided a vital alternative for oil exports disrupted by Iran’s restrictions at Hormuz. Separately, the Houthis captured Mokha and Perim, also known as Mayun, strengthening their position at Bab el-Mandeb, the southern gateway to the Red Sea and the trade route through Suez. Again, despite both the Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement and the Mecca accord, Pakistan and Turkiye have not shown up to defend Saudi Arabia, concerned with themselves being drawn into the crisis, after being threatened by Houthis that they both would pay a “high price” if they intervened. 
The military picture extends the problem. Turkiye brings decades of NATO experience and a substantial domestic defense industry, while Pakistan increasingly relies on Chinese equipment, and Saudi Arabia remains heavily dependent on foreign suppliers. According to SIPRI’s 2026 data, China supplied 80 percent of Pakistan’s major arms imports in 2021–2025, while the United States supplied 77 percent of Saudi Arabia’s. If Pakistani and Saudi forces were fighting together, they would need to exchange relevant operational intelligence and coordinate forces using different military systems. However, integrating those systems could require sensitive technical information and assistance from their suppliers. Washington could object to arrangements that exposed information about American equipment to Chinese technicians, while Beijing could have similar concerns about Western access to its technology. Both would want to prevent a rival from learning how their weapons operate, identifying their vulnerabilities, or developing ways to defeat them. Suppliers could therefore have more power to limit how closely Mecca accord parties could operate together, even if those governments agreed on the need for joint military action. 
Turkiye has seen how serious these restrictions can become. In July 2019, the United States excluded Ankara from the F-35 fighter program following its purchase of Russia’s S-400 air defense system, arguing that the Russian system could collect sensitive information about the aircraft’s capabilities. Turkiye’s longstanding NATO membership did not overcome Washington’s security concerns. The implication for the Mecca accord is that political agreement among its members may be insufficient to secure the military integration they need. If competing suppliers’ security concerns could obstruct cooperation inside NATO, there is little reason to assume that American and Chinese equipment can be easily integrated for the Mecca accord parties. 
Turkiye’s NATO membership creates another complication. Even though the NATO Treaty places limits on collective defense obligations through Articles 5 and 6, which define the attacks and geographical areas they cover, Turkiye cannot extend NATO’s protection to Pakistan or Saudi Arabia simply by signing another agreement. However, an armed attack on Turkish territory resulting from Turkiye’s intervention in defense of either country would raise a separate Article 5 question which limits Turkiye’s freedom of action under the Mecca accord, as Ankara would have to consider how far it could go in defending its new partners and what consequences its involvement could have for its NATO allies. 
Moreover, from an economic perspective, the economic imbalance among the three members makes the Mecca agreement hard to sustain. Saudi Arabia brings substantial oil wealth, Turkiye brings industrial capacity but continues to struggle with inflation, and Pakistan remains an IMF borrower. These differences raise questions about how they would divide the costs of preparing for, fighting, and recovering from a common war. NATO members finance their own forces while contributing to common budgets through an agreed formula based on national income. The Mecca accord’s statement announces a secretariat and industrial cooperation without explaining an equivalent financial arrangement. 
If Saudi Arabia is expected to provide most of the money, would it demand greater influence over deployments and procurement? Would Turkiye and Pakistan accept that influence while supplying forces and bearing casualties? Conversely, would Riyadh finance military commitments over which its partners retained a veto? Paying for weapons is also different from funding years of operations, replacing losses and compensating for disrupted trade. A further difficulty is that attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure could weaken the revenue supporting any Saudi financial commitment. According to current reports, oil loadings at Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea port of Yanbu have stopped following drone attacks by the Iran-backed Houthi militia. The port has served as a major outlet for Saudi oil exports following the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, and, according to experts, this pause in loadings could cause further severe disruption to global energy markets. 
The difficulty goes further: the three countries do not share the same enemies. Pakistan shares a border with Iran, and both Islamabad and Ankara maintain relations with Tehran, while Saudi Arabia faces attacks from Iranian rockets in its territory as well as from its Houthi allies. More importantly, Turkiye has said the accord is not directed against Iran, which puts Saudi Arabia’s situation in limbo, as it’s not clear what is in this accord for Saudi Arabia and what protection Riyadh can expect if its partners prioritize preserving relations with Tehran. 
Moreover, the Mecca accord countries have different approaches to Israel, the other major player in the region. Turkiye’s relations with Israel are confrontational, and Pakistan does not recognize Israel as a state, while Saudi Arabia remains the subject of efforts to expand the Abraham Accords, although Riyadh conditions normalization on Palestinian statehood. 
On the other hand, with India, Pakistan’s principal strategic rival, the complications are amplified Saudi Arabia maintains a close partnership with India, with bilateral trade reaching $41.88 billion in fiscal 2024-2025. Would Riyadh jeopardize that relationship to fight New Delhi on Islamabad’s behalf? Would Pakistan confront Iran for Saudi Arabia? If each member preserves its own partnerships while expecting the others to absorb its security risks, what does the promise that an attack against one is an attack against all mean when a crisis arrives?

Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, bases its claim to leadership on its custodianship of Mecca and Medina and its established position in Islamic diplomacy. In the meantime, while Mohammed bin Salman wants to preserve that position and keep religion as a source of legitimacy, he is also making the kingdom a center for investment, technology, and regional diplomacy to serve the country’s economic and political ambitions. Saudi Arabia therefore wants a form of Islamic leadership that reinforces its own position, which raises the question of how far it would support an alliance that also strengthens Turkiye’s competing claim to that leadership. 
For its part, Pakistan has long sought to turn its military strength into a claim to leadership of the Muslim world. This ambition is visible in how its leaders have explained the purpose of its nuclear program. Prime Minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto famously said that other civilizations already possessed nuclear capability, writing: “Only the Islamic civilization was without it, but that position was about to change.” He was presenting Pakistan’s nuclear ambitions as an achievement that would alter the position of the entire Islamic civilization. Almost half a century later, addressing religious scholars in December 2025, Field Marshall Asim Munir, Pakistan’s first chief of defense forces and the country’s top military official,  declared: “Among all Muslim countries, Allah has given Pakistan the honor of helping safeguard the Haramain,” referring to Islam’s holy sites in Mecca and Medina. Munir was thereby presenting Pakistan’s military role as a religious responsibility extending beyond its borders, giving Islamabad another basis for claiming a special position in the Muslim world. 
Further, in 2020, Foreign Minister Shah Mahmood Qureshi threatened to organize Muslim countries outside the Saudi-led OIC over Kashmir. Pakistan has therefore shown a willingness to challenge the existing framework of Muslim diplomacy led by Saudi Arabia or Turkiye when it fails to serve Pakistani priorities, and this is where these ambitions could become difficult to reconcile with Saudi Arabia and Turkiye’s.
These three countries have also had differences in their foreign policies, and those differences have sometimes led them to work against one another’s regional objectives. For instance, during the 2017 blockade of Qatar by Saudi Arabia, it was Turkiye that sent troops and food supplies to Doha, helping Qatar to resist pressure from Saudi Arabia and its partners. Pakistan has also resisted Saudi expectations of military support. In 2015, after Riyadh requested Pakistani troops, aircraft, and warships for its intervention in Yemen, Pakistan’s parliament voted to remain neutral; this refusal showed that close relations did not mean Islamabad accepted Riyadh’s judgment about when military action was necessary. 
Pakistan has also not shown up to defend Saudi Arabia against the current attacks by Iran, despite the so-called “NATO-like” agreement that both countries signed last September. Most recently, on September 11, Saudi Arabia announced a precautionary shutdown of its East-West pipeline following drone attacks that Riyadh said originated in Iraq. The pipeline provided a vital alternative for oil exports disrupted by Iran’s restrictions at Hormuz. Separately, the Houthis captured Mokha and Perim, also known as Mayun, strengthening their position at Bab el-Mandeb, the southern gateway to the Red Sea and the trade route through Suez. Again, despite both the Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement and the Mecca accord, Pakistan and Turkiye have not shown up to defend Saudi Arabia, concerned with themselves being drawn into the crisis, after being threatened by Houthis that they both would pay a “high price” if they intervened. 
The military picture extends the problem. Turkiye brings decades of NATO experience and a substantial domestic defense industry, while Pakistan increasingly relies on Chinese equipment, and Saudi Arabia remains heavily dependent on foreign suppliers. According to SIPRI’s 2026 data, China supplied 80 percent of Pakistan’s major arms imports in 2021–2025, while the United States supplied 77 percent of Saudi Arabia’s. If Pakistani and Saudi forces were fighting together, they would need to exchange relevant operational intelligence and coordinate forces using different military systems. However, integrating those systems could require sensitive technical information and assistance from their suppliers. Washington could object to arrangements that exposed information about American equipment to Chinese technicians, while Beijing could have similar concerns about Western access to its technology. Both would want to prevent a rival from learning how their weapons operate, identifying their vulnerabilities, or developing ways to defeat them. Suppliers could therefore have more power to limit how closely Mecca accord parties could operate together, even if those governments agreed on the need for joint military action. 
Turkiye has seen how serious these restrictions can become. In July 2019, the United States excluded Ankara from the F-35 fighter program following its purchase of Russia’s S-400 air defense system, arguing that the Russian system could collect sensitive information about the aircraft’s capabilities. Turkiye’s longstanding NATO membership did not overcome Washington’s security concerns. The implication for the Mecca accord is that political agreement among its members may be insufficient to secure the military integration they need. If competing suppliers’ security concerns could obstruct cooperation inside NATO, there is little reason to assume that American and Chinese equipment can be easily integrated for the Mecca accord parties. 
Turkiye’s NATO membership creates another complication. Even though the NATO Treaty places limits on collective defense obligations through Articles 5 and 6, which define the attacks and geographical areas they cover, Turkiye cannot extend NATO’s protection to Pakistan or Saudi Arabia simply by signing another agreement. However, an armed attack on Turkish territory resulting from Turkiye’s intervention in defense of either country would raise a separate Article 5 question which limits Turkiye’s freedom of action under the Mecca accord, as Ankara would have to consider how far it could go in defending its new partners and what consequences its involvement could have for its NATO allies.
articles.summary: If each member preserves its own partnerships while expecting the others to absorb its security risks, what does the promise that an attack against one is an attack against all mean when a crisis arrives?

articles.title: Missing the Forest for the Trees in Taiwan’s Defense Preparations
articles.full_text:
Beyond exercises and equipment, strategic developments in Taiwan’s military preparedness are being overlooked.
A guided-missile fast attack craft with the ROC Navy participates in the 2026 Han Kuang exercise, Aug. 8, 2026.
In recent years, Taiwan’s military issues have received considerable discussion, from changes in Taiwan’s annual large-scale Han Kuang exercises to recommendations on equipment procurement. These are all quite important areas of change, but the most core issue seems to have received much less discussion: how exactly the Taiwan military may fight. The aforementioned changes in exercises and equipment procurement, in the end, are all meant to serve the kind of war Taiwan is prepared to fight. Taiwan has had some developments in this area that have received limited attention and discussion, but their importance is definitely no less than the developments in exercises and equipment.
The key is to comprehensively understand Taiwan’s efforts and preparations from the strategic level, using what the Taiwan military most often says about what kind of war to fight, what equipment to have, what kind of force structure is needed, and what training to conduct. Taiwan has moved from its past concepts of defeating the enemy on the opposite shore or seeking a decisive battle in the littoral area to actually carrying out an erosion strategy and sustained operations in recent years. To that end, Taiwan has continued to strengthen the army’s active-duty combat power in the northern region to build a layered defensive network and regional force superiority. Meanwhile, the cumulative duration of large-scale exercises in 2026 has already accumulated to nearly one month. There is also something that many people might have noticed but not realized: the significant expansion of Taiwan’s navy in recent years. 
At the same time, these developments also bring out the current difficulties Taiwan faces in joint operations across the services. This is one of the most critical areas to watch in Taiwan’s future defense development. In recent years, experts have paid considerable attention to the Taiwan military’s efforts toward decentralization, but in practice, joint command and control is the key to whether Taiwan’s combat capability can be improved.
Further Concentration of Forces in Northern Taiwan
The key to an erosion strategy and sustained operations is to delay and strike enemy forces through layered forces. Although Taiwan emphasizes decentralized command and control, this means emphasizing that a single operational unit can continue to carry out assigned actions based on higher-level operational objectives when command and control is disrupted. In terms of military operations, strategically concentrating forces to make it difficult for the enemy to break through and advance is quite important. And this is also what Taiwan is doing.
Northern Taiwan is where the political center is located, and it also concentrates important operational command organizations and transportation hubs. More than one-third of Taiwan’s population lives there. More than about half of the Taiwan active-duty brigade-level forces of the Republic of China (ROC) Army and Marine Corps are normally stationed in the northern region (north of Miaoli and Yilan), including the main combat forces, combined arms brigades, Army Aviation units, and Marine Corps forces.
In particular, in recent years Taiwan has continued during exercises to additionally move units from other regions into the northern region to conduct reinforcement missions. This makes the forces concentrated in the northern region possibly reach nearly two-thirds of Taiwan’s active-duty ground forces. During the 2025 Han Kuang Exercise, the main reinforcement was carried out by units from the Marine Corps 99th Brigade moving north from southern Taiwan to reinforce Taoyuan and the greater Taipei area. The 2026 Han Kuang Exercise further expanded the reinforcement forces, including forces under the Marine Corps 99th Brigade and Army 564th Combined Arms Brigade from southern Taiwan, and the Army 586th Combined Arms Brigade from central Taiwan, which moved and deployed to the northern region.
This kind of deployment and training concentrates forces in northern Taiwan and is, to a considerable degree, a focus of Taiwan’s current sustained defensive operations. In September 2026, during the ROC Army’s annual large-scale Lu Sheng exercise, Maj. Gen. Lin Shih-wei, deputy commander of the Army Education, Training, and Doctrine Development Command, clearly stated at a press conference that this exercise was centered on the concept of successive resistance and sustained operations under Chief of the General Staff Admiral Mei Chia-shu’s erosion strategy. Most importantly, the exercise area was changed to northern Taiwan in order to conform with the focus on defensive operations and allow troops to become familiar with key terrain in the area of operations and the deployment and employment of troops and firepower.
Nearly One Month of Large-Scale Military Exercises
Another development deserving more attention is that in recent years the Taiwan military has begun extending the training duration of various live-force exercises. In addition to extending existing exercises such as the nationwide Han Kuang exercise and the brigade-level Lu Sheng exercise, it has also added several large-scale exercises. 
The accumulated time of these military exercises has led the Taiwan military this year to spend almost an entire month participating in various live-force exercises, far more than in the past few years. This includes the five-day Immediate Combat Readiness Exercise in June, the five-day Joint Defense Exercise in July, the 10-day Han Kuang Exercise in August, and the 10-day Lu Sheng Exercise expected in October. 
Besides allowing units to have more time to complete continuous training events that could not be conducted in the past, this also allows participating units to become familiar with scenarios related to long-duration sustained operations during a future Taiwan conflict. The longer training and exercise duration allows units to validate operations under prolonged combat scenarios, as well as the maintenance of combat capability and coordination with civilian sectors in the use of civilian resources, including manpower and material mobilization.
Another aspect worth attention in recent years is that the ROC Navy has been playing more and more roles in Taiwan’s current defensive operations. In the past, the Taiwan government mainly planned naval units in wartime as fleet task forces. In recent years, there have been three notable changes.
First, the Marine Corps under the Navy has undergone a major transformation in recent years, shifting from a force responsible for offensive amphibious operations and power projection in the past to a defensive force for urban areas. In recent years, Taiwan’s Marine Corps has gradually given up its tanks and self-propelled artillery in favor of drones and anti-tank equipment. As the strategic reserve directly under the General Staff Headquarters, the Marine Corps has been deployed to the Taipei area, with its mission shifting to become a defensive force for the capital garrison area.
Second, the ROC Navy this year established a new Coastal Operations Command within the service. Its commander holds the same vice admiral rank as the Fleet Command commander, and it integrates units related to shore-based anti-ship missiles, shore-based radar, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR), and unmanned aerial systems, with the goal of establishing a coastal operations system across units and platforms.
Third, Taiwan’s Coast Guard this year added one new deputy director-general position, and in late September formally appointed a vice admiral from the Navy to the position. The purpose is to bring the Navy’s tactical thinking into the Coast Guard, inject key new momentum into the Coast Guard’s transition from peacetime to wartime, effectively connect communication channels between the military and Coast Guard, and deepen joint maritime-air defense and response mechanisms. 
In addition, Taiwan’s Coast Guard has also begun, during the military’s annual exercises, to expand training events related to the transition from peacetime to wartime, allowing its Coast Guard vessels to undertake part of the sea-denial strike missions during wartime. Specifically, this year’s Han Kuang exercise had the Coast Guard conduct exercises under the control of the Navy’s Coastal Operations Command.
These changes all show that the ROC Navy is playing an increasingly important role in Taiwan’s current defensive operations. This includes sea denial and coastal operations, and also includes the capital garrison mission during the defense-in-depth phase.
Taiwan’s current defense preparations are not only changes in concepts and efforts in equipment procurement, but have also seen quite significant developments in military training and deployment validation. More importantly, as the relatively weaker side in the cross-strait military balance, Taiwan must necessarily concentrate its resources to a greater degree and use them more efficiently. Therefore, we can also notice that there is now more Navy involvement in maritime and coastal denial operations, and even in the land-based attrition strategy and the defense-in-depth phase. The Coast Guard is also practicing the transition from peacetime to wartime, 
But at the same time, these changes also point to a more critical area to observe in the future, which is whether Taiwan’s joint operations across the services, especially its command and control preparations, are in place. In the past, land operations were usually considered something for the Army to handle by itself. In a hypothetical scenario where the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) would be able to conduct an amphibious assault on Taiwan and then offload follow-on forces, it was typically assumed to mean that Taiwan’s air and naval combat power had already been largely paralyzed, while China had air and sea superiority. Now, this situation has changed to a considerable degree. Navy shore-based units and Air Force air defense units will also play important roles during the defense-in-depth phase, and therefore preparations for joint operations become quite important.
The first question mark is the joint command and control capability under the concentration of large numbers of forces, including Army and Navy forces concentrated in the northern region, as well as Air Force air defense assets. Efficient command and control of different units in conducting joint operations is quite critical.
Second, and even more critical, is whether Taiwan can increase the capacity of its joint operations training. The Taiwanese military’s only Joint Operations Training Base has limited training capacity. Because of geographic space limitations and the need to avoid disturbing nearby residents, it can usually only provide battalion-level training. The ROC Navy, Army Aviation, and Air Force also have difficulty participating together as formed units in exercises because of the limited airspace. Although annual large-scale exercises can validate and train service members’ ability to conduct joint operations, in practice they cannot fully replace basic joint operations training.
Taiwan has far fewer resources compared with China, so joint operations capability is key to allowing Taiwan’s combat power to be used more efficiently. This is also a key area of Taiwan-U.S. military cooperation. In January 2026, media reports stated that U.S. personnel had been stationed at Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defense Joint Firepower Coordination Center, which is responsible for cross-service fires deployment and coordination, and that joint staff work had reportedly already been conducted.
It is important to know that decentralization is a key capability when the command and control system is cut off, in order to maintain operational resilience. But for Taiwan, in the event of war, the best situation for resisting a Chinese invasion to the greatest extent should be to have a sound joint operations capability, so that resources can be converted into combat power to the greatest extent. Therefore, although experts in recent years have paid considerable attention to the Taiwan military’s efforts toward decentralization, joint operations capability is also critical.
In recent years, Taiwan’s military issues have received considerable discussion, from changes in Taiwan’s annual large-scale Han Kuang exercises to recommendations on equipment procurement. These are all quite important areas of change, but the most core issue seems to have received much less discussion: how exactly the Taiwan military may fight. The aforementioned changes in exercises and equipment procurement, in the end, are all meant to serve the kind of war Taiwan is prepared to fight. Taiwan has had some developments in this area that have received limited attention and discussion, but their importance is definitely no less than the developments in exercises and equipment.
The key is to comprehensively understand Taiwan’s efforts and preparations from the strategic level, using what the Taiwan military most often says about what kind of war to fight, what equipment to have, what kind of force structure is needed, and what training to conduct. Taiwan has moved from its past concepts of defeating the enemy on the opposite shore or seeking a decisive battle in the littoral area to actually carrying out an erosion strategy and sustained operations in recent years. To that end, Taiwan has continued to strengthen the army’s active-duty combat power in the northern region to build a layered defensive network and regional force superiority. Meanwhile, the cumulative duration of large-scale exercises in 2026 has already accumulated to nearly one month. There is also something that many people might have noticed but not realized: the significant expansion of Taiwan’s navy in recent years. 
At the same time, these developments also bring out the current difficulties Taiwan faces in joint operations across the services. This is one of the most critical areas to watch in Taiwan’s future defense development. articles.title: Farewell to Russia: The View From Kazakhstan
articles.full_text:
Karaganda and its environs are home to some of the largest-scale coal-mining on the planet. And once, the home to an immense gulag.
In “Farewell to Russia: A Journey Through the Former USSR” journalist Joe Luc Barnes travels across the 15 states that once comprised the Soviet Union. In the excerpt below, Barnes stops off in Karaganda, the heart of Kazakh coal country and once the site of a notorious gulag.
The steppe stretches in all directions under the massive sky. There are no trees, no hills, no natural points of interest of any sort, save for a herd of horses grazing by the roadside. The openness of Central Asia makes itself felt immediately. Kazakhstan alone spans an area larger than Western Europe. 
But these northern plains are not featureless. Factories dot the landscape, their chimneys raised like middle fingers in defiance of the mighty heavens. Thin trails of smoke seep from them and a vast network of pylons and railway tracks sprawl from their feet. Karaganda and its environs are home to some of the largest-scale coal-mining on the planet. At the time of my visit, much of this industrial landscape belonged to steel giant ArcelorMittal. 
“We don’t like them here. They don’t care about employees; they pay us nothing, and don’t give a shit about our safety,” my taxi driver tells me.
“Used to. I’m an invalid now; was forced to retire. My lungs can’t take it any more.”
“Of course!” he says, displaying that gritty courage you often get in mining communities, where a hard day’s graft is the highest form of honor.
As it happens, this former miner is taking me to one of the predecessors of ArcelorMittal – another institution that has a rather patchy record when it comes to worker rights.
Around a century ago, Karaganda didn’t really exist. Coal had been discovered here in the late 19th century, but the nascent mines were soon abandoned – for some reason it proved difficult to persuade people to leave their families behind and toil down the pit in the middle of the frigid steppe. Besides, there were too few houses and nowhere near enough food to supply a large-scale mining settlement. But all that changed in February 1927, when Article 58 of the Russian penal code was brought into force.
Article 58 justified the arrest of those suspected of counter-revolutionary activity. The law cast a wide net as the precise meaning of “counter-revolutionary activity” was left deliberately vague, leaving Alexander Solzhenitsyn to ask: “Who among us has not experienced its all-encompassing embrace? In all truth, there is no step, thought, action, or lack of action under the heavens which could not be punished by the heavy hand of Article 58.”
People may not have fancied moving to the steppe, but fortunately for economic planners the Soviet justice system had suddenly created a large pool of laborers who had little choice in the matter.
Between 1921 and 1953, an estimated 18 million people passed through the Soviet forced-labor camp system known as the Gulag. The number of those who died is disputed, but is thought to be around 1.5 to 1.6 million. These numbers suggest that while the Gulag experience was unimaginably brutal, it was not necessarily the death sentence it is often portrayed as.
The Karaganda Camp (or Karlag) was created in 1930 to solve the problem of supplying the coal mines. It grew so rapidly that, by 1940, the area of the camp covered 6,500 square miles and was home to 65,000 prisoners. The Kazakh SSR became a repository for all manner of “undesirables,” from the political dissidents convicted under Article 58 to the so-called rich peasants, or kulaks, who were seen to be standing in the way of the equal distribution of land. They were joined by whole groups of “disloyal” ethnicities such as Poles and Chechens, Koreans and Crimean Tatars. In the early 1940s, half a million ethnic Germans, who had been living along the banks of Russia’s Volga River for almost two centuries, were also forced to relocate here. 
Between them they played a large part in the building of Karaganda, which went from a small settlement in the late 1920s to a city of over 200,000 twenty years later. The camp headquarters, and now the site of the Karlag Museum, was in a small town called Dolinka, about 30 miles from Karaganda proper. There are few other visitors, so the young woman at the ticket office is happy to give me a free tour.
She takes me to the dormitories first. It’s draughty even at the height of summer. Rough woolen sheets filled with straw are draped over bunk beds whose supporting planks are so thin I doubt they would have supported any but the scrawniest of inmates – though I suppose the diets here were unlikely to have left anyone particularly rotund.
“Local people used to ride here on horseback and throw kurt over the walls of the camp for the prisoners to eat,” my guide tells me.
Kurt is a hard, extremely salty ball of dried cheese. It’s not particularly appetizing but lasts a long time and has been used for centuries as a protein-rich snack for those spending days in the saddle. The traditional Kazakh diet is heavy on these milky staples. Another is kumis – fermented horse’s milk – which I was made to sample on my first evening here. It wasn’t the tastiest of concoctions, but I imagine that both kurt and kumis would hit the spot if you’ve been forced to build a coal mine on Oliver Twist’s rations. 
I also imagine that this story isn’t true – the idea of noble, empathetic Kazakh horsemen coming to the aid of the desperate, oppressed prisoner is, well, a stretch. However, there is well-documented evidence of large-scale black-market trade in food and rations in the Karlag, whose walls were more porous than other camps due to its size and proximity to Karaganda.
We come to the commandant’s study, set up as it would have been in the early 1950s: portrait of Stalin on the wall behind the desk and some heavy bookshelves, well stocked with the works of Lenin, Marx, and Engels. The only touch of personality is betrayed by an old gramophone.
“Concerts were organized on Sundays and Mondays,” she tells me. “Those were the days when the prisoners were tortured; the music drowned out the screams.”
The other rooms are dedicated to the fate of the Kazakhs – that is, the people who had lived here for centuries before these lands became an integral part of the Gulag.
In 1897, under the tsars, the land we now call Kazakhstan was 82 percent Kazakh. The early years of the 20th century saw the authorities encourage Slavic people to settle in the areas that had traditionally been inhabited by Kazakh nomads.
“Kazakhs lived at one with the steppe,” Klara, an IT worker who lived in Kazakhstan’s capital, Astana, had told me before my trip. As soon as she found out about my post-Soviet odyssey, she made it her mission to make her country my next destination. 
“They traveled to where food and water was before moving on. This way, the land was allowed to recover in the meantime. The European arrivals began to change that, and the Soviets put it on fast-forward. They were obsessed with collectivizing people. The idea of being a nomad didn’t fit into their concept of a worker-led revolution. Maybe Marx skipped our role in his grand theory of history,” she said, giving me a wan smile.
The result of this crash-collectivization was famine. The room has exhibits on the famines of 1919–22 and 1932–3. Kazakhs suffered disproportionately as they lived on fertile land that could produce a lot of wheat. They were forced to abandon their nomadic lifestyle and produce food first for the Red Army, and then for Stalin’s five-year plans. Those who resisted were shot. Many fled to China or Mongolia. Many more starved.
In the Soviet census of 1926 the Kazakh population was 3.6 million; by 1939 this had dropped by a third to 2.3 million. By 1959 Kazakhs numbered a mere 30 percent of the population of the Kazakh SSR.
Along with the demographic assault came the attempts to destroy Kazakh identity. The room next door has a small exhibition dedicated to the entire class of Kazakh intellectuals who were exterminated in the purges of the late 1930s. Just as their way of life was destroyed and their people forced onto farms, their thinkers, authors, and anyone who might be able to articulate the uniqueness of the Kazakh identity were wiped out by NKVD bullets.
Klara had told me about the legend of the Mankurt.
“When a warrior was captured in battle, his head would be shaved by his captors and a piece of damp camel skin would be wrapped tightly around it. He would then be left, tied up in the desert sun, which would dry the camel skin and cause it to contract. His hair would also have no room to grow, so it would grow inwards, into his skull. The resulting pressure on the head would break the prisoner’s mind, causing him to lose all memory, all sense of self, all knowledge of his past and his family. Once broken, he became the perfect slave: the Mankurt, loyal only to his master.”
The story sounds like an ancient steppe legend, but it actually comes from “The Day Lasts More Than a Hundred Years,” a novel by the celebrated Kyrgyz writer Chingiz Aitmatov. The Mankurt became a powerful metaphor across Central Asia for a people stripped of their history and identity. That was precisely how Klara saw the Soviet experience.
articles.summary: Karaganda and its environs are home to some of the largest-scale coal-mining on the planet. And once, the home to an immense gulag.

articles.title: South Korea’s $60 Billion Semiconductor Exports to Drive the KOSPI’s Resurgence
articles.full_text:
South Korea’s economy has become intrinsically linked to the ongoing artificial intelligence boom.
With semiconductors amounting to around two-thirds of the Korea Composite Stock Price Index’s (KOSPI) market capitalization, South Korea’s economy has become intrinsically linked to the ongoing artificial intelligence boom. As exports reach record highs, optimism is growing among investors that the KOSPI can recapture momentum to close out 2026. 
Monthly export value for semiconductors surpassed $60 billion in September, breaking the $120 billion total export threshold for the first time in South Korea. The trend was driven by accelerating demand for AI and memory chips and is paving the way to $1 trillion in annual exports domestically. 
Critically, September’s export figures represented an 83.5 percent boost compared to the same period last year, while daily averages for the month reached a 105 percent year-over-year increase to $5.63 billion per day.  
The KOSPI responded to the news with a 2 percent jump. Despite a clear heavy reliance on semiconductor stocks following years of exponential growth, signs of strength in South Korea’s export activity are likely to instill a newfound confidence in the long-term outlook for the nation’s markets. 
South Korea’s strength in exports has helped to further deepen the growth of the KOSPI’s star players, Samsung and SK Hynix, which posted growth of 2.79 percent and 3.21 percent, respectively, after September’s figures were released by government sources. The two stocks now account for 66 percent of the entirety of the KOSPI index by market capitalization, underlining the nation’s reliance on the performance of the semiconductor giants. 
“There’s a clear case for South Korea as the most impacted market by the rise of artificial intelligence,” explained Vsevolod Smirnov, CMO at Just2Trade. “Since the launch of ChatGPT by OpenAI in November 2022 and the beginning of the GenAI boom, the KOSPI gained more than 270 percent to reach its 2026 peak, but the fact that the index has since tumbled 22.5 percent over the past three months is a warning sign of overreliance.” 
The KOSPI surpassed 9,000 in June, a historic high water mark for the index. But it didn’t remain there long. The KOSPI dropped back into the 8,000s just a week after hitting its all-time record, and spent most of July, August, and September in the 6,000-range.
However, Smirnov sees cause for optimism moving forward. “The good news is that export momentum means that these two semiconductor leaders aren’t selling magic beans. There’s a clear product and evident investor appetite,” he explained. “Both Samsung and SK Hynix have a relatively grounded trailing price-to-earnings ratio of around 10.9 and 7.4, respectively, indicating that both companies are well-positioned to fill their boots moving forward.” 
Analysts expect a return to the positive momentum that helped to push the KOSPI to new highs. Mirae Asset Securities analyst Kim Young-gun noted that DRAM and NAND memory chips are likely to stay undersupplied through 2028, which is likely to drive prices higher in the mid-term future. 
The climate surrounding Samsung, in particular, has remained more optimistic in recent weeks, with the company avoiding a workers’ strike by offering bonuses averaging $400,000. Given that the tech leader is single-handedly responsible for a quarter of South Korea’s exports, the resolution is set to support the national economic outlook. 
The biggest threat to the long-term performance of the KOSPI is wider economic uncertainty, which has become increasingly pertinent as the conflict in Iran has brought higher global oil prices and U.S. Treasury yields. Although the index naturally correlates to the ongoing AI boom, the KOSPI tumbled into the 6,600 range earlier in September as a result of international oil prices climbing beyond $100 a barrel and 10-year U.S. Treasury yields exceeding 5 percent. 
These factors could lead to shortfalls in net buying due to macroeconomic uncertainty. This, coupled with the traditional underperformance of the KOSDAQ following the Chuseok holiday season, could create a weaker conclusion to 2026 for South Korean markets. 
However, the sheer strength of the AI boom appears to be offering some resilience. There is increasing U.S. demand for AI infrastructure, as Wall Street’s “Magnificent Seven” collective of hyperscalers and AI adopters have committed more than $750 billion in capex toward their own AI buildouts. 
With competition over AI investment accelerating beyond GPUs and memory chips toward infrastructure and power, as well as servers and communications, Samsung and SK Hynix are well-positioned to continue achieving their collective potential on the KOSPI throughout the fourth quarter and beyond – in spite of ongoing macroeconomic concerns. 
Although a return to 9,000 is unlikely at a time when U.S. Treasury yields are expected to rise further, South Korea’s positive export figures show a level of resilience that should encourage investors. The KOSPI has been one of the world’s best performers since 2022, following the emergence of the AI rally. While headwinds are continuing to mount, there’s no reason the optimism has to subside looking ahead. 
The upcoming earnings season for South Korea’s semiconductor giants will be critical. Should the likes of Samsung and SK Hynix show that they can justify their momentum, there’s no reason why 9,000 can’t be a legitimate target for the first quarter of 2027.

The two stocks now account for 66 percent of the entirety of the KOSPI index by market capitalization, underlining the nation’s reliance on the performance of the semiconductor giants. 
“There’s a clear case for South Korea as the most impacted market by the rise of artificial intelligence,” explained Vsevolod Smirnov, CMO at Just2Trade. “Since the launch of ChatGPT by OpenAI in November 2022 and the beginning of the GenAI boom, the KOSPI gained more than 270 percent to reach its 2026 peak, but the fact that the index has since tumbled 22.5 percent over the past three months is a warning sign of overreliance.” 
The KOSPI surpassed 9,000 in June, a historic high water mark for the index. But it didn’t remain there long. The KOSPI dropped back into the 8,000s just a week after hitting its all-time record, and spent most of July, August, and September in the 6,000-range.
However, Smirnov sees cause for optimism moving forward. “The good news is that export momentum means that these two semiconductor leaders aren’t selling magic beans. There’s a clear product and evident investor appetite,” he explained. “Both Samsung and SK Hynix have a relatively grounded trailing price-to-earnings ratio of around 10.9 and 7.4, respectively, indicating that both companies are well-positioned to fill their boots moving forward.” 
Analysts expect a return to the positive momentum that helped to push the KOSPI to new highs. Mirae Asset Securities analyst Kim Young-gun noted that DRAM and NAND memory chips are likely to stay undersupplied through 2028, which is likely to drive prices higher in the mid-term future. 
The climate surrounding Samsung, in particular, has remained more optimistic in recent weeks, with the company avoiding a workers’ strike by offering bonuses averaging $400,000. Given that the tech leader is single-handedly responsible for a quarter of South Korea’s exports, the resolution is set to support the national economic outlook. 
The biggest threat to the long-term performance of the KOSPI is wider economic uncertainty, which has become increasingly pertinent as the conflict in Iran has brought higher global oil prices and U.S. Treasury yields. Although the index naturally correlates to the ongoing AI boom, the KOSPI tumbled into the 6,600 range earlier in September as a result of international oil prices climbing beyond $100 a barrel and 10-year U.S. Treasury yields exceeding 5 percent. 
These factors could lead to shortfalls in net buying due to macroeconomic uncertainty. This, coupled with the traditional underperformance of the KOSDAQ following the Chuseok holiday season, could create a weaker conclusion to 2026 for South Korean markets. 
However, the sheer strength of the AI boom appears to be offering some resilience. There is increasing U.S. demand for AI infrastructure, as Wall Street’s “Magnificent Seven” collective of hyperscalers and AI adopters have committed more than $750 billion in capex toward their own AI buildouts.
articles.summary: South Korea’s economy has become intrinsically linked to the ongoing artificial intelligence boom.

articles.title: China’s Revised Defense Mobilization Law Touches Nearly Every Sector
articles.full_text:
The circumstances under which mobilization can be declared are wider than ever, and a large number of entities – including private firms – are legally obligated to the state during wartime.
The revised version of China’s National Defense Mobilization Law came into effect on October 1. It’s the first major overhaul since the statute came into existence in 2010. On its face, the law governs how China can convert civilian economic capacity into military capability during wartime, facilitating a rapid transition for national defense. However, a closer reading of the law indicates that it involves many critical stakeholders and has bearing on many aspects of the economy.
The law, in its original conception in 2010, was construed as Taiwan-centric. It helped build an underlying legal and military architecture to respond if Taiwan were to declare independence. Thus, it had a very clear purpose: war preparation in relation to the longstanding mission of national unification.  
However, the recent revision goes beyond the war preparation narrative and Taiwan contingency. Now, the circumstances under which mobilization can be declared are widened, and the law encompasses a large number of entities that are legally obligated to the state during wartime, including private organizations that are required to assist in mobilization. It also mandates that anything required for mobilization can be levied or expropriated by the state. These revisions make the law relevant for a wide variety of stakeholders, including foreign governments and firms, in scenarios beyond Taiwan – and even in peaceful conditions.
The revision defines defense mobilization as steps taken by the state in response to threats to national sovereignty, unity, territorial integrity, security, and, interestingly, “development interests.”
“Development interests” can’t be read in the same breath as the former categories. Sovereignty, unity, and territorial integrity, and security can be broadly defined with strict bounds, but the definition of “development interests” can be as loose as officials want it to be.  
The Chinese Defense Ministry spokesperson mentioned that the law need not be overinterpreted and is line with similar legislation in place in other countries. In general, the mention of “development interests” in Chinese national discourse acts as a central legitimizing framework, linking the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) authority with continuous economic growth and modernization. 
However, with the phrase’s invocation in the operative definition of the defense mobilization statute, “development interests” has acquired a new extension. A blockade on the Strait of Malacca would not be an attack on territory or sovereignty but might hamper China’s development interests. The long-standing maritime dispute in the South China Sea may also be counted as jeopardizing China’s development interests. 
This raises the question of what would qualify as a development interest – and thus authorize the conversion of civilian resources into military resources. The law delineates no threshold test. The revision has an expansive breadth with abysmally low precision, and it has been designed this way. An elastic law allows authorities to potentially co-opt private resources across a variety of scenarios, not just armed conflicts. 
The law, with loosely defined and vague triggers, keeps a wide variety of stakeholders in its range. There is an obvious Taiwan angle, of course. Taiwanese media outlets report that experts perceive the law as wielding a clear legal warfare dimension for Taiwan. Taiwan’s independence is antithetical to the law, just as it was with the first version from 2010. 
But the new revision has implications far beyond Taiwan. Foreign and domestic firms, under the revised law, become another stakeholder. Military-civil fusion has been a high-priority national strategy of the CCP to systematically eliminate barriers between its commercial civilian research sector and its military-industrial complex. The revised law provides a framework to establish a “data service support system,” giving the state explicit legitimate authority to “collect and use data closely related to defense mobilization” (Article 7).
The law also envelops emerging technologies, including AI. Article 8 of the law states that the state “promotes the application of advanced technologies in national defense mobilization and develops national defense mobilization forces in emerging fields.” It should be read along with Article 7. 
The law requires strategic materials stockpiling and formal security assessments of military product supply chains. It allows the requisition and expropriation of civilian facilities, equipment, vehicles, and premises once mobilization is declared. As a whole, these revisions pave the way for a self-contained system, where a state systematically maps its own dual-use industrial base, making a massive share of the Chinese economy a contingency-based defense asset, while insulating itself against external disruption. 
The “development interests” trigger matters to New Delhi as well. India’s exposure to China is mostly economic, including pharmaceutical inputs, rare earths and magnets, electronics components, solar modules, and capital goods. The new defense mobilization law is elastic enough to cover economic disputes with India as well in its purview, which can act as a formal extension to export restrictions on India already in place since April 2025.
The law plays on an undefined threshold and an expansive perimeter. This makes the revision a significant move by Beijing, given the almost exhaustive list of contingency sectors including transport, telecom, network security, medical, food supply, construction, energy and chemicals, nuclear facilities, news media, and municipal infrastructure. For firms in the Chinese market, due diligence now includes not only asking whether a Chinese partner has identifiable military links, but whether the partner operates in any listed sector, which would be most likely given the vast breadth of the law.
The law doesn’t imply that an emergency is imminent. The revised law can be seen as a part of Beijing’s wider institutional project to restructure its mobilization architecture into an all-encompassing trigger that legitimizes economic coercion. That new reality should shape how the world rates risk in China.
