articles.title: Will US President Donald Trump Visit Central Asia?
articles.full_text:
No U.S. president has ever traveled to Central Asia while in office. Could Donald Trump be the first? Sure. But will he be? That’s a different question.
U.S. President Donald Trump speaks with leaders of C5 Central Asian countries after a dinner in the East Room of the White House, Nov. 6, 2025.
As U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s planned trip to Uzbekistan – at the head of a large delegation of American businesses – approaches, once again Central Asian governments and people are angling for a presidential visit. Both Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan have repeatedly invited Trump to make the trek; he’d be very welcome in the region and they’re hoping the novelty of being the “first” will get them on the presidential calendar. 
In an interview with an Uzbek TV station, U.S. Special Representative for Global Partnerships Paolo Zampolli, said, “I know [Trump] wants to come to Uzbekistan. The president has an extremely busy schedule. But he told me about his intention to visit Uzbekistan. I myself am constantly promoting this issue. So, he will definitely visit Uzbekistan one day. We hope this visit will take place as soon as possible.”
That’s not exactly a firm commitment from a notoriously fickle administration, no matter the rabid headlines about the comments. 
There has been no shortage of U.S. officials traveling to Central Asia since the dawn of the second Trump presidency. These include an October 2025 trip to Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan by Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau and Sergio Gor, concurrently the U.S. ambassador to India and also special envoy for South and Central Asian affairs. In February 2026, Gor returned to Central Asia, visiting Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan. In July 2026, Senator Steve Daines, a Republican from Montana – who co-founded the bipartisan Senate Central Asia Caucus in 2024 – traveled to Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan (and also Azerbaijan). 
U.S. engagement with Central Asia has shifted from Afghanistan – an all-encompassing subject that dominated relations from 2001 to 2021 – to critical minerals, an especially hot topic for governments keen on dealmaking.
In November 2025, amid the fanfare of the C5+1 summit in Washington, in which all five Central Asian presidents were welcomed to the White House for the first time (although it was not the first presidential level C5+1 summit, as some have erroneously reported) – Rubio declared his intention to visit all five Central Asian states in the coming year. 
“I personally intend to visit in the coming year,” he said during a reception after meeting with his Central Asian counterparts, as reported by Reuters. “All five,” Rubio added. “So I know it would probably be a week-long trip. So we’ve got to work on that and make that happen together.”
To date, the highest-ranking U.S. official to complete what I dubbed the “grand Stan slam” was then-Secretary of State John Kerry in 2015. It was during that trip that the C5+1, at the foreign ministers level, was launched in Samarkand, a month after a preview event on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly.
Rubio’s own envisioned  “grand Stan slam” has been apparently whittled down to a trip to Samarkand, with a heavy business focus. According to a September 24 press release published by the U.S. embassy in India, and attributed to Gor, Rubio “will lead a historic business delegation of more than 100 American companies to Samarkand, Uzbekistan in mid-October to advance the U.S.-Central Asia strategic partnership and strengthen bilateral diplomatic and commercial cooperation.”
The Diplomat has heard rumored dates for the trip, but they have yet to be confirmed publicly. And that’s of little surprise. Not only is Rubio serving as secretary of state, but he’s also national security adviser – a role he took over on an interim basis in May 2025 after Michael Waltz flamed out by inviting a journalist into a high-level Signal chat. That role was made permanent on September 22. Rubio’s the second person to wear both hats simultaneously – the first was Henry Kissinger under Presidents Richard Nixon and Gerald Ford. All that to say: Rubio is a busy guy. The planned trip to Samarkand could, frankly speaking, be spoiled by any number of sudden crises.
Aside from Zampolli’s recent comment that Trump “wants” to come to Uzbekistan, there’s been no official word on that front. Trump is often discussed as disliking international travel. Of the three most recent presidents – Barack Obama (2009-2016) Trump 1.0 (2017-2020), and Joe Biden (2021-2024) he’s made the fewest international trips and visited the fewest foreign countries. Obama made a total of 25 foreign trips during his first term, Trump made 19, and Biden 21.
The statistics alone don’t tell the full story. Trump’s presidency ended with the COVID-19 outbreak, and Biden’s began with its lingering impact. So far in his second term, Trump has made 14 foreign trips – six in 2025 and eight so far in 2026. Trump is scheduled, officially, for one more international trip this year: from November 16 to 19, to attend the ASEAN Summit and the East Asia Summit in the Philippines and then to attend the APEC Summit in Shenzhen, China.
The year is drawing to a close, rapidly. The looming mid-term elections, scheduled for November 3 – and not looking good, per most polls, for the president’s party – might jerk Trump’s attention back to the domestic arena, making a late-year junket to Tashkent nearly impossible and potentially ruining future plans, too.
Trump does have two years left in his term, so a Central Asia visit may eventuate – he could also visit any of the more than 75 other countries a U.S. president has never traveled to while in office.  Spoilers abound both internationally and domestically that could dash the highest of hopes for a U.S. president to finally step foot in Central Asia. But hope springs eternal.

articles.title: What Would Europe Do in a Taiwan Crisis?
articles.full_text:
Washington should not take European assistance for granted, especially if states can’t agree on how to label Beijing’s actions.
Imagine that, one morning, Chinese coast guard vessels begin stopping commercial ships approaching Taiwan. Beijing offers the official explanation that the operation is necessary to enforce customs regulations and maritime safety and makes clear that it does not consider this a blockade, let alone an act of war. Taipei clearly sees things differently and calls it an attempt to blockade the island. Washington agrees with Taipei.
Europe, however, is less certain, with some governments demanding that China stop its actions while others start calling for restraint and dialogue. Officials begin debating whether the operation constitutes an armed attack, what international law permits, and whether sanctions against China would be justified. Meanwhile the effects on global trade start to be felt as insurers raise premiums, shipping companies start to reroute vessels, and financial markets react nervously.
At that point, Washington steps up and asks its European allies to impose economic costs on Beijing. The answer from Europe could very likely be an attempt to win more time to determine what is happening. That delay could incidentally be precisely what Beijing is aiming to achieve: deliberate ambiguity, namely the systematic creation of legal and political uncertainty designed to make an adversary hesitate over how to respond.
We have already seen elements of this approach tested on Taiwan. In June 2026, Chinese coast guard vessels conducted patrols east of Taiwan, described by Beijing as lawful maritime enforcement, while Taiwan accused China of asserting jurisdiction over commercial shipping. The United States, Britain, France, and Germany subsequently expressed concern about the operations but their protest remained at the level of rhetoric. Barely a week later, in July, Taiwan observed a sharp increase in Chinese coast guard and research vessel activities and publicly warned that such operations could be connected to preparations to disrupt maritime supply routes.
Even though such actions can be seen as acts of rehearsal, they cannot be interpreted as definitive proof that Beijing has undeniably decided to blockade Taiwan. They definitely show one thing, though: namely, how easily a future crisis could be presented in opposite ways by different sides, and how this difference could complicate a unified response between Washington and its allies.
This is one fallacy Washington should avoid: assuming that because Europe is an ally and it has enormous collective economic power, that power will automatically be available as a coherent instrument in a crisis, side by side with Washington. It may not be. The United States should therefore be encouraging and, where necessary, nudging, European governments to develop contingency plans before a crisis begins, precisely so that their institutional structure does not become an advantage for Beijing.
There is a structural reason why Europe could struggle to use its leverage quickly. The European project was built above all through economic integration – a common market, common rules and, for much of the European Union, a common currency. Foreign and security policy evolved differently and remains largely in the hands of national governments. The EU’s Common Foreign and Security Policy generally requires unanimity, as do the sanctions decisions that would be among the most important instruments available in a Taiwan crisis. 
This division matters because a blockade would sit precisely at the intersection of economic and foreign policy: European governments could agree that Taiwan’s security matters while disagreeing over whether Chinese actions constitute a sufficient trigger for collective economic measures. The European Parliament has already recognized the need for contingency planning, explicitly calling for preparations for scenarios including an economic blockade of Taiwan. But planning for a contingency is not the same thing as having a common response ready to deploy.
A blockade could therefore confront Washington with two crises at once: a crisis around Taiwan and a crisis within the coalition supporting Taiwan.
Beijing could exploit precisely those divisions by threatening restrictions against particular European countries or companies, using its monopoly on critical materials and rare earths as leverage, or offering selective economic incentives. The objective would be to make European governments reluctant to support measures that might trigger further retaliation.
And to this point, there is another complication that Washington should not overlook in its strategic planning. European governments are already reassessing their dependence on the United States as they assume a greater share of the burden for Ukraine and confront uncertainty over the future of the transatlantic relationship under President Donal Trump. At NATO’s 2026 summit, European allies and Canada acknowledged that they now finance the vast majority of security assistance to Ukraine, while Reuters has reported growing European efforts to diversify away from U.S. defense technology amid doubts about the reliability of American commitments. 
European governments are not abandoning the alliance – many continue to emphasize its importance – but they are increasingly preparing for a world in which U.S. priorities may shift more abruptly than in the past. In such an environment, a Taiwan crisis could arrive at precisely the wrong moment: when Washington expects Europe to follow its lead, some European governments may opt instead for asking how far they should go in assuming the economic and political costs of confronting China and of following the United States, in spite of the obvious fact that a Taiwan crisis would have direct consequences for Europe’s own security, economy, and strategic interests.
Europe and the world should prepare for such contingencies. In less than two years Taiwan is scheduled to hold another presidential election on its regular four-year cycle, following the January 2024 election. This makes 2028 a useful planning horizon, since a new government in Taipei could produce renewed tensions with Beijing, depending on its policies and Beijing’s reaction. The point is not to predict that a crisis will occur in 2028, but to ensure that Washington and its European allies do not discover the limits of their respective contingency plans only after a new political configuration in Taiwan has already raised tensions.
Therefore, the United States and its European allies should privately work through concrete scenarios – prolonged inspections of commercial vessels, selective denial of port access, Chinese coast guard “escorts,” restrictions on shipping insurance, interference with critical infrastructure, and economic retaliation against individual European states. The objective would not be to predetermine every possible scenario or response, but to prevent the first days of a crisis from being consumed by arguments over terminology and definition.
More concretely than that, such preparation also needs to extend beyond the level of governments by including shipping companies, insurers, ports, banks, technology firms, and semiconductor manufacturers – actors who would would make decisions before diplomats reached an agreement. This would also have a plus side: European governments will be more willing to support collective measures if they know that the costs of Chinese retaliation will not fall disproportionately on one or two vulnerable countries.
None of this would require Europe to adopt Washington’s China policy or promise military intervention in a Taiwan conflict. The goal, instead, is agreement in advance about which forms of coercion would cross a line, what economic measures could be considered, and how their costs could be shared.
The United States has spent years strengthening military deterrence around Taiwan, yet the next Taiwan crisis may not begin with an invasion but with a disagreement over what to call what is happening. Washington’s task, therefore, is not to lament Europe’s fragmentation or demand that it simply follow the American lead, but to work with European governments now to overcome the structural obstacles that could turn hesitation into paralysis when a Taiwan crisis comes.

The United States should therefore be encouraging and, where necessary, nudging, European governments to develop contingency plans before a crisis begins, precisely so that their institutional structure does not become an advantage for Beijing.
There is a structural reason why Europe could struggle to use its leverage quickly. The European project was built above all through economic integration – a common market, common rules and, for much of the European Union, a common currency. Foreign and security policy evolved differently and remains largely in the hands of national governments. The EU’s Common Foreign and Security Policy generally requires unanimity, as do the sanctions decisions that would be among the most important instruments available in a Taiwan crisis. 
This division matters because a blockade would sit precisely at the intersection of economic and foreign policy: European governments could agree that Taiwan’s security matters while disagreeing over whether Chinese actions constitute a sufficient trigger for collective economic measures. The European Parliament has already recognized the need for contingency planning, explicitly calling for preparations for scenarios including an economic blockade of Taiwan. But planning for a contingency is not the same thing as having a common response ready to deploy.
A blockade could therefore confront Washington with two crises at once: a crisis around Taiwan and a crisis within the coalition supporting Taiwan.
Beijing could exploit precisely those divisions by threatening restrictions against particular European countries or companies, using its monopoly on critical materials and rare earths as leverage, or offering selective economic incentives. The objective would be to make European governments reluctant to support measures that might trigger further retaliation.
And to this point, there is another complication that Washington should not overlook in its strategic planning. European governments are already reassessing their dependence on the United States as they assume a greater share of the burden for Ukraine and confront uncertainty over the future of the transatlantic relationship under President Donal Trump. At NATO’s 2026 summit, European allies and Canada acknowledged that they now finance the vast majority of security assistance to Ukraine, while Reuters has reported growing European efforts to diversify away from U.S. defense technology amid doubts about the reliability of American commitments. 
European governments are not abandoning the alliance – many continue to emphasize its importance – but they are increasingly preparing for a world in which U.S. priorities may shift more abruptly than in the past. In such an environment, a Taiwan crisis could arrive at precisely the wrong moment: when Washington expects Europe to follow its lead, some European governments may opt instead for asking how far they should go in assuming the economic and political costs of confronting China and of following the United States, in spite of the obvious fact that a Taiwan crisis would have direct consequences for Europe’s own security, economy, and strategic interests.
articles.summary: Washington should not take European assistance for granted, especially if states can't agree on how to label Beijing's actions.

articles.title: Taiwan’s Maritime Law Enforcement Operations Spark Anger in Chinese Society
articles.full_text:
The reaction to a Taiwan Coast Guard confrontation reflects the existence of a particularly hardline strand of opinion on Taiwan among mainland Chinese.
Taiwan Coast Guard personnel board and inspect a fishing vessel from mainland China , Oct. 1, 2026.
On October 1, a Chinese mainland fishing vessel came into a confrontation with a Taiwan Coast Guard vessel near the Pratas (Dongsha) Islands. After the fishing boat refused to leave the waters, the Taiwan Coast Guard vessel used a water cannon against it, eventually forcing it to leave the area. 
Just one day earlier, the Taiwan Coast Guard had detained another Chinese fishing vessel near Penghu and taken control of its seven crew members.
The incident quickly attracted widespread attention on Chinese social media. Videos showing a Taiwan Coast Guard vessel spraying the Chinese fishing boat with a water cannon were widely circulated, prompting widespread criticism of what many described as the Taiwanese vessel’s heavy-handed conduct. Some commentators interpreted the incident as a deliberate provocation by Taipei on the National Day of the People’s Republic of China. 
However, much of the criticism was directed not only at Taiwan, but also at the Chinese government itself. Some argued that Beijing’s repeated “concessions” toward Taiwan had encouraged Taipei to become increasingly assertive. Others even questioned whether Beijing is capable of effectively protecting Chinese fishermen. The reaction reflects the existence of a particularly hardline strand of opinion on Taiwan in mainland Chinese society, which frequently criticizes the government for being “too weak” toward Taiwan.
This challenges a narrative in which Beijing is portrayed as the main driver of coercive pressure against Taiwan, while mainland Chinese society simply passively absorbs Chinese Communist Party (CCP) propaganda about national (re)unification. In fact, in recent confrontations between Taiwan’s government vessels and civilian vessels from the mainland, Beijing has often exercised restraint and refrained from using its superior military capabilities in response. 
Following the October incident, for example, the Taiwan Affairs Office of the PRC State Council merely called on Taiwan not to “use dangerous methods to treat mainland vessels and crew members in a heavy-handed manner.” Beijing has so far refrained from escalating the situation through its maritime forces.
This resembles Beijing’s handling of the February 2024 fishing boat incident near Kinmen, in which two mainland fishermen died after their vessel capsized during a confrontation with Taiwan’s Coast Guard. At the time, visible anger emerged on mainland Chinese social media. Related Weibo posts received more than 50 million views, accompanied by calls for retaliation against Taiwan. However, Beijing ultimately responded in a relatively restrained manner. 
This raises an important question. Beijing has conducted repeated military drills around Taiwan in recent years, and confrontations between Chinese fishermen and the Taiwan Coast Guard might appear to provide convenient opportunities to demonstrate Chinese military power. So why has Beijing refrained from doing so?
Beijing must strike a balance between military deterrence and the image of itself as a guarantor of peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait. A forceful response to Taiwan might satisfy public anger in the short term, but it could also reinforce Taiwanese society’s perception of the mainland as a security threat over the longer term.
Beijing frequently uses military exercises as a signal to Taipei and the international community of its determination to safeguard national unity. However, although Beijing continues to insist that such activities are directed only at the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) and “Taiwan independence separatist forces,” polling suggests that a substantial share of the Taiwanese public regards these activities as a threat to Taiwan. Against this backdrop, any retaliatory action by the China Coast Guard or the People’s Liberation Army Navy against Taiwan could be presented by Taipei as further evidence of a military threat from the mainland. 
Therefore, it is necessary for Beijing to calibrate the use of force carefully, lest coercive measures produce the opposite of their intended effect and undermine the credibility of deterrence. This may help explain why incidents such as fishing boat confrontations are not necessarily regarded in Beijing as occasions warranting a military response.
However, growing public dissatisfaction with Taiwan in mainland China could push cross-strait relations into a more dangerous direction. It could transform tensions between the CCP and the DPP into a broader conflict between two societies across the Taiwan Strait. Although direct interaction between people on the two sides has declined substantially since 2016, the remaining interpersonal, economic, and cultural ties between the two societies continue to play an important role in preserving peace across the strait.
A recent poll found that mainland respondents still held broadly positive attitudes toward Taiwan. Their average feeling toward Taiwan rose from 57 points in 2025 to 61 points in 2026, on a 100-point scale. At the same time, 38 percent agreed that force should never be used to achieve (re)unification under any circumstances, while 47 percent disagreed. When asked what measures could be taken if Taiwan formally declared independence, 81 percent supported “limited military operations on offshore islands,” but only 32 percent supported “a full-scale military attack.” 
When asked why (re)unification between the mainland and Taiwan was important, 71 percent pointed to the two sides’ shared cultural heritage. These findings reveal an important ambivalence in mainland Chinese attitudes toward Taiwan: Opposition to the independence of Taiwan coexists with a sense of cultural affinity toward Taiwanese society.
Maritime confrontations, however, could cause this attitude to deteriorate, and the Chinese government itself could become an early target of public anger. For years, alongside military deterrence, Beijing has sought to improve Taiwanese attitudes toward the mainland through economic incentives and other forms of preferential treatment. However, these policies are often interpreted within mainland Chinese society as evidence of the failure of Beijing’s Taiwan strategy. These sweeteners have not persuaded Taiwanese society to move toward support for (re)unification. When PRC citizens see Taiwan’s Coast Guard forcibly enforcing its regulations against mainland fishing vessels, Beijing’s preferential policies toward Taiwan may instead be interpreted as a betrayal of the interests of the Chinese people. After Japan proceeded with the nationalization of the islands, Beijing significantly intensified its response.

Taiwan’s firm maritime enforcement may appear to reinforce the DPP’s longstanding hardline position toward Beijing, but its immediate effect may be felt not only by the Chinese government but also by Chinese society. articles.title: Iranian Ships Test Sri Lanka’s Sovereignty Again
articles.full_text:
The U.S. has threatened Sri Lanka with sanctions if it provides supplies to Iranian vessels stranded off its coasts.
On Sept. 30, 2026, the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported that U.S. officials threatened Sri Lanka with sanctions if it continued supplying around 20 Iranian tankers stranded off its coast. According to WSJ, the tankers are running short of food, fuel, and fresh water.
Sources in Sri Lanka’s Foreign Ministry told The Diplomat that the U.S. embassy in Colombo and visiting American civilian and military officials have repeatedly warned Sri Lanka against providing the Iranian vessels with essential supplies, despite the potential humanitarian crisis. Sri Lanka’s national security establishment reportedly objected to these demands and called on the government to convey its displeasure to Washington, as they are opposed to leaving the Iranian crew stranded and suffering.
With the WSJ report, the matter has now become public, restricting the maneuvering space of the Sri Lankan government.
The incident reveals the limits of sovereignty of small states like Sri Lanka that depend on exports to the Global North. Washington has considerable means to punish any resistance from Sri Lanka, and the question before Colombo now is how it can protect its economic interests while retaining the freedom to provide basic humanitarian assistance to friendly nations.
Foreign Minister Vijitha Herath has tried to distance the government from any private suppliers who might be supplying the stranded Iranian ships. Speaking to the Sunday Times, Herath said that the authorities had identified 15 Iranian vessels among 47 foreign ships outside Sri Lanka’s territorial waters. He confirmed that Iran had requested essential supplies for the stranded ships but said that the government had provided nothing and did not intend to do so.
Herath described provisioning the ships as a private business. Companies could make their own decisions, he said, after considering the possibility of U.S. secondary sanctions. Foreign Ministry spokesman Thushara Rodrigo told local media that U.S. sanctions apply globally and that these are not threats targeted at one country.
Colombo’s caution has an obvious economic explanation. The Export Development Board’s report for the first six months of 2026 puts the United States’ share of Sri Lanka’s merchandise exports at approximately 22 percent. The European Union accounts for 25.5 percent, with Britain providing another substantial market. These figures explain why Sri Lankan policymakers worry about disputes with Western governments.
Yet accepting every U.S. demand also carries costs.
If Colombo does not provide drinking water to hundreds of stranded Iranians due to the fear of economic punishment, it invites further U.S. interference in decisions that should be its own. Officials urging a firmer response recognize that Sri Lanka must sometimes express disagreement to preserve any freedom of action.
In the past, Sri Lanka has indicated that it is willing to risk U.S. ire on humanitarian grounds.
After an American submarine sank an Iranian naval frigate, IRIS Dena, off the Sri Lankan coast in March, Sri Lanka rescued survivors. Colombo subsequently took custody of IRIS Bushehr, brought its sailors ashore and repatriated over 230 Iranians to safety.
India’s recent conduct complicates the decisions before Colombo. New Delhi presents itself as a regional security provider and has had a longstanding relationship with Tehran. Smaller neighbors expect India to take charge when external powers take military action in its backyard. However, when the U.S. sank IRIS Dena, India was nowhere to be found. Sri Lanka had to do the heavy lifting without any military support or diplomatic cover from India.
In recent years, India has grown closer to the United States and Israel. On the other hand, Sri Lanka has taken a strong pro-Palestinian stance and refused to sponsor a Bahrain-led United Nations Security Council resolution against Iran in March 2026.
However, these pressures must not let Sri Lanka diminish its sovereignty. Economic dependence on the West makes exercising its sovereignty difficult, but surrendering its foreign policy decision-making to Washington now would gradually reduce the matters over which Sri Lanka exercises meaningful control.
Sri Lanka cannot afford a reckless confrontation with the United States. Its government must consider the Sri Lankan livelihoods that depend on Western markets. But protecting those livelihoods also requires judging which risks the country can bear. Treating every American objection as a veto would leave Colombo with little foreign policy of its own. Fear of U.S. pressure has already constrained Sri Lanka’s willingness to pursue Russian oil and nuclear energy agreements or certain investments with China.
The government should convey its objections to American officials and allow willing private suppliers to deliver essential provisions to the stranded Iranian vessels. It should explain the risks to the public and defend its decision to prevent a humanitarian emergency.
Sri Lanka took a calculated risk when it rescued Iranian sailors in March. It must now show the same willingness to act before hunger and thirst endanger lives. Dependence on Western markets cannot become a justification for abandoning people at sea.

articles.title: Urban Rail in Southeast Asia Is Booming
articles.full_text:
Due to rapid economic growth and Chinese knowhow, public transit in the region’s cities is entering something of a golden age.
Line 2A of Hanoi’s metro system, close to Van Quan station.
The last few years have seen a rapid expansion of urban rail systems throughout Southeast Asia, with major new lines going into operation in Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Vietnam, and the Philippines, and more on the way. From 2015 to 2026, well over 400 kilometers of new track and extensions were completed across Bangkok, Kuala Lumpur, Jakarta, Manila, Hanoi, and Ho Chi Minh City. Between now and 2032, at least 200 kilometers are in an advanced stage of planning or already well into construction.
In addition to that, Chinese-backed high-speed rail lines are already operating in Indonesia and Laos, with construction on additional lines in Thailand and Malaysia well underway. For rail enthusiasts and fans of public transit generally, the region is going through something of a golden era. And that’s not even counting Singapore, which has an extremely comprehensive transit system spanning the entire island.
In 2015, Bangkok was operating its famous Skytrain, a single subway line and a rail link. The Philippines had an MRT that was over a decade old and two light rail lines, one of which was built in the 1980s. Kuala Lumpur had an airport link and commuter system, along with three rapid rail lines. In the decade since, tens of billions of dollars have poured into new and expanded lines all across the region, boosting capacity by hundreds of millions of passengers.
Between 2016 and 2023, Bangkok opened the Purple, Yellow, and Pink lines at a combined cost of around $5 billion. The Orange line, with a price tag in excess of $4 billion, is expected to become operational in phases between 2028 and 2030. The Skytrain was extended, a commuter line was added, and extensions to the Purple line are underway. Ridership across the system increased from 359 million in 2017 to 520 million last year.
Malaysia inaugurated its Shah Alam Line earlier this year, a project that cost approximately $5 billion, including five new stations still under construction. The Putrajaya line, which fully opened in 2023, cost around $7 billion and added over 50 kilometers of track. Kuala Lumpur and the surrounding area now have six rapid rail lines, not including commuter rail or bus, with total ridership of 330 million in 2025. Malaysia is also one of the few countries in the region that is starting to build urban rail in cities outside of the capital.
Manila has been operating at least one light rail service since 1984. The MRT was fully opened in 2000 and a second LRT in 2003. Then very little progress was made, despite the fact that the system carried over 411 million passengers in 2014. That will change soon, as a new MRT line is nearing completion and should open next year. A $7 billion subway project is also underway, which is expected to be operational in the next few years, along with the 147-kilometer North-South Commuter Rail valued at around $14 billion.
Indonesia and Vietnam are the newest entrants to the region’s modern urban rail club. Until recently, commuters in Jakarta had to make do with an aging commuter rail system that traces its roots to the colonial era. In 2019, the Jakarta MRT was opened, followed by a pair of light rail systems. The total cost was around $4 billion, and the system carried over 81 million passengers in 2025. Expansion plans, particularly for the MRT, are in various stages of development and construction.
Vietnam opened its first metro line in Hanoi in 2021, and in Ho Chi Minh City in 2024. A second Hanoi metro line is partially operational, with full operations expected in 2027. More lines are planned. Progress on Vietnam’s metro lines has been very slow, however, in large part because of cumbersome land acquisition. If that bottleneck can be solved, we should expect the pace and scale of urban transit in Vietnam’s major cities to pick up in the years ahead.
It’s clear that urban rail in the region is experiencing a huge resurgence. But what is driving this trend? One obvious factor is economic growth. Manila, Bangkok, and Kuala Lumpur invested in their metro systems in the late 1990s, but momentum slowed with the onset of the Asian Financial Crisis. It took over a decade to reach a point where they were comfortable investing in urban rail again and as their economic resources increase, more of those resources are being directed to building out urban infrastructure.
We should also consider the role of China. It would be wrong to say that China is driving all of this. We see a range of financing and development arrangements across these projects, including a major role for Japanese development finance, multilateral lenders like the Asian Development Bank, European firms and even some domestic players.
But Chinese capital and technology are certainly an important part of the story. It gives rapidly growing economies in the region more options as they look to upgrade and expand their urban transit systems, and it may encourage competitors to more aggressively pursue projects for fear of losing market share. We can debate the mechanism, but the result is clear: urban transit in Southeast Asia is absolutely booming, and looks set to keep growing in the years ahead.

articles.title: Laos Replaces Prime Minister in Major Leadership Reshuffle
articles.full_text:
Saleumxay Kommasith, a former foreign minister and permanent representative to the UN, has been appointed to the top job.
Lao Foreign Minister Saleumxay Kommasith meets with ASEAN Secretary-General Dr. Kao Kim Hourn on the sidelines of the 56th ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ Meeting and Related Meetings in Jakarta, Indonesia, July 12, 2023.
Laos’ National Assembly yesterday approved a major leadership change that included the removal of Prime Minister Sonexay Siphandone.
In what the state-run Vientiane Times described as “a significant change in senior state leadership,” lawmakers yesterday voted unanimously to appoint Sonexay’s deputy Saleumxay Kommasith as the country’s new prime minister. Sonexay was appointed president of the National Assembly, succeeding the late Xaysomphone Phomvihane.
The position has been vacant since Xaysomphone, the son of revered communist leader Kaysone Phomvihane, died in August at the age of 70. The Central Committee of the ruling Lao People’s Revolutionary Party described his passing as “an immense loss for the Party, the State and the Lao people of all ethnic groups.”
According to the Laotian Times, 57-year-old Saleumxay has a background in diplomacy, having spent much of his career in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. He has previously served as Laos’ representative to the United Nations and as foreign minister between 2016 and 2024, and was also appointed as a deputy prime minister in 2022.
Beyond the need to fill the vacant National Assembly position, Lao media reports were reticent about the reasons for Sonexay’s removal, and in Laos it is often hard to separate performance-based from patronage-based appointments. Nonetheless, the fact that he was kept on as prime minister at the last national congress of the LPRP in January, presumably with the expectation that he would serve for a full five-year term, suggests that the reasons for his removal are probably more short-term.
Indeed, his successor’s address to the National Assembly after yesterday’s vote may offer some clues as to the change. articles.title: China’s AI Governance Push and the Race to Shape Global AI Rules
articles.full_text:
In contrast to Washington’s fragmented approach, Beijing is showing an impressive ability to enact and coordinate regulations, policies, technical standards, and enforcement.
On September 12, China’s National Data Administration (NDA) announced that it would develop standards for embodied artificial intelligence (AI) data. The announcement followed a September 10 meeting chaired by NDA head Liu Liehong, where seven key digital companies called for shared public data infrastructure for smart physical machinery and robotics, along with unified data standards. The participants included the startups ModelBest, Infinigence AI, and X Square Robot.
While much remains to be seen regarding raw AI development and emerging technologies in general, this announcement is an indicator of a broader trend, with China increasingly building a centralized and coordinated framework for governing how AI is developed and deployed. This is critical because establishing usable rules around AI has significant implications, potentially becoming nearly as vital as the ability to develop the underlying AI models themselves. As a result, safety and governance are becoming strategic components of the global competition over AI.
AI governance is a critical front in the broader arena of non-kinetic competition between China and the United States. Instead of direct armed conflict, some have described a new “Silent Cold War,” which focuses on topics like AI, semiconductor chips, and foreign investment. AI is especially important because of its dual-use nature, with its capabilities ranging from advising a fifth-grade child on her homework to providing a 99 percent facial verification match on a suspected human trafficker at a border crossing.
China’s history of increased AI model exportation, which could result in increased information influence, has been detailed as one of the implications originating from the AI arms race between the U.S. and China. This is particularly important for countries in the Global South, due to the influx of Chinese infrastructure designed to support AI, with many of these efforts being made as part of the Belt and Road and Digital Silk Road Initiatives.
If Chinese firms become major providers of AI models and their corresponding cloud services, data centers, and energy grids, then China may also gain influence over technical standards, data practices, content controls, and what defines responsible AI in the first place.
This makes AI governance a regulatory issue that must be tackled at an international level rather than at a regional or domestic level. For developing countries deciding which AI systems to adopt, governance frameworks can be a key driver for these nations, with a country selecting an AI provider simultaneously adopting the same standards for data management, content moderation, privacy, and system oversight.
Consequently, AI governance has become a key frontier topic that must be top-of-mind for policymakers worldwide. AI has and is already being leveraged for nefarious purposes, ranging from human-driven prompts promoting deepfakes and impersonation to AI-generated misinformation.
Most recently, U.S.-based Claude maker Anthropic and ChatGPT’s OpenAI faced significant backlash due to key AI safety concerns, with both AI makers disclosing that their own models went rogue in their own capacities. This was compounded by the resignation of a former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher around the same period, with this researcher openly citing these same elements as the reason for his resignation.
Therefore, the core regulatory dilemma has become how to regulate AI while still enabling innovation. The U.S. has often approached this challenge through things like voluntary commitments, state-level laws, and a smattering of sector-specific rules. This approach prioritizes flexibility, but at the cost of fragmentation.
For example, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology released an AI Risk Management Framework in early 2023, with this currently being revised as part of the White House AI Action Plan released in early 2025. However, this framework remains entirely voluntary. Fragmentation in America’s governance space has remained significant, with some states like Colorado, New York, and California issuing AI-specific legislation, while the vast majority of other states have not.
In stark contrast to America’s fragmented approach, China’s top-down approach has resulted in the creation of a multi-layered regulatory system that covers different parts of the AI lifecycle. This model gives specific regulators concrete levers over AI deployments, even as AI development continues to advance at a blistering pace.
The National Data Administration’s approach is the most recent epitome of this approach. It is focusing on developing standards for the data used to train AI for physical machinery and robotics, while also establishing common standards. This is significant because embodied AI depends heavily on data collected in the physical world. Establishing common approaches to collecting, organizing, and evaluating this data could become an important part of building an AI-enabled domestic robotics ecosystem.
China has pursued similar governance measures in other efforts in AI. On July 15, the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC), China’s top internet regulator, brought its Interim Measures for the Administration of Anthropomorphic AI Interaction Services into effect. This law specifically regulates AI systems that simulate human personality traits, with the CAC introducing prohibited content, rules for minors, and highlighting necessary safety assessments for compliance, among others.
Additionally, on May 8, the CAC, the National Development and Reform Commission, and the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology jointly released the Implementation Opinions on the Standardized Application and Innovative Development of Intelligent Agents. This marked China’s first comprehensive national policy framework specific to agentic AI, introducing tiered risk governance, priority scenarios, and “off-switches” for exigent circumstances.
The rapid and cohesive pace of this legislation highlights China’s desire to govern AI in a more stringent and systematic manner. Chinese regulators are already connecting policy, technical standards, data infrastructure, and implementation. These efforts could increase the amount of Chinese-built AI systems used on a worldwide scale, particularly as Beijing increasingly positions its systems as usable and trusted due to its leadership in AI governance.
For many, the AI race seems to be determined by who will create the fastest and most advanced AI system. However, China is demonstrating that this race is instead being decided by which country creates an environment in which AI can be trusted, deployed, and adopted at scale.
China’s growing advantage is increasingly visible in its ability to connect regulations, policies, technical standards, and enforcement. As Chinese AI systems and infrastructure become more prevalent internationally, establishing clear governance practices could enable China increased influence over how AI is regulated and deployed on an international level. If America continues to rely on its fragmented and voluntary approach, it risks enabling China to play a larger role in setting the rules that shape the future of the world’s AI economy.

articles.title: At Least 8 Dead in Myanmar Air Strikes, Rakhine Rebel Group Claims
articles.full_text:
In a desperate bid to claw back territory from the Arakan Army, the Myanmar military has ramped up its use of air power.
Myanmar’s military has launched airstrikes on camps for internally displaced people in Rakhine State, killing at least eight people and leaving more injured, according to a local ethnic rebel organization.
The Arakan Army (AA), a Rakhine nationalist group that controls much of the state in western Myanmar, said yesterday that a Y12 aircraft bombed a displacement shelter and a nearby village in AA-controlled Ponnagyun Township, The Irrawaddy reported. One civilian was killed and two injured in the attack, it added.
This came after six were killed in an air attack on a separate displacement camp in the township on Sunday night, the AA claimed. Several more were injured in the attack, which also destroyed buildings.
The two attacks were also confirmed by ​the Ponnagyun Youth Association, which told Reuters that everyone killed or injured was a “displaced civilian.”
“Attacking these civilian targets with aircraft was a deliberative move,” Wai Hun Aung, a prominent Rakhine writer and aid worker, told The Irrawaddy, adding that the camps were located far from the active combat zone in Rakhine State.
This week’s airstrikes are just the latest to take place in Rakhine, as the Myanmar armed forces attempt to claw back territory from the AA. Much of the state has fallen under the control of the AA since late 2023, when the group and its allies launched an offensive known as Operation 1027. The military has only a few precarious footholds in the state now, including the state capital Sittwe and several other coastal areas. As it has done in other parts of Myanmar, it has begun to lean heavily on its air power to punish civilian populations and stave off further losses.
The attacks came a week after a major aerial attack in neighboring Kyauktaw township on September 28, which killed 50 people and wounded at least ​58, according to the AA and other local sources. In December, an attack on a hospital in Mrauk U township killed at least 30 people.
The attacks indicate that despite the efforts of the new quasi-civilian government to project a sense of stability and normalcy, the situation in much of the country is unstable. Since taking office as president in April, coup leader-turned-President Min Aung Hlaing has launched a diplomatic offensive aimed at normalizing Myanmar’s relations with its neighbors. This includes the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), which has excluded Myanmar from its summits since late 2021 over its failure to implement the bloc’s Five-Point Consensus conflict resolution plan.
In a response to the September 28 attack, the Philippines, ASEAN’s current chair, said that it was “closely monitoring developments” and expressed “concern” over the attacks, ​Foreign Affairs Assistant Secretary for ASEAN Affairs Ana Marie ​Hernando told Reuters on Saturday. The air strike was also condemned by U.N. human rights chief Volker Türk.
While Myanmar’s military has recently succeeded in halting the loss of territory to ethnic armed groups and other resistance factions, nearly 3.8 million people remain displaced across the country, according to the United Nations, and the central state’s hold on much of the country remains either loose or non-existent.
With the failure of a recent military offensive aimed at seizing territory around Sittwe, the Myanmar armed forces will likely compensate by relying ever more heavily on the use of air power in Rakhine State.

articles.title: How Christian Networks in Asia Are Shaping Support for Israel
articles.full_text:
As Israel faces growing pressure in the West, Eagles’ Wings mission brings Christian leaders from across the globe to show support for the Jewish people and Israel
With much of the international discourse, specifically in North America and Europe, focused on criticizing Israel, a large group of international Christian leaders congregated in Jerusalem to show support. One of the key participants was senior Filipino pastor Bishop Dr. David A. Sobrepeña who leads a large evangelical community across the Philippine islands. Bishop Sobrepeña is the founder of Word of Hope Christian Ministries which includes 43 satellite churches and hosts 70 services on any given Sunday across Manila.  Partaking in this year’s event, Bishop Sobrepeña stated, “For Christians in the Philippines, the opportunity to come here and pray in Jerusalem is deeply meaningful. We also come to listen to the people of Israel and to carry their stories back to the churches and communities we serve.”
The Bishop was one of more than 550 prominent Christian leaders with vast followings who recently participated in a 10-day Eagles’ Wings delegation organized in conjunction with Bishop Sterns and Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Attendees hailed from 51 different nations and congregated around the Jewish holiday of Sukkot (Feast of Tabernacles) in Jerusalem, commemorating the third anniversary of the October 7th attack.  The gathering offers a window into a less frequently discussed dimension of the Israel debate: the continued mobilization of Christian communities in parts of Asia and the wider Global South around Israel.
Taking a closer look at Israel sentiment in Western countries, antisemitism interwoven with anti-Israel sentiment is on the rise. In 2025 the Anti Defamation League (ADL) recorded 6,274 antisemitic events in North America alone. The Hillel organization reported 2,334 incidents across U.S. campuses in the 2024-2025 academic year, stating that, “Antisemitic incidents on campus are at a record high in the past school year.”
In Western Europe the Community Security Trust (CST) recorded a staggering 3,700 antisemitic incidents across Britain over the course of 2025, the second highest annual total of such events ever recorded. French authorities cited 1,320 antisemitic acts in 2025, with France’s Interior Ministry calling it a “historically high” figure.
As sentiment over Israel grows increasingly polarized in the West, there are a number of well-educated Asian evangelical Christian communities who unequivocally support Israel, comprising the backbone of its support in the region. South Korea is home to nearly 9 million evangelical and Pentecostal Protestants who display the Israeli flag during rallies and prayers. Roughly 8 percent of Singapore’s population run a network of influential evangelical megachurches while boasting an active Christian Zionist movement that mobilizes fundraising initiatives, educational tours and pro-Israel forums.
The Philippines is a particularly heavy hitter on the East Asian evangelical pro-Zionist front with an estimated 13 million evangelical adherents within a predominantly Catholic milieu. A Pew study surveying Pentecostals across 10 nations highlighted that 67 percent of Filipino Pentecostals surveyed said they sympathized with Israel.
In this context, Eagles’ Wings has been working for the last three decades to bring tens of thousands of evangelical Christians from around the globe to Israel. The organization was founded by Bishop Robert Stearns who is a staunch supporter of Israel and an outspoken supporter of moving the United States Embassy to Jerusalem. In Stephen Spector’s 2008 book Evangelicals and Israel: The Story of American Christian Zionism, Bishop Stearns discusses Israel’s regional threat profile while declaring himself willing to “die defending Israel.” He has spoken on Israel’s behalf both at the House of Lords in London and the Israeli Knesset.
Stearns founded Eagles’ Wings with a clear mission in mind: Firsthand encounters with Israel can be utilized to strongly shape how large Christian networks around the world understand Israel and antisemitism. They have been working to achieve this goal by having brought 25,000+ Christians to the Holy Land, organizing Nexus Leadership Missions which offer intensive educational tours to global pastoral leaders, as well as spearheading the Christian answer to Birthright, dubbed the ‘Israel Experience’, bringing college-age Christian students to Israel.
One of the key events as part of this year’s Eagles’ Wings 10-day delegation was “Awake Jerusalem at the Tower of David.” The event took place on October 3 at Jerusalem’s iconic Tower of David with hundreds of Christian leaders from 51 different countries in attendance. The event showcased international Christian artists while also including communal worship being covered and broadcasted by Daystar Television Network, a media partner of Eagles’ Wings.
For Israel, the challenges that lie ahead are not merely diplomatic. As the international stage becomes increasingly harder to navigate the relationships that Israel fosters with Asia and the Global South may become of increasing strategic importance. This gathering of 550 Christian leaders from 51 nation-states demonstrates merely one aspect of this shifting climate. Prominent religious communities from the Philippines to Korea and Brazil to Kenya will be able to shape the conversation about Israel within their respective societies. The mobilization of these groups shows the potential benefits that Israel stands to reap from fostering non-traditional alliances and that vis-à-vis culture, religion and interpersonal connections a new path to diplomacy may emerge.

Attendees hailed from 51 different nations and congregated around the Jewish holiday of Sukkot (Feast of Tabernacles) in Jerusalem, commemorating the third anniversary of the October 7th attack.  The gathering offers a window into a less frequently discussed dimension of the Israel debate: the continued mobilization of Christian communities in parts of Asia and the wider Global South around Israel.
articles.summary: As Israel faces growing pressure in the West, Eagles’ Wings mission brings Christian leaders from across the globe to show support for the Jewish people and Israel

articles.title: The Scam Industry Is Becoming a Big Problem in India
articles.full_text:
According to the FBI, American nationals lost around $50 million to one network of online scammers based in India.
On September 15, investigators raided three call centers in Pune and Patiala, finding around 220 people at work. According to India’s Enforcement Directorate, the premises were being used to defraud Americans. Investigators said that they were establishing the workers’ identities and roles.
Officers also searched a Chandigarh property linked to a suspected organizer. They seized 66 mobile phones, 13 laptops, and unspecified records. Investigators said that they were examining calling scripts, internet telephony systems, and payment routes. 
The published account did not provide an overall figure for victims’ losses. 
Months earlier, another investigation exposed the damage one India-based network could inflict. An American woman’s $1.7 million loss helped investigators connect other victims to the operation. The FBI subsequently attributed more than $48.7 million in reported losses among over 600 American victims to the network. Indian authorities arrested six alleged leaders in December 2025. 
These cases reveal an enduring threat to American households, while also hurting India’s image abroad. Organized networks operating from India can reach victims thousands of miles away. As has happened with Cambodia’s scam centers, a raid may shut down one office while the people who hire workers, move the money, and coordinate from outside remain untouched.
The criminal organizations behind these calls can resemble a conventional business. A 2024 study published by Itad and commissioned by Britain’s Home Office described larger Indian scam centers with management structures, staff shifts, human resources departments, and quality control functions. It also documented recruitment agencies, prepared scripts, English and accent training, and performance incentives.
Roles can be divided between “openers,” who establish contact, and “closers,” who persuade victims to surrender money. Beyond the telephone operators sit facilitators who supply websites, deceptive pop-ups, recruitment services, and various forms of money laundering. The study also identified markets for phone numbers, calling scripts, and victim profiles. These arrangements allow different participants to specialize in separate parts of the fraud. 
Reuters reported in 2016 that former workers at scam centers near Mumbai described memorizing scripts, learning from floor managers, and receiving commissions or incentives. The accounts describe a workplace where securing a payment from a victim could increase an employee’s earnings. 
Technology helps conceal the operation. In a Noida case announced in July 2025, Britain’s National Crime Agency described spoofed telephone numbers and internet calls routed through servers in several countries. The scam center in Noida targeted both British and American victims. A familiar-looking number on a screen offered no reliable indication of where the caller actually worked. 
An office can make a scam look like a real business. Reporting from Maharashtra has described scam centers posing as IT or outsourcing firms, while poor verification of businesses made such operations harder to detect.
The details differ between networks, but documented cases show a recurring progression from an alarming first contact to demands for money. 
Stage one is intended to trigger initial fear and gain attention from the intended victim. In technical support fraud, a person browsing the internet sees a warning claiming that their computer has been infected or compromised. The message supplies a telephone number. Calling it connects the victim to someone offering to resolve the supposed emergency. In the Noida case, investigators said callers falsely presented themselves as Microsoft employees and charged for unnecessary repairs. 
Other schemes begin with unsolicited calls claiming unpaid taxes, compromised identities or criminal investigations. The goal is to create a false sense of urgency and then urge action before the victim has time to check it. 
Scammers reinforce their claims through multiple impersonations. A supposed technical support worker may introduce a bank representative, followed by someone claiming government authority. Each apparent handover makes the preceding story seem independently confirmed.
The FBI’s warning about “Phantom Hacker” scams describes forged correspondence on government letterheads and instructions to keep transfers secret. The victim is encouraged to distrust the very people who could interrupt the fraud. The caller says the conversation must stay private to protect the victim. That stops the victim from asking someone else for advice.
Some operators persuade victims to install remote-access software. This can allow the scammer to inspect the computer and watch as the victim opens financial accounts. The supposed repair becomes an opportunity to identify available savings. A second impersonator then claims those funds face immediate danger and must be moved to a supposedly secure account. 
In other schemes, threats of arrest or deportation supply the pressure. American prosecutions have documented India-based callers impersonating tax and immigration authorities to extract payments. The victim is made to believe that following instructions will protect a home, retirement account, or legal status. That belief is central to the deception.
Payment methods vary. Gift cards and prepaid cards allow scammers to demand value without asking victims to send money directly to an identifiable caller. Once card details are surrendered, criminals can use or transfer the value.
Cryptocurrency offers another route. Victims may be instructed to withdraw savings, buy digital assets and send them to wallets controlled by the fraud network. Wire transfers can similarly move money into accounts controlled by intermediaries. These methods feature in documented call-center investigations. 
Cash and gold introduce a physical collection stage. The FBI has warned that scammers direct victims to buy precious metals or withdraw cash for supposed safekeeping, then dispatch couriers to collect them. The person arriving at an American doorstep can therefore be part of a fraud directed from abroad. 
Money laundering adds further distance between the victim and the organizers. In one India-based operation that was prosecuted in the U.S. state of Virginia, American authorities documented couriers, bank accounts, and hawala transfers used to move proceeds. Such arrangements complicate efforts to trace the money and identify who ultimately received it. 
After the transfer, the scammers may cease contact, leaving victims with unanswered calls and missing savings. But some schemes continue demanding transfers over days or months, so the first payment does not necessarily end the manipulation. 
Either way, by the time a victim recognizes the fraud, the lost money may already have moved through several hands. 
The same methods are used against victims in other countries. Canada’s Project OCTAVIA targeted callers impersonating tax officials; reported losses to that particular scam fell from C$6.4 million in 2018 to C$1.4 million in 2019. 
In Australia, police alleged that Hyderabad-based Ridge IT Solutions had taken 80-100 million rupees from Australians over roughly two years. The allegations included payments passing through Australian accounts before moving toward India. 
India is not unique in hosting these scam centers. The online scam industry is global, and the financial scale is substantial. The FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) received 1,008,597 complaints in 2025, with reported losses of $20.9 billion. People aged 60 and older reported approximately $7.7 billion in losses. Complaints involving technical or customer support fraud and government impersonation together exceeded 80,000, with losses above $2.9 billion. 
Those totals cover perpetrators worldwide, and IC3 also receives complaints from outside the United States. These figures cannot be presented as American losses caused entirely by India-based centers; IC3 has not established the share of the 2025 losses originating from operations in India.
Nevertheless, India’s role is well documented: in a 2022 podcast, the FBI said most technical-support and telephone scams targeting Americans originated from India. And while scam operations based in Southeast Asia, especially Cambodia, have received more attention of late, scam centers operating out of India remain less discussed.
Recovering money presents a daunting challenge. Investigators must identify recipients, trace subsequent transfers, and seek the necessary legal cooperation. American agents cannot simply conduct arrests in India. Even successful prosecutions do not guarantee that every victim will receive full repayment. Often, the scammers are able to keep their ill-gotten gains, and use them to fund further crimes.
articles.summary: According to the FBI, American nationals lost around $50 million to one network of online scammers based in India.
